It also happened at that time that a certain Christian man who was bringing an offering to the same church was seized; and because he confessed Christ, he was cast into the fire, and in place of the offering, he became an offering to Christ. The remains of these, a woman—the wife of another prince of the race of the Goths, who was a Christian and orthodox—gathered together with priests and laymen; and leaving her goods to her son, she went from place to place until she came into the land of the Romans, accompanied by her daughter. Then, having returned to her own region, she left the remains to her daughter; and she, having gone away to Cyzicus, gave a portion of them to that city, and thus she finished her life.
And the contest of the holy martyrs Philemon and Domnus.
Philemon and Domnus, martyrs of Christ, were natives of the city of Rome. In the time of persecution, having journeyed into the province of Italy, they preached Christ, and having converted many of the unbelievers by their doctrine from the error of idols to the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, they baptized them. For this reason, having stirred up the idolaters to anger, they were seized and
bound with chains, and delivered to the governor of the province. The governor, upon seeing them, first attempted through flattery to draw them away from the faith of Christ, promising them honors and gifts of great value. Afterwards, when he saw that they counted all things as nothing and invoked only Christ, he ordered them stripped and stretched out on the ground by their four limbs, and cruelly beaten, that they might be forced to sacrifice to the idols. But when he could not persuade them, he shut them up in prison; and having later led them out of prison, and punished them again inhumanly, he beheaded them.
The Contest of the Holy Martyrs Callinicus and Basilissa.
Callinicus and Basilissa, martyrs of Christ, lived during the reign of Decius in the province of Galatia. Since Basilissa abounded in wealth, she would give money to Callinicus to go to the prisons and provide food to the Christians detained there, so that they might pray for her, and that she might make them ready for martyrdom, that they might not fail in their tribulations. On a certain day, therefore, Callinicus was seized, and being asked of what religion he was, not knowing how to lie, he confessed. Having been bound, he was delivered to the governor. Holy Basilissa was also caught and presented before the tribunal. Both of them, freely confessing Christ, were first tortured with various torments, being pressed to deny Christ and sacrifice to the idols. But, as they could not be persuaded, their sacred heads were cut off with a sword; and thus, having excellently conquered the devil, they received the kingdom of heaven.
IN THE SAME MONTH.
THE 27TH.
The Contest of the Holy Martyr Philetus the Senator, and his wife Lydia, and their children.
These lived under the Emperor Hadrian. Therefore, the blessed Philetus was seized and presented to the emperor. But the emperor, being unable to resist the wisdom of the martyr, delivered him to the duke Amphilochius, who immediately hung both up on timbers and tore them. Soon he cast them into prison along with Cronides the jailer, who had already believed. But at night, as they were chanting psalms and praying, angels came and encouraged them for their struggles. On the following day, the tyrant said to the saints standing before him: "Many torments are prepared for you." Then he cast them into a bronze cauldron, heated and filled with oil and resin. But they, having made the sign of the cross, cooled the cauldron. The duke, seeing this, believed in Christ and cast himself into the cauldron, saying: "Lord, help me." Then a voice came down from heaven: "I have heard your prayer; come up to me with joy." The emperor, seeing them come forth unharmed, departed; but they, having prayed, made an end of living.
And the contest of the holy martyrs Manuel and Theodosius.
Manuel and Theodosius, martyrs of Christ,
coming from the region of the Orient, and seeing the Christians daily being slaughtered by the idolaters, agreed among themselves to act freely, and to die for Christ. Therefore, having gone forth—or rather, having gone forth of their own accord—to the governor of the region, who was at that time examining many of the Christians and slaughtering them, they stood before him and with boldness proclaimed Christ, and confessed themselves to be Christians; they astonished not only those who were present, but the governor himself by their courage and boldness. Then, having been seized, they were cast into prison; and after a few days the governor, having brought them out of the prison, compelled them to deny Christ and to sacrifice to the idols. But as he did not persuade them, having tortured them severely, and having hung them upon wooden stakes, and having lacerated their sides, he then took them down from the wood, and having placed them upon sharp thorns, at last he beheaded them.
And the contest of the holy hieromartyr Codratus
Codratus the hieromartyr, being a bishop, and having been expelled by the idolaters from the city in which he had been ordained, and having received an interdiction not to teach in the name of Christ if he wished to live, not only did not cease to do this, but even going around the whole city, whoever he found as catechumens he baptized; and he visited those held in the prisons, not only Christians, but also unbelievers; and some he rendered more prompt to persevere in the faith of Christ, while others he exhorted by his teaching to abandon the idols, saying to them: "Since you are about to die, being put to death by those who cast you into this prison, bestir yourselves to die for Christ, that you may obtain the good things laid up there." Recognized, therefore, by the idolaters, and seized, after many tortures and sufferings, he was put to death by the sword: and thus finishing his life, he departed to Christ.
And the contest of the holy Stephen the Confessor
Stephen the confessor of Christ was, during the reign of Leo the Armenian, a monk adorned with all virtues, and also made superior of the monastery of Triglia at the request of the monks, where he helped many by his institutions, and offered them pure to God. But afterwards, when the aforementioned impious emperor had moved a heresy against the holy and venerable images, and had raised a bitter persecution against the orthodox, he himself was also summoned and compelled to abjure the adoration of the holy images, and to subscribe against the orthodox faith. And when he refused to do so, but even called those who compelled him to this act impious, having been tormented by many tortures beforehand and held in custody, he was finally deported into exile; and having been overtaken by illness in his exile, he joyfully departed to the Lord, for whom he had endured many long labors.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The twenty-eighth day.
A 32 The Contest of Saint Matrona of Thessalonica.
Matrona, a martyr of Christ, was from the city of Thessalonica, and was the slave of a Jewish woman whose husband was the stratopedarch (military governor) of Thessalonica. Following her mistress as far as the synagogue of the Jews, she would not enter it, but turning away, would depart to the church of the Christians and pray there. Having been discovered by her mistress, she was beaten severely and was shut up in prison. After remaining there for many days, macerated by lack of food, she was brought out and scourged mercilessly, and was forcefully compelled to deny Christ. But when she would not be persuaded, she was cast into prison again, where she gave up her soul to God. Her mistress threw her corpse from the wall, but the Christians took it up and buried it by night. Later, when Alexander the bishop had built a church within the city of Thessalonica in the name of the saint, he deposited them there.
The contest of the holy apostle Herodion, one of the Seventy.
Herodion, the apostle of Christ, was one of the seventy disciples. Following the holy apostles, he assisted them in the preaching of Christ, serving them in all things, and being in subjection to them as a disciple of Christ, mindful of the words: "Whoever wishes to be first of all, let him be the servant of all, and the minister of all." After this, he was ordained by them as bishop of the city of New Patras, and he converted many of the Greeks to the Lord by his teaching. But the Jews, envying him, conspired with the idolaters, and having seized him, they vexed him with most grievous tortures; some striking him, others smashing his mouth with stones, and others beating his head with clubs. Finally, the lawless ones, like fierce and bloodthirsty beasts, slaughtered that illustrious ram with a sword, and thus he delivered his blessed soul to the Lord, for whom he endured a violent death.
33 And the commemoration of our holy Father Hesychius.
Hesychius, our Father among the saints, was both born and bred in Jerusalem; having studied all Scripture to the highest degree, he became rich in knowledge of God. Therefore, having withdrawn and become a monk, he lived in the deserts, going from one holy father to another, and gathering the flowers of virtue from each one, like a laborious bee. Because it was not possible for such a virtue to remain hidden, he was constrained by the archpriest of Jerusalem of that time and was ordained a presbyter. And remaining at the tomb of the Lord and in other places where our Lord Jesus Christ endured his holy passion for our sake, he drew from the fountains of knowledge and wisdom. Whence he interpreted and expounded all Scripture, and set it forth for the benefit of many. Thenceforth, becoming renowned and wondrous to all, he […].
having served God most perfectly, joyfully hastened to Him.
And the commemoration of our holy Father Hilarion, abbot of the monastery of Pelecetes: as also of Martin, bishop of the Arethusians, and of Cyril the Deacon.
IN THE SAME MONTH.
The twenty-ninth day.
The contest of the holy martyrs Jonas and Barachisius.
In the reign of the great Constantine, these men were. Being monks, they went into Persia; and finding there nine holy martyrs locked in prison, they encouraged them to contend bravely. Wherefore, having been apprehended and brought before the princes of the Persians, they were compelled to deny Christ. But as they could by no means be persuaded to do so, Jonas was the first to be bound according to the law of the Persians: for it is the custom of the Persians, if they are to subject anyone to scourging, to lay him upon the ground and bind his hands and feet to a piece of wood. He, however, like an immovable stone, received the blows while he was being struck with rough rods; and finding him still whole, they cast him forth and exposed him for the whole night to the frozen ice. Then they cut off the fingers of his hands and feet, and having compressed him into a vice, they sawed him in half, and cast him into a pit; and thus he ended his life. Barachisius, however, was dragged naked through thorns, and cast into a vice, and when boiling pitch was poured into his throat, he finished his life.
And the commemoration of the holy Confessor Acacius.
Our holy Father Acacius, the confessor of Christ, lived during the reign of the wicked Decius. And when he was preaching Christ, he was seized by idolaters: and being bound, he was brought to Marcianus, the prefect of the region, before whom he stood and confessed the name of the Lord. He discoursed concerning the Divinity, and concerning the dispensation of Christ, and concerning the Cherubim and Seraphim; he mocked the gods of the Greeks and refuted their error. Wherefore, having been most grievously tortured, he was cast into prison. Meanwhile, Marcianus transmitted reports concerning him to the emperor Decius, who commanded that the holy man should be released without injury or torture. Released in this manner, carrying the stigmata of Christ in his flesh, enlightening many and leading them to the flock of Christ, being highly renowned for his miracles and teachings, he rested in peace.
And the memory of our holy Father Eustathius, bishop of Bithynia.
IN THE SAME MONTH.
The thirtieth day.
The contest of the holy Marcus, bishop of the Arethusians.
When the Christian religion was spreading widely during the reign of Constantine the Great, Marcus, bishop of the Arethusians, having overturned a temple of idols, built a church. When
the Great Constantine died, and Julian the Apostate, by the permission of God, took hold of the empire, the idolaters, having regained their courage, and bearing anger against the holy Marcus, seized him, and having bound his feet with ropes, they dragged him along beating him. Then, having smeared him with honey and brine, they hung him from ropes at a height, it being summer and intensely hot, that he might be devoured by bees. But when they saw him remain unyielding, they changed their counsel, took him down from the torture, released him, and henceforth held him in the place of a teacher, deeming his patience a miracle, and even asking forgiveness for their deed. Having escaped death in this manner, and having well shepherded his flock for the remaining time of his life, he rested in extreme old age.
And the contest of the holy deacon Cyril and many others
Cyril the deacon was in a city of Phoenicia; and because he himself, during the time of Constantine the Great, had smashed many idols, he was seized during the reign of Julian by the idolaters and suffered a violent death. For having cut open his belly, they devoured his liver, and drank his blood like dogs; and immediately their teeth fell out, and their tongues rotted away, and their eyes were blinded. The martyr, having finished his contest, ascended rejoicing into the heavens. On that same day, in the cities of Ascalon and Gaza, the idolaters seized a multitude of Christians—virgins, women, monks, and men consecrated to God—and having split open their bellies with swords and filled them with barley, they set them before swine for food. And while their bodies endured such tortures, their holy souls were deposited into the hands of the living God.
And the commemoration of our holy Father John of the Ladder
Our holy Father John of the Ladder, when he was sixteen years old, offered himself to God as a most holy sacrifice, having ascended Mount Sinai; and after nineteen years, he gave himself over to silence, five miles from the main monastery in a place called Tholas. He spent forty years in the love and desire to serve God, given to fasting, weeping, and prayer; he partook of sleep only as much as was necessary so that the essence of his mind would not be harmed by vigilance. Thus, having practiced every virtue and lived well, and having surpassed in virtue all the monks struggling for God on that mountain, and having been deemed worthy of the greatest gifts and visions from God, he composed many soul-benefiting discourses and wrote a book, entitled the *Ladder*, because it hands down in order the ascent of the virtues, and he finally ended his life.
And the contest of the holy thirty-eight martyrs
During the reign of the impious Julian, these holy thirty-eight martyrs were serving as soldiers in the region of Cappado
Cappadocia. And having heard of the noble endurance of the holy forty martyrs of Christ, and how they struggled, defeated the devil, and were crowned, they themselves also became zealous, and casting down their arms before the governor, they confessed with a loud voice that Christ is the true God, and themselves his true servants. Then they were seized and stripped of their clothing, and their flesh was so flayed by the beating of rods that they could scarcely be recognized as having human form. Afterward, they were thrown into prison without any care, and a little later were brought out, their hands bound behind their backs and their heads burdened with iron collars, and brought before the governor; and because they remained steadfast in their holy purpose and were longing for a glorious death for the sake of Christ, by the command of the governor they were beheaded.
And the commemoration of the holy prophet Jodad.
When Jeroboam, the servant of Roboam the son of Solomon, had revolted together with the ten tribes from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, and having rejected the true God, had made golden calves and worshipped them with all his people, this prophet was sent to rebuke him on God's behalf. He came therefore and rebuked him. But Jeroboam stretched out his hand to strike him; but he saw it withered. Soon, led to repentance, he earned the favor of the prophet to heal it. When he had done this, he urged him to eat bread: but he could not induce him to do so, because it was forbidden to him by God. But as he was returning, a certain false prophet met him and compelled him to enter his house and eat bread. Because of which transgression, a lion meeting him on the way killed him. When the false prophet learned of this, he went and, having taken his remains, buried them.
And the commemoration of our holy Father John, patriarch of Jerusalem.
IN THE SAME MONTH.
The thirty-first day.
The contest of the holy martyrs Abdas the bishop, and Benjamin the deacon.
This man flourished in Persia during the reign of Theodosius the Younger. But after he destroyed a temple of fire, he was seized and brought before the king; who at first urged him with great gentleness to rebuild the temple. But when he said that it was impossible for this to be done, he sent out a mandate and destroyed all the churches of the Christians. Hence, the persecution against the Christians took its beginning, by which every age of the faithful was taken away by various torments; of whom the first, the most holy Abdas, finished his life by the sword. Afterward, for thirty entire years, many martyrs were manifested, among whom were wealthy men, who after various tortures were beheaded. Then also Benjamin the deacon, after he had received twenty sharp reeds fixed under his nails, and another into his member
and inserted into his private parts, he yielded up his blessed spirit.
IN THE MONTH OF APRIL. THE FIRST DAY.
1. Commemoration of Saint Mary of Egypt.
Our holy mother Mary was formerly a harlot, destroying many souls of young men through the way of carnal intercourse, and persisting for seventeen years in Egypt in the shameful trade of her body. But later, she gave herself to God in this manner: When some were departing for Jerusalem to worship the precious Cross, she went also. But being forbidden by an angel from entering the temple and from worshipping the precious Wood, she was grieved. But when she had promised to serve God, she obtained entry. Then, having bidden farewell to the Theotokos, she crossed the Jordan and struggled in the desert for forty-seven years, seeing no human being. But God, wishing to manifest her, arranged for the holy Zosimas to enter the desert, that he might receive from her a secret account of her affairs, and returning (as one who crossed the Jordan by walking upon the waters), he might bring the divine communion and offer it to her. And visiting her again, he found her dead, read her name written upon a shard, and buried her, with the help of a lion.
IN THE SAME MONTH. The second day.
 The struggle of the holy martyrs Apphianus and Ædesius.
Apphianus and Ædesius, martyrs of Christ, were brothers by the same mother, originating from the region of Lydia during the reign of Maximian. When they came to Berytus, they were taught the faith in Christ by the martyr Pamphilus. Whence, having been apprehended, they were brought before the governor of the city. And Apphianus first, preaching Christ openly and freely, was struck in the face and, falling to the ground, was trodden under the feet of the soldiers; and being hung upon wood, he was swollen and burst asunder by kicks. Yet, still remaining steadfast in his confession of Christ, he was cast into the depths of the sea, and there he finished his life. But Ædesius, having been condemned to be punished in the copper mines, was sent to Alexandria. And one day, seeing the governor of the city raging fiercely against the Christians there, he ran up and struck him with a rod. Whence, having first been vexed by many tortures, he was at last cast into the sea and finished his martyrdom.
And the struggle of the holy martyr Polycarp.
This holy Polycarp was also a martyr of Christ during the reign of the impious and iniquitous Maximian, from the city of Alexandria. Being a Christian and burning with great zeal for God, and seeing every day those who confessed the faith of Christ being apprehended
and examined with multiple torments, he could not bear it any longer. Therefore, seeing the governor sitting before the tribunal, pouring out the blood of men like water, he stood before him and rebuked him, saying: "Why have you so forgotten human nature, O insatiable dog, that you hack to pieces men who are of the same nature as you, like wood with swords, because they preach the true God and expose the error of idols; as I also do, who am a servant of Christ?" Therefore, having stirred the governor into a rage, he was seized and cruelly tortured; and carrying Christ in his mouth until the end of his life, he was beheaded.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The third day.
The contest of the holy martyr Theodosia the virgin.
Theodosia was a martyr of Christ from the city of Tyre. When she was in her eighteenth year, she was apprehended because she was a Christian and brought before the governor of Palestine; and being questioned, she confessed Christ. Wherefore she was struck in the sides and breasts. But being commanded to deny Christ and sacrifice to idols, since she could not be persuaded to do so, she was thrust into prison; and a mandate was given to the jailer that he should not only guard her diligently, but that he should not permit anyone to enter to visit her or to bring her food, until she should deny Christ and sacrifice to the so-called gods. When many days had already passed, she was led out of prison, and when she was again compelled to sacrifice to the impure demons—and she would not even hear of this—she was first cruelly tortured; then, being thrown into the sea, she rendered her spirit to the Lord.
The contest of the holy women Irene, Agape, and Chionia.
Irene, Agape, and Chionia were martyrs of Christ under the Emperor Maximian, from the city of Thessalonica. When, because of the persecution, they had left all things, they withdrew to a certain mountain, and there lived a quiet life, fasting and offering prayers assiduously to God. But being discovered and apprehended, they were brought before the governor, by whom they were commanded to deny Christ, but they did not agree. Wherefore he burned Agape and Chionia with fire. Finding Irene with the sacred books which the holy women had been accustomed to read, he burned those, but he ordered her to be taken to a brothel, that she might be defiled by the profligate. But protected by the grace of God, she was preserved inviolate, with no one daring to approach her. When the governor understood this, he ordered her to be brought before him again, urging her to desert Christ. But when she refused to do so, he also delivered her to the fire. And thus were consummated the three martyrs of Christ, having attained the kingdom of heaven.
And the memory of our holy Father and confessor Nicetas.
Nicetas, our father among the saints and confessor of Christ, lived by the permission of God during the reign of the Iconoclasts. From his childhood, according to the commandment of Christ, he left behind father, mother, brothers, sisters, kinsmen, his home, his country, and his wealth, and taking up his cross eagerly, he followed Christ, having become a worthy disciple of His. For when he had retired to the monastery of Medicius, he strove after virtue with such intensity that he excelled all the monks who were there. He was also deemed worthy of the gift of miracles. On account of his virtue, at the request of the monks, he became their hegumen and rightly presided over his flock. But since the time of his martyrdom was approaching, those sent by the Iconoclasts arrived and summoned him, and compelled him to renounce the veneration of the venerable icons and to join their heresy. Since they were unable to persuade him, they subjected him to exile, famine, and other hardships, and thus put him to death.
And the memory of the holy Joseph, the writer of canons.
The holy Joseph, the writer of canons, was from Sicily, the son of Plutinus and Agatha. When his native land was captured by the race of the Africans, he came to Thessalonica, and having entered a certain monastery, and having become a monk, he contended in his struggle, diligently exercising himself in the meditation of the divine Scriptures. Having thus been ordained a presbyter, he came to Constantinople with Gregory the Decapolite. Being then sent to Rome on account of the heresy of the Iconoclasts, he was seized by the Saracens, taken captive to Crete, and thrust into prison. After the death of Theophilus the Iconoclast, having been delivered from prison by the aid of Saint Nicholas, he returned again to Constantinople; where, having been subjected to calumnies and slanders, he was relegated to Cherson. Recalled from there, he went again to Byzantium, and became the custodian of the sacred vessels of the Great Church. Being enlightened with the gifts of God, after he had honored many saints with canons, or hymns, he passed from this life.
ON THE SAME MONTH. THE FOURTH DAY.
The contest of the holy martyrs Agathopodes and Theodulus.
Agathopodes, the most sacred deacon, and Theodulus, the most religious reader, the martyrs of Christ, were from the city of Thessalonica. Being seized on account of their faith in Christ by the idolaters, they were brought before the ruler of the city and were compelled to offer sacrifice to the idols. Because they refused to do so, they were cast into prison, in which that same night they both had this vision. They seemed to themselves to board a ship and sail upon the sea; but a great tempest of waves having been raised, they saw the ship broken in pieces, and those sailing in it submerged in the sea; yet they themselves alone safely escaped, and
ascended a high mountain. And the vision portended their perfection by the sea, and their ascent to heaven. For in the morning, when the governor had brought them out of prison, he commanded them to sacrifice to the idols; but as they could by no means be induced to do so, he ordered them to be cast into the depths of the sea: and thus they were perfected.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The fifth day.
Contest of the holy martyr Pherbutha and her companions.
Pherbutha, the martyr of Christ, after the contest and death of her brother Simeon the bishop, living quietly in her house together with her sister and handmaid, taught those who approached her the faith in Christ. But the Jews were jealous, and taking this ill, provided an occasion, and plotted their slaughter in this manner. The wife of Sapor, king of the Persians, was a protector of the Jews: but at that time she was using ill health. Therefore the Jews approached her, and slandered the holy ones, saying thus: "Because Simeon the bishop was killed by your husband, his sisters are trying to destroy you by magic arts. If, however, you desire to recover your former health, command them to be sawed in two, and their dissected limbs to be hung up: then do you pass through them, and thus you will escape safe and sound." This having been performed, the holy martyrs of Christ attained the kingdom of heaven: but the queen not only did not recover her health, but she obtained hell as her lot.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The sixth day.
Memory of our holy Father Eutychius, Archbishop of Constantinople.
Our holy Father Eutychius was born in the region of Phrygia, during the reign of Justinian the Great. He was excellently educated by Hesychius the presbyter and wonderworker, his own grandfather, and having been thoroughly versed in the holy scriptures by constant meditation and study, he was taken in by the bishop of Amasea: and having been initiated first as a monk, then as a presbyter, he led a tranquil life in the monastery of Saint Meletius. But when the fifth council was gathered by Justinian, and the bishop of Amasea was detained by ill health, Eutychius was sent in his stead, who so excelled in the council that the Patriarch Menas said: "This man will be my successor." And so, in very deed, after his death, he was elected patriarch. But when he had fallen into the hatred of the emperor, he was driven into exile. But after the death of Justinian, he received his see again from Justin and Tiberius. And when he had already performed many miracles, and by his prayers had checked the onset of a deadly and great pestilence, and had also predicted the death of Tiberius, just as he had earlier predicted his reign, he departed from this life, and was buried in the church of the holy apostles.
And the contest of the holy hundred and fifty martyrs crowned in Persia.
Sapor the impious king of the Persians, against the Roman
dominion during the time of the Roman emperor Constantius (God allowing this on account of the incited heresy of the senseless Arius, who had persuaded the emperor himself, through Eusebius the praepositus who was an Arian, to think the same as he did), having made an incursion and having destroyed many forts and regions, led away many captives from the Christians; of whom some were slaughtered, and others perished on the way. Only one hundred and fifty survived, who were deported into Persia, bound in chains, and cast into prison, where they were afflicted for many days with incessant hardships. But when at some point Sapor was free from his vain occupations, and had lit a great pyre of wood, he brought the holy men out of the prison and compelled them to deny Christ and to sacrifice to the fire. Because he could not persuade them, he ordered them to be thrown into the fire, and thus they were perfected.
IN THE SAME MONTH
The seventh day
Memory of our holy Father George, bishop of Mitylene.
Holy and God-bearing Father George, a most fervent confessor of Christ, was the son of noble, wealthy, and pious parents; he, hating their riches but embracing piety, and despising nobility and glory for the sake of his love and longing for Christ, went away into a monastery and became a monk, in which he achieved many other virtues, but especially almsgiving. For the whole day, according to that Davidic saying, he ceased not to show mercy and lend. Therefore, by the pleading of the clergy, he was ordained bishop of the church at Mitylene, retaining in that office the same mercy in giving alms that he had previously displayed. And when later the heresy of the Iconoclasts arose, he was its most bitter enemy, but a most fierce champion of the orthodox religion. For he, revering and worshipping the holy images, taught others also to honor them. But when he had already performed many miracles, he was made certain of his future death by a revelation, a divine star portending it; and thus he migrated to the Lord. D
And the contest of the holy martyr Calliopius.
Calliopius, martyr of Christ, lived during the reign of Maximian, born in the region of Pamphylia, the son of a certain Theocleia, a Christian woman of wealth. Having been piously and religiously raised by his mother, he was occupied in the constant meditation of the divine Scriptures. When a persecution was stirred up, he departed of his own accord to Pompeiopolis, where he stood before the governor Maximus and freely confessed Christ. His hands were therefore bound behind his back, and having been cruelly beaten, he was cast into prison, into which his mother also entered, and she wiped away his blood with a sponge: for having distributed all her wealth to the poor, she had followed her son. But he was led out of prison and condemned to be crucified: being a sharer in Christ not only in the passion and the torments, but also in the days
in which He suffered. For it was the fifth day of the Great Week on which he was crucified. But his mother, giving the executioners five pieces of gold, begged them not to crucify her son in the same way Christ was crucified, but head downwards. And thus, being crucified at the third hour of the Preparation, he gave up the spirit; and his mother, rushing upon him, likewise gave up her soul.
47 And the contest of the holy martyrs Rufinus the deacon and his companions.
When a grave persecution against the Christians had been stirred up under the impious emperor Maximinus, whoever confessed Christ was seized by the idolaters and, after being tormented with many tortures, was finally delivered unto death. At that time there was Saint Rufinus, a deacon of the Church of Christ, who, because he was instructing many in the name of Christ, was cast into chains and thrust into prison. A certain Christian woman, named Aquilina, while visiting him, was likewise seized; and both, having been brought before the governor and subjected to various tortures, whereas they performed many wonders, brought it about that two hundred of the soldiers who were present embraced the faith of Christ. Wherefore the governor, becoming immediately enraged, ordered all of them to be put to the sword. Then the executioners having bound them, led them to the place of execution; and they beheaded them all, while they gave thanks to God until the end.
OF THE SAME MONTH. EIGHTH DAY.
The contest of the holy martyr Pausilypus.
Pausilypus, the martyr of Christ, lived during the reign of the impious and iniquitous Hadrian. Being denounced because he worshipped Christ and taught in His name, he was seized and cast into chains, and brought before the emperor. Standing before him, he was asked if he confessed Christ to be God. With free confidence of soul, he proclaimed Him the true God and Creator of the universe. He was delivered to the prefect of the region of Europe, and was beaten with rods so unsparingly that three hundred blows were cruelly inflicted upon him. Having been delivered from this torture, he was again ordered to deny Christ and to sacrifice to idols. As he would not do this, he was bound in chains and brought to the place of execution, that he might there be beheaded. But his bonds having been broken on the way, he took flight and was delivered from perishing by the sword. Having escaped to a certain place, he remained there, offering continual prayers to God, and with a glad soul he rendered his life, having fulfilled his martyrdom, unto God, having obtained an unfading crown and immortal life.
48 And the memory of our holy Father Celestine, pope of Rome.
Our holy Father Celestine, in the reign of Theodosius the Younger, flourished in the Roman Church, occupied in the practice of every virtue and in the meditation of the Divine Scriptures. After the death
of the holy bishops Innocent, Boniface, and Zosimus, he was ordained Pope of great Rome. Since his doctrine also corresponded to his life, he showed himself venerable and admirable to all, in many things indeed, but especially in the exposition and dissertation of the right dogmas. For, striving together with the holy Cyril, by means of a dogmatic letter full of orthodoxy, which he sent from the city of Rome to the synod in Ephesus, he overthrew the impious Nestorius and cast him out of the Church of the orthodox, as he was blaspheming against the Son of God and against the holy Theotokos. Thereafter, by other decrees also, he delivered the Churches of the East from this most pestilential plague, and having enlightened many, he departed in peace.
ON THE SAME MONTH. 9th Day. The contest of the holy martyr Badimus the Archimandrite.
Saint Badimus was from the region of the Persians, the son of wealthy parents; when they had ended their lives, he distributed all his wealth to the poor, went away to a monastery, and there became a monk, and later an archimandrite. Preaching Christ, he brought many to Him and baptized them. When Sapor, the king of the Persians, learned of this, he sent and seized him, together with seven of his disciples, and shut him up in prison. And after four days, Sapor commanded the executioners to bring them out of the prison and behead them. But the holy man, seeing one of the executioners by the name of Nersas, who had previously been a Christian but had denied Christ out of fear, as he was drawing his sword to behead them, groaned and lamented; and he reminded him of the retribution of the day to come. Nersas, beginning to tremble from fear, inflicted four wounds upon the holy man, and in this way, through much violence, he yielded up his spirit.
And the contest of the holy martyrs who attained martyrdom in Persia.
Sapor, the king of the Persians, having set out on an expedition into Roman territory in the fifty-third year of his reign, and having taken by right of war a very populous city, ordered all the soldiers who were in it to be killed; but as for the people unfit for war—namely, the old men, women, children, the bishop Heliodorus, the presbyters, the deacons, and all who were of the clergy—he commanded them to be kept unhurt. But the bishop Heliodorus, when he felt himself near to death, ordained one of the presbyters as bishop in his place. As the glorification was being offered to God in church according to custom, a certain Persian went and reported to Sapor: "Those Christians, O King, to whom life was granted by you, have chosen a prince for themselves, and they reject our religion and despise your authority." Whereupon, having been brought to the king, they were ordered to adore the sun. And when they refused to do so, they were all beheaded.
The Contest of the Holy Martyr Eupsychius of Caesarea
Eupsychius, a martyr of Christ, was from the region of Cappadocia, under the reign of Julian the Apostate. Having attained an irreproachable life and a simple manner of conduct, he burned with the greatest desire and love for Christ. When he saw the idolaters approaching the temple dedicated to Fortune, and sacrificing therein—to which the apostate Julian, in his belief, was accustomed to offer victims daily—he was kindled with divine zeal. Taking with him other Christians as companions, he went and razed the temple from its foundations, and crushed the idols that were within it. When Julian learned of this, he was vehemently enraged and ordered them all to be arrested. Some of them he deprived of their property and, having afflicted them with various torments, he sent them into exile. As for the martyr Eupsychius, being the author of the crime committed, he first ordered him to be thrust into prison; later, having brought him forth from the prison, he ordered him to be tormented with multiple tortures. Finally, when he was commanded to deny Christ and refused, he was beheaded.
ON THE SAME MONTH. THE TENTH DAY.
The Contest of the Forty Holy Martyrs, Terentius, Africanus, and Others
Terentius, a martyr of Christ, was from Africa, under the reign of Decius. When a persecution was stirred up and Christians were being killed, many who had previously taken to flight from fear were arrested and ordered to sacrifice to idols; and because they would not obey, they were cast into prison by the order of the governor of Africa. Then, being led forth from the prison, they were again compelled to desert Christ, and were tortured with many torments. For first they were scourged until their viscera were exposed. Afterwards, they were pierced in the loins with glowing spits, and vinegar mixed with salt was poured into their wounds. But since, by the prayers they poured forth to God, they overthrew the idols, altars, and temples, thirty-six of them were beheaded; but the remaining four, with hands and feet bound, were cast into prison, from which they were later led out and they too were beheaded.
And the Memorial of the Holy Apostle Agabus.
Agabus, apostle of Christ, was endowed by God with many heavenly gifts on account of his virtue and merit; but he especially obtained the prophetic spirit. For, taking the girdle of the great apostle Paul, and binding his own hands and feet with it, he prophesied, saying: "Thus says the Holy Spirit: The man to whom this girdle belongs, the Jews will bind him in this way in Jerusalem, and will scourge him with whips." And so it came to pass just as he had predicted. For when the holy Paul had gone to Jerusalem, the Jews not only cast him into chains, but also attempted to kill him. And this was his first prophecy. Afterwards, he predicted many other things as well. Having truly illuminated with his doctrine and with countless miracles that part of the world which had fallen to his lot,
he set the flock entrusted to him toward the knowledge of God, and having overthrown and destroyed the worship of idols, he departed in peace.
OF THE SAME MONTH. THE ELEVENTH.
Contest of the holy hieromartyr Antipas, bishop of Pergamon.
Antipas, the adversary of demons, lived during the times of Domitian the king, at the time of the holy apostles, when also John the Theologian was in exile on the island of Patmos. Being bishop of Pergamon, and very advanced in years, he was seized by the idolaters, to whom demons had appeared and said that the place could not be inhabited on account of Antipas. For this reason, having been brought before the governor and compelled to deny Christ and sacrifice to idols, and having refused, but rather having refuted the error of the Greeks with the example (for the governor had set forth, as an objection, that the religion of the Greeks is ancient, while that of the Christians is new; and the holy man had replied that Cain also was ancient, and yet a fratricide), he was cast into a brazen bull, heated, and accomplished his martyrdom.
OF THE SAME MONTH. THE TWELFTH.
Contest of the holy martyr Artemon.
Artemon, the martyr of Christ, lived during the reign of Diocletian, being a presbyter of the holy church in Laodicea. One year before his passing, having entered the temple of the Greeks together with his bishop Sisinnios, he overthrew the idols. And the governor of the region, having learned this from the idolaters, went off to seize the bishop, but was seized by a disease and brought into grave danger of life. He then asked the bishop to offer prayers in his behalf, and promised that if it should happen that he were restored to health, he would erect a golden statue for him. Having regained his health, he set off for Caesarea; and having found Artemon the presbyter on the road, he seized him, dragged him bound, and having led him into the city, cast him into prison. Then he compelled him to deny Christ; and since he could not persuade him, he cut off some members of his body and roasted them on a gridiron. And then he ordered a cauldron to be heated, into which he was to be cast and burned. But two eagles suddenly took hold of the governor and threw him into the cauldron; and the holy man, having lived a little longer, departed in peace.
OF THE SAME MONTH. THE THIRTEENTH.
Contest of the holy martyr Crescens.
Crescens, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Myra, venerable no less for his piety than for his old age. Seeing many worshipping idols, he rushed into their midst, exhorting them to detest their error, to draw near to Christ, and thus to be saved.
Having learned of this, the governor seized him and, bringing him before his tribunal, asked his lineage, country, and name. He replied nothing else but: "I am a Christian." The governor said: "Sacrifice to the gods at least in outward appearance, and worship your God in your heart and soul." But the saint, refusing this, and with a loud voice confessing Christ and rejecting and despising the idols, was first suspended on the wood and long scraped, and his sides were seared with torches. Afterwards, he was taken down from the wood and again compelled to offer sacrifice to the idols. Since he would not be persuaded, he was cast into a great furnace of fire and rendered his spirit to God.
The Commemoration of our Holy Father Basil the Confessor.
Our holy Father Basil loved God from an early age; and having attained every virtue, he was created Bishop of Parium during the times of the impious iconoclasts. Because, following the example of the divine and great apostle of Christ, Paul, he would not consent to the impious heresy of those who despised the venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of his immaculate, glorious, and all-holy Mother, the Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary, and of all the saints; and because he refused to subscribe to the iniquitous document [composed] for the subversion of the orthodox faith, he passed his whole life in persecutions, temptations, afflictions, and tribulations, always migrating and fleeing from place to place. And thus, adhering to the institutions of the Fathers and contending for them, and abhorring the assemblies of the heretics until the end, he departed to the Lord.
The Contest of the holy Martyr Eleutherius the Persian.
Eleutherius, martyr of Christ, was a native of the region of Persia. Being a Christian and loving Christ, he went to the holy bishop Simeon, and by him was more perfectly taught the word of truth. Then, returning to his own home, he himself taught others who came to him the things pertaining to the dispensation of Christ: how God, being in need of nothing, willed to become man, that he might save man, and did not change his essence on account of the union with humanity; but remaining whole God, he was made whole man. When the holy Eleutherius taught thus, and converted many from the infidels and baptized them, it became known to the Persians, who worshipped fire, and by them he was denounced to the king. He was therefore seized and brought to the king; who, when he had interrogated him and recognized his constancy, handed him over to the princes of the Magi, commanding them to persuade him to renounce Christ. They, having tormented him with many tortures, and unable to turn him from Christ, cut off his head.
MONTH OF THE SAME. The fourteenth day.
The contest of the holy hieromartyr Simeon and his company.
Simeon, the hieromartyr of Christ, flourished during the reign of Sapor, King of the Persians. When he beheld the lawless deeds of the Persians and could no longer bear their exactions, he wrote to the king, saying: "We are servants of Jesus Christ our God, and we do not suffer to be your tributaries. Do, therefore, what you will." Consequently, by the king’s order, he was brought bound along with his companions. Upon entering, he did not offer him the sign of reverence as he had done before. When asked why he did not render reverence, he replied: "When I was in peace, I was accustomed to reverence the king; but now that I come as a prisoner, I reverence him no more." Furthermore, when a certain prefect, who had previously been a Christian but had later fallen away from Christ, saw him departing, he attempted to embrace him. But being repelled by Simeon, he said: "If Simeon, being a man, looks down on me, how will Christ, whom I have denied, receive and love me?" Learning of this, the king ordered that the prefect himself, along with the bishop, priests, deacons, and others to the number of one hundred and fifty, be beheaded.
And the contest of the holy martyr Phasic, and of his daughter, a nun.
This martyr, when the holy martyrs with the holy Simeon were being beheaded, was present and watching their martyrdom. Seeing a certain priest among them who was about to have his head cut off, and who was fearful and trembling, he said to him: "Do not fear; close your eyes, and Christ will enlighten you." Thus, having been identified as one who held the beliefs of the Christians, he was brought before the king. Being interrogated and having confessed the name of Christ, first his tongue was cut out, and then, after the skin of his whole body was cruelly flayed, he yielded up his soul. He had a daughter who was a Christian nun; the king ordered her to be brought before him and compelled her to renounce Christ and to offer sacrifice to the sun and fire. But when she could not be persuaded to do this, he first ordered her to be stripped, beaten unsparingly with scourges, and burned with torches. Then, having bound her, he tore her with iron claws, and finally cut off her sacred neck with a sword.
And the contest of the holy thousand martyrs, and of Azat the eunuch.
The saving feast of the holy and great Friday being at hand, the Christians who were in Persia were celebrating it and commemorating it with glorious recollection, giving thanks to Christ, because for our salvation He deigned to suffer. Now, after the holy Bishop Simeon had been seized and put to death, and many others with him had been slain (for from the day of Great Friday for ten consecutive days, every Christian who was seized was executed), these holy ones were also seized, and with them Azat the eunuch, who was a man of wealth
and first in the palace, very much beloved and held in honor by Sapor. And so, when they were brought before the king and questioned, and having confessed Christ with a confident spirit, they were all executed. But Sapor, moved to repentance by the death of the holy Azat, issued a law that from then on no Christian should be put to death; and for some time this edict was observed.
56 And the contest of the holy martyrs James the presbyter and Aza the deacon.
These holy martyrs also, James the presbyter and Aza the deacon, were in Persia during the time of the persecution of the impious Sapor. But when they preached Christ, the prince of the Magi ordered them to be arrested and thrown into prison, where he tormented them with hunger for many days. After this, he ordered them to be brought out of the prison and into his presence, and impelled them to deny Christ. When they would not comply, he first cast mustard and vinegar into their nostrils; then, having stripped them naked and hung them upon wood for the whole night, he tormented them with the cold. In the morning, while they were still hanging, he ordered them, naked as they were, to be beaten with rods, and to be thrown back into prison. Finally, they were led out of the prison and were beheaded. But when the executioner had gone down to a nearby marsh and washed his sword there, the water of the marsh itself was turned into blood; and it remained so for a long time, and finally it dried up.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The fifteenth day. The contest of the holy martyr Sabas the Goth.
Sabas, the martyr of Christ, was from the region of the Goths, in the reign of the emperor Valentinian. Since he had been a Christian from his youth, he not only abhorred foods sacrificed to idols, but also turned others away who wished to taste them. For instead of those things, he set forth the faith that is in Christ, and having converted many, he baptized them. The idolaters, therefore, rising up against him, forcibly expelled him from the city. But after some time, when Athanaricus, the prince of the Goths, had stirred up a persecution against the Christians, Sabas himself was arrested and beaten with rods. Then he was bound to the axle of a chariot and hung from the beam of a house. And when he refused to taste the foods sacrificed to idols, he was led to a river, and a large piece of wood having been tied to his neck, he was thrown into it and drowned, being in the thirty-first year of his age: and thus he departed eagerly to Christ.
57 And the contest of the holy apostles from the Seventy, Aristarchus, Pudens, and Trophimus.
These three holy apostles of Christ, Aristarchus, Pudens, and Trophimus, being from the seventy apostles, followed the great apostle Paul, themselves also preaching Christ and teaching the word of truth. Together with their master, they were affected by the same hardships and were partners in all his persecutions. Finally at Rome, after his death,
and his departure to our Lord Jesus, they themselves were also beheaded by the command of the mad Nero. All these things the most holy and most blessed man Dorotheus, who was born in Rome, recorded in his commentaries in the Roman dialect; and he left a history written not only concerning these, but also concerning the rest of the apostles and many other saints, as well as the holy prophets. For this saint, by reason of the great felicity of his genius, far surpassed all others in manifold doctrine and learning.
And the contest of the holy martyrs, the women Basilissa and Anastasia.
Basilissa and Anastasia were martyrs of Christ from the great city of Rome, noble and wealthy, and disciples of the holy apostles. But after the death of the latter, when they had taken up their venerable relics by night and given them burial, they were discovered and denounced as Christians to the impious and mad Nero. He immediately sent men who seized them and brought them before him bound in chains, and compelled them to deny Christ. But when he could not persuade them to do so, he ordered that they be thrown into prison. Afterward, he brought them out of prison and tormented them with various tortures. For he ordered first that their breasts be cut off and their tongues amputated; then, that they be suspended and torn, and burned with torches; and finally, that their venerable heads be cut off with swords.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The sixteenth day.
The contest of the holy martyr Leonides and his companions.
These holy martyrs were from the region of Greece. Now Leonides, while he was chanting and celebrating the feast in the church in the presence of a large crowd of people on the feast of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, was seized by the idolaters, bound, and led to Corinth. The remaining men and women, who were from various places, were brought before the governor of the province. They too were seized and shackled, and, joined to the holy Leonides, were thrown into prison. Then, being brought out of the prison, they were again set before the governor of Corinth, and were compelled to deny Christ and to sacrifice to the idols. But because they were not persuaded, Leonides was suspended from a wooden post and cruelly raked, and his sides were burned with torches; then, having been taken down from the wood, he was, together with his holy companions, cast into the depths of the sea.
And the contest of the holy martyr Irene.
And the holy martyr Irene, during the same time of the holy Pascha and in the same region, while she was glorifying God in her private oratory, together with those who were with her then, was denounced to the governor by impious idolaters. She was therefore seized, bound in chains, and set before him. And being interrogated, she confessed Christ with confidence, as the true God
and as the Savior of all men and the destroyer of idols. Being then seized, she was confined in a dungeon, as the governor was busy with public affairs. When he later had leisure, she was again brought out of prison and lead before him. And after being harshly tormented and suffering many things, she was cruelly tortured; for her tongue was cut out, her teeth were pulled out, and finally her head was severed with a sword.
59 And the contest of the holy martyr Adrian.
Adrian also, a martyr of Christ, was one of those who were seized at that time and pushed into various prisons. But being led out of prison, when a sacrifice was being offered to false gods, and all the Greeks led astray by error were sacrificing, he also was compelled to approach the altar and burn incense. He not only refused to do this but, being strong and noble, he jumped onto the altar, overturned it, scattered the victims placed upon it, and dispersed the fire. Having thus provoked the anger of the governor and inflamed the spirits of the idolaters who were present, he was seized and cruelly beaten; for one man struck him with a rod, another crushed his mouth with a stone, and another struck him on the head. Finally, they cast him into a burning furnace and thus he surrendered his holy soul to the Lord.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The seventeenth day.
The contest of the holy martyr Ardalion.
This man, during the reign of Maximianus, was a mime. It pleased him, among other theatrical performances, to exhibit this act as well: he pretended to be a martyr contending for Christ. And when on stage, while being hung and lashed by the one who was representing the tyrant, and being applauded by the spectators for his feigned constancy, he cried out with a loud voice, and having commanded silence, he turned to the people and said: "Do not imagine that I am acting in a play; but in truth consider me a Christian, for I am a Christian." Then the governor, his face changed, first exhorted him to change his mind and not die a shameful death. But when he would not assent, but affirmed he wished to persist in the faith of Christ even to death, a great pyre of wood was kindled, and he was thrown into the midst of it. He accepted the end of this life with joy, dealing a timely wound to the devil.
60 And the memory of our holy Father Agapetus, Pope of Rome.
Our holy Father Agapetus was born in ancient Rome during the reign of Justinian, and because of his exercises in the religious life and other virtues, he ascended to the dignity of the supreme pontificate. He was also illustrious for miracles. For when he once departed from the city of Rome and was sailing for Constantinople,
and had come into Greece, and found there a certain man who was mute and, by reason of infirmity, immobile, he took him by the hand and made him whole. Then, as he was entering the Golden Gate and happened upon a certain blind man sitting there, he laid his hand upon him and restored his sight. Thus did he become so venerable in the eyes of the emperor and the senate that he expelled Anthimus, the bishop of Trapezus, who had illicitly ascended the throne of Constantinople and held the heresy of Eutyches, and in his place ordained the most holy Mennas. Afterwards, having been taken ill, he departed this life and was buried in the temple of the holy Apostles.
The Memory of Saint Anthusa
Saint Anthusa was the daughter of Constantine Caballinus, by whom she was bidden to marry a husband, but she did not consent. Truly, having obtained freedom after his death, she distributed all her wealth: some parts she scattered among the poor, other parts she spent on the construction of churches and monasteries, and other parts she devoted to the redemption of captives, while the golden garments which she herself possessed she converted into the ornament of churches. She was, moreover, a mother to many orphans; for she would gather up abandoned infants, and would educate and instruct them; and those indeed who died she would commend to God, but those who lived she would place in a hospice for the aged. Often, however, being summoned by the most religious Irene and her son Constantine to rule together with them, she steadfastly refused. Finally, having become a nun under Saint Tarasius, she migrated to the Lord in the monastery of Eumenia.
THE SAME MONTH. 
THE EIGHTEENTH DAY.
The Memory of Saint Cosmas the Confessor
Cosmas, the most holy pontiff and confessor of Christ, took his origin from the city of Constantinople. From his early youth, he pursued God with love, left the world, and departing, became a monk. And when he had purged himself through religious exercises and the remaining virtues, and had become a tabernacle of God, he was ordained bishop of Chalcedon, during the time of the impious iconoclasts. For this reason, on account of the orthodox faith, he sustained many struggles. For, being pressed by those who then held the mastery to deny the veneration of the holy and venerable icons, and not being persuaded, he was cast into exile and endured very many calamities. But having been recalled from exile and compelled to consent to their heresy, since he was unwilling even to hear them, he was subjected to manifold miseries together with Saint Auxentio, with whom he also underwent the same struggles. And thus, having been tempted and having triumphed, he migrated to the Lord.
The Memory of Holy John, Disciple of Saint Gregory the Decapolite
Our holy Father John, from his tenderest years, hated the world; and having embraced Christ with love, he departed to the great Gregory the Decapolite and...
becoming a monk under him, he thereafter lived alongside him, struggling with him and serving God in all things. And he became so famous for his obedience, so compliant in his submission, and so ready for any ministry, that the great Gregory greatly rejoiced in him and glorified God. After the passing of the holy Gregory and his departure to God, he went away into a far and unknown land—for the Lord Himself had acted as a foreigner and been born a stranger among strangers—and he endured much. Then, seeking the holy places, he betook himself to the Laura of the blessed Chariton, and there he dedicated himself to many exercises of virtue. And having thus lived rightly, in peace he emigrated to the God of peace, whom he had loved exceedingly.
The contest of the holy martyr Victor and his companions.
At the time when the impious emperor Diocletian stirred up that great and horrible persecution against the Christians, and the holy and many-times-tried martyr of Christ, George, had been seized and subjected to manifold torments, during these very tortures he performed signs far more admirable and greater than human strength, and seeing these miracles, many believed in the Lord. And some of them were immediately beheaded or burned, while others were thrust into prisons to be tortured later. Among these were those holy martyrs of Christ: Victor, Acindynus, Zoticus, Zenon, and Severianus, who, having seen the holy George bound to the wheel and yet in no way harmed, embraced the faith of Christ. Therefore, Diocletian, flaring up with rage, ordered them to be tortured first with various punishments, and when they refused to sacrifice to idols, they were beheaded.
The memory of the holy confessor George.
The holy confessor of Christ, George, also flourished in the days of the iconoclasts. Having from infancy pursued God with love and become a monk, because of the many labors and struggles he endured, he became a temple of the Holy Spirit. Then, being ordained bishop of Antioch, he rightly governed the flock entrusted to him. Thereafter, by the evil counsel of the devil, the heresy of the iconoclasts emerged, and all the bishops were summoned by the emperor through letters to arrive at Constantinople as quickly as possible. He came there as well, desiring to obey kings in accordance with the commandment of Saint Paul. But being ordered to abjure the veneration of the holy images, since he would not consent, he was driven into exile, in which, having endured many hardships for the orthodox faith, he rested in peace.
OF THE SAME MONTH.
The nineteenth day.
The contest of the holy martyr Christopher and his companions.
These three also, on the same day, with various torments
the great martyr George was tormented. There stood by the emperor soldiers bearing spears, and having seen those wonders, they threw down not only their arms, but also their belts, and stood before him, and confessed Christ. And being seized and bound with chains, they were shut up in prison; and on the morrow, being brought out of prison, they were led in as prisoners and stood before him; and they were compelled first by threats to deny Christ, and then by moderate tortures. But since they had an unchangeable purpose toward Christ, they were suspended and flayed, and their sides were scorched with torches; then they were shut up in prison. And after this, being brought out of the prison, they were again compelled to deny Christ and to sacrifice to the idols. And not being persuaded, they were perfected by fire.
OF THE SAME MONTH. Twentieth.
Memory of our holy Father Theodore the Trichinas.
Our holy Father Theodore, who was surnamed Trichinas, was by birth and upbringing from Constantinople. Being the son of wealthy parents, he left behind both parents and riches and glory, and departing to the monastery which for his sake was called Trichinas, he became a monk; and he subjected himself to such austerity that he seemed as one dead to all. For day and night, struggling against the cold and the frost, he stood in prayer, clothed in only one garment, and that of hair, and coarse; for this reason he was named Trichinas. He was also unshod, and kept his head uncovered and bare; whence also, having received authority over demons, he performed many miracles, and at the end of his life he did not cease to work wonders, but offered healings to all who approached him.
And the memory of our holy Father Anastasius the Sinaite.
Our God-bearing Father Anastasius, leaving the world and the things in the world, and taking up his cross, according to the command in the holy Gospel, zealously followed Christ, and departing, he became a monk in a monastery. Desiring, however, to undergo greater struggles and to attain more perfect virtue, he went to Jerusalem. And when he had worshipped in the holy and venerable places, he went to Mount Sinai; and having found holy men there practicing the monastic life, he remained among them, obeying them and serving them zealously. And on account of his humility, he received from God the gift of knowledge and of much wisdom. Whence he also recorded the lives of holy Fathers, and composed many soul-profiting discourses, most of which, being found, are set before those who are studious of learning for the salvation and benefit of souls; and after these things, having pleased God, he rested in peace.
OF THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-FIRST DAY.
Contest of the holy martyr Alexandra the empress.
Alexandra, the martyr of Christ, was the wife of the emperor Diocletian. When she also had seen the holy George being tormented, namely by a spear in the belly, and yet in no way harmed; then bound to a wheel composed of sharp iron, and by aid from above released from his chains; and furthermore, when he had been cut into pieces and was restored to health, and appeared before the emperor who was sacrificing to idols, and stood fearlessly, and by that wondrous spectacle summoned many to the faith of Christ, some of whom were beheaded outside the city, while others were thrown into prisons: when she, I say, had seen these things, Alexandra, casting away the glory of the empire, herself also believed in Christ, and confessed before the emperor that she was a Christian. By the order of Diocletian, therefore, she was committed to prison. And after the sentence was passed that George and Alexandra should be beheaded, having learned of this, she poured out prayers to God in prison and surrendered her soul.
And memory of the holy prophet Micah.
The glorious and great prophet Micah was one of the sixteen prophets and was from the tribe of Ephraim. Reproving king Achab for his many and various transgressions, he was indeed held in hatred by him, but was by no means killed, because the king feared God and revered the virtue of the prophet. Yet, being struck with fear, the king withdrew, and for the most part dwelt in the mountains, so that by not appearing frequently and reproving him, he might not arm his heart against him to commit murder. After the death of Achab, when he reproved his son Joram for the same iniquities, and he would not bear the reproof of the prophet with a calm mind, he was seized and thrust into prison. Where, having remained for a long interval of time, he constantly endured sorrows and very many afflictions. Then, being led out of prison, he was cast over a precipice by the executioners; and having surrendered his soul to God, he was buried.
And memory of the holy Maximian, patriarch of Constantinople.
Maximian, the pontiff of Christ, drew his origin from ancient Rome, the son of wealthy and noble parents. But when, on account of some business, he had departed from Rome, he came to Constantinople, where, on account of his good disposition and manifold learning, as well as the exact rectitude of his life, he was ordained a presbyter of the holy church of Constantinople by the most renowned patriarch Sisinnius. And demonstrating his probity in all virtues, he persevered in that course until Nestorius the heretic, who had succeeded the most holy Sisinnius, was condemned. But after the deposition of that heretic Nestorius, Maximian, as a faithful and orthodox man, by the common
a faithful and orthodox man was chosen as patriarch of Constantinople; and having shepherded the flock of Christ well and piously, and having preserved the Church free from scandals, and having held office for two years and five months, he rested in peace.
*And the contest of the holy martyr Isaacius and those with him.* These three holy martyrs, Isaacius, Apollo, and Codratus, were servants of the Empress Alexandra; and seeing her having despised the fleeting glory of this age, corruptible power, and a mortal emperor, and having run to Christ, and having believed in Him as an immortal and eternal King, and having died for Him, they themselves also believed in Christ; and speaking with boldness, they reproached the emperor, calling him lawless, and cruel, and beastly, since he did not even spare his own wife, with whom he had begotten children. Then the emperor, being enraged, ordered the executioners to seize them and commit them to prison. And this having been done, he himself deliberated throughout the night as to how he might put them to death (for he was greatly angered), and the next day, having brought them into his presence and forced them to deny Christ, and failing to persuade them, he beheaded them.
EODEM MENSE. Die vicesima secunda.
*Memoria sancti Patris nostri Theodori Sicæota.*
Theodore, the high priest of Christ and great wonder-worker, was from the region of Galatia, from the village of Sicaea, during the reign of Justinian the Elder; he was born in an inn, his mother, Maria, having drawn to his begetting, by reason of the beauty of her face, a certain Cosmas, one of the imperial couriers; his mother also saw in a dream a star descend from heaven and fall into her womb; the star signified the future virtue of the child; for he became so virtuous from infancy that he acquired the holy George as a friend, who conversed with him openly and walked with him, and guided him toward every good; from whom he also acquired the power to work countless miracles. Having become a monk, he was ordained bishop of Anastasiopolis, and having become celebrated for his many other miracles, both to emperors and to the whole world, he departed in peace to the Lord.
*And the memory of the holy apostle Nathanael.*
Nathanael, the friend and apostle of Christ, was from the city of Cana of Galilee, where Christ our God, having been called to a marriage along with His immaculate Mother and the holy disciples, performed the first miracle, changing water into wine. And he himself also awaited the arrival of Christ, as he was skilled in the law, and knew what was said by those—
who were led away from prison, and again seized, surrendered his spirit to God.
The struggle of the holy martyr Sabas the commander.
Sabas, a martyr of Christ, held the office of commander of soldiers under the emperor Aurelian in the city of Rome. Being a Goth by race, but a Christian in religion, he was accustomed to visit the holy men confined in prison and to serve them. Moreover, because of his pure life and his exercises, he drove wicked spirits out of the bodies of possessed men. Accused, therefore, and arrested, he was brought before the emperor. He cast down before him the military belt with which he was girded, and confessed Christ. He was, therefore, suspended and stretched, and smitten with torches, from which tortures he miraculously escaped safe and unharmed. He called seventy men to the faith of Christ, who were immediately beheaded. Afterwards he was cast into prison, where being seen by Christ, he was granted much greater strength. Being led out of the dungeon, and commanded again to deny Christ and to sacrifice to idols, and refusing to do so, his holy head was severed with a sword.
ON THE TWENTY-SIXTH DAY OF THE SAME MONTH.
The struggle of the holy hieromartyr Basileos, bishop of Amasea.
The most holy martyr Basileos was bishop of Amasea under the emperor Licinius. He suffered martyrdom in this manner. A certain maidservant of the wife of Licinius, named Glaphyra, because she wished to avoid the concubinage of the emperor for the sake of modesty, by the counsel of her mistress, fled secretly with a large sum of money to the Eastern regions. When she had come to Amasea, she was received as a Christian by Bishop Basileos. When Licinius learned of this, he ordered both to be brought to him. But Glaphyra, having already passed away, escaped his hands. Basileos, however, the bishop, was brought in chains to Nicomedia; and when he had rebuked the emperor, he was beheaded, and cast into the sea, the body separately, and the head separately. But by the providence of God, his body was joined to his head, and floating across the current, it was found in the city of Sinope, and was then deposited at Amasea.
The struggle of the holy martyr Publius.
This holy martyr of Christ, Publius, was a soldier, assigned to the troops of the emperor Licinius, and much beloved by him because he had comported himself strenuously and bravely on many occasions in war. But when the most holy martyr Basileos was brought in chains from the city of Amasea before Licinius, and boldly rebuked him and the deception of the impure demons, he described what pertains to the dispensation of the true God and our Savior Jesus Christ; and having cast down the military belt with which he was girded, and his weapons, he professed himself a Christian, and
a servant and soldier of the heavenly Divinity. The emperor, being moved to wrath and his countenance suddenly changed by great fury, first endeavored to move him from such a purpose by flatteries; but since he could not attain this, he ordered that he be cruelly tortured, and finally that his head be cut off with a sword.
EODEM MENSE. Die vicesima septima.
Memorial of the Holy Apostles Sosipater and Jason
Jason and Sosipater were disciples of the apostle Paul. Jason was born in Tarsus in Cilicia, and became bishop of that same city; Sosipater was born at Patras in Achaia, and became bishop of Iconium. When they had governed their own churches for some years, they went away to the West, that they might help some people. And having arrived at the island of Corcyra, they built a church in the name of the holy protomartyr Stephen. When Cercylinus, the ruler of the island, learned of this, he ordered them to be thrown into prison; where seven robbers who were imprisoned there saw them and believed in Christ; likewise also the jailer, Antonius, who was also beheaded. And after fire descended from heaven and consumed the ruler's two sons and his wife, the holy men were released from their bonds; and having benefited many, they later departed in peace.
The Passion of the Holy Martyr Cercyra
After the sons of the ruler Cercylinus and his wife had perished by the heavenly fire, and the aforementioned holy men had been released from their bonds, Carpianus, the governor of the island, seized them and, by the command of the ruler, subjected them to tortures. But Cercyra, the ruler’s own daughter, looking out from a window and seeing the holy men being afflicted with tortures, embraced the faith of Christ; and having professed herself to be a Christian, she stood before her father. When she was commanded by him to deny Christ, and did not consent, she too was delivered to the governor. And the governor gave her to a certain Ethiopian, that he might corrupt her. But by the will of God, a bear coming from elsewhere intercepted the Ethiopian in his attempted crime and guarded the virgin uncorrupted. Upon seeing this miracle, the Ethiopian himself believed in Christ and was beheaded with a sword. But the holy Cercyra was first hung up, and tortured by smoke emitted from a fire placed beneath her, then transfixed with arrows, and finally, being pelted with stones, she consummated her martyrdom.
The Passion of the Holy Martyr Saturninus and his Companions
These holy saints were the leaders of the seven robbers who, in prison, through the teaching of the holy apostles Jason and Sosipater, gave their names to Christ; and together with those who later embraced the Christian religion through the holy Cercyra, after her death they were led out from prison. They themselves, the seven, were led outside the city and cast into cauldrons filled with pitch, wax, and oil, and being boiled, they consummated their martyrdom. The remaining brothers were deported to a small island and devoted themselves to divine prayers. And having learned of this
their failure to entrap Paul, turned against James. And having seized him, they compelled him to deny Christ. And having led him to the pinnacle of the temple, they said to him: Tell us, O Just One, since the multitude is led astray after Jesus, which is the door of Jesus? But he said: Why do you ask me about Jesus? He is sitting in the heavens at the right hand of the Father, and is about to come to judge the inhabited world in righteousness. And when they had said, Lo, even the Just One is led astray, they cast him down from the temple. And while he still breathed, one of the fullers, striking him with a club, killed him.
MONTH OF MAY.
On the first day.
The falling asleep of the holy prophet Jeremiah.
Jeremiah, the elect prophet of God, was from the region of Judea, and he prophesied many things, but especially concerning the destruction of Jerusalem. Wherefore he took the Ark of the Law and all the holy things within it, and having hidden them in a rock, he thus addressed those who were present: The Lord has departed from Sinai into heaven, and will come again to Sinai with power; and this will be a sign to you of his presence, when all nations shall adore wood. When he had said this, immediately upon the rock where he had hidden the Ark, a cloud appeared, overshadowing that place until the present day. Afterwards he suffered many tribulations from the Jews, because he reproved their iniquities. When he had gone into Egypt, he prophesied that it would come to pass that their idols would be shattered and fall down because of the Savior, the child born of a Virgin in a stable. And at last, while he was dwelling in the Egyptian city of Taphnis, he was stoned by the people, departed from this life, and was buried near the house of Pharaoh.
The struggle of the holy martyr Batas.
The holy martyr Batas was from the region of Persia, having been taught the faith of Christ by his parents. When he had reached his thirtieth year, he left behind his father, mother, wife, children, and all the riches with which he was blessed, and departed and took up the monastic life: in which, when he had exercised himself most excellently, he desired to end his life by martyrdom.
