When therefore a persecution was stirred up against the Christians, and the rest of the monks who were with him had fled from the monastery, he alone remained: where, being seized, he was delivered to the governor of Nisibis, and by him was compelled to deny Christ, and to adore the sun and fire. When he refused to do this, and with the greatest confidence of spirit confessed Christ, both his hands were stretched out by ten satellites, and his shoulders were dislocated from the excessive violence. Then, when his genital parts were tightly bound with ropes, he was dragged along and beaten with rods. Finally, being cruelly flayed in all the members of his body, he ended his life by the sword.
ON THE SAME MONTH, THE SECOND DAY
The Contest of the Holy Martyrs Hesperus, Zoe, and their Children
The holy martyrs Hesperus, and Zoe with their children, were from the region of Italy, serving a certain rich man during the reign of Hadrian. Now when Cyriacus and Theodulus had been instructed in the Christian faith by their parents, they said to them one day: "Why do we serve these impious men, and not rather Christ, lest we perish with them?" Their mother, hearing this, said: "Resist him who bought our bodies, and we shall sustain martyrdom for Christ." Then the boys went and said to their master: "Our bodies are indeed subject to your power, but the Lord of our souls is Jesus Christ, who rules over all. From now on we shall not serve you, but Him." Their master, being astonished at this, sent them at that time to Hesperus, their father, who was residing in the city of Tritonium. Afterward, however, he summoned both the father and the mother, ordered them to be tortured, and finally, having heated a furnace, cast them into it and burned them with flames.
And the Falling Asleep of our Holy Father Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria
Our holy Father Athanasius, born in the city of Alexandria, flourished in the time of the emperors Constantine the Great and his son Constantius. From his boyhood he loved God and sought to imitate the ecclesiastical order. For while still a boy, he took his companions and went to the seashore, and acting like a child, he simulated being a bishop, and from those who were with him, he ordained some as presbyters and deacons; the rest of the Greek and Jewish boys he baptized with the water of the sea. Alexander, the Bishop of Alexandria, observing these things from afar, was struck with amazement; but discerning in the spirit that those things which had been done were presages of the future, he completed the rite by anointing the boys with the divine Chrism. Athanasius was instructed in letters first by him, soon became a lector, and finally was ordained bishop. After suffering many struggles for piety, he finished his life.
ON THE SAME MONTH, THE THIRD DAY
The Contest of the Holy Martyrs Timotheus and Maura
Timotheus, Christ's martyr, was a lector of the most holy Church of God. Having taken Maura as his wife by the law of marriage, after scarcely twenty days had passed, he was seized by idolaters, bound, and led to Arrianus, the governor of the Thebaid, to whom he was delivered. The governor said to him: "Bring your books and burn them before me." But when the saint refused to do this, glowing iron plates were inserted into his ears, and immediately the pupils of his eyes fell out. Then he was bound by the ankles to a wheel, a piece of wood was placed in his mouth; and with a stone tied to his neck,
he was suspended upside down. And since he could not persuade him, he commanded his wife to try to persuade him to abandon Christ. But she chose rather to suffer martyrdom. Wherefore he ordered the hair of her head to be torn out, and finally both of them to be nailed to a wall: where, persevering for the space of nine days, they ended their lives. Et memoria sancti Patris nostri Petri Thaumaturgi. Καὶ μνήμη τοῦ ὁσίου Πατρὸς ἡμῶν Πέτρου τοῦ Θαυματουργοῦ. Our holy Father Peter had Constantinople as his homeland, being the son of pious parents, who eventually became monks. And he strove in virtue to such a degree that it is not easy to explain. For not only did he surpass everyone in vigils and the study of the holy Scriptures, but also in almsgiving and compassion for the poor. Hence, being compelled to become the archbishop of Corinth, because of his humility of mind and modesty, he could not be induced to consent. Therefore, his brother Paul having been ordained, he followed him. But by the prayers of the Argives, being consecrated bishop of Argos, he laid such hold of almsgiving that every day there was nothing to be found in his storehouse except the tunic he was wearing; and he turned away no poor person who came to him. Whence, having performed many miracles and served God, he departed in peace. EODEM MENSE. Die quarta.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
Δ´. § Certamen sancti Silvani martyris. ῎Αθλησις τοῦ ἁγίου μάρτυρος Σιλβανοῦ. The holy martyr of Christ, Silvanus, was from the region of the Gazaeans. He was first a soldier, but afterwards, having renounced the camps of the earthly king for Christ, he undertook the warfare of the heavenly King, Christ. Wherefore, being held worthy of the priesthood, he was first ordained a presbyter, then a bishop. When he diligently applied himself to the rule of the Church committed to him, and brought many of the Greeks to the Lord by his teaching, he was seized by idolaters, and brought forth into the midst of the Caesarean people, he was cruelly beaten; then hung up and severely lacerated, and condemned to the digging of bronze mines: where, having endured many hardships, and not ceasing not only to profess Christ, but also to preach the true God to others, and especially to those who were with him, he was beheaded with a sword together with forty other martyrs who had been instructed by him. Et certamen sacrosancti martyris Olbiani, et discipulorum ejus. Καὶ ἄθλησις τοῦ ἁγίου ἱερομάρτυρος Ὀλβιανοῦ, καὶ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ. Olbianus, the divine holy martyr, was a bishop when Maximian was emperor and Aelianus was governor of Asia. When a certain priest of the idols, named Agrippinus, was offering sacrifice to Juno, being seized himself, he was compelled to sacrifice and to burn incense on the altar. But he, with many arguments and pious speeches, exalted the Christian faith,
deprecating and condemning the worship of idols. Wherefore his entrails and loins were first scorched with red-hot irons; then, being cruelly beaten with rods, he was cast into prison. Afterwards, led out from prison and again compelled to deny Christ and to sacrifice to idols, when he refused to do this, he was adjudged to the fire along with his disciples; and accordingly, a great furnace having been kindled, he was cast into it with them and finished his life.
The Contest of Saint Nicephorus, Hegumen of the Medicius Monastery.
Saint Nicephorus lived during the time of the Iconoclasts. From childhood, he burned with love for Christ, and seeing the heresy increasing, he forthwith renounced the world and all that is in it, became a monk, and withdrew to the mountains. He lived a tranquil life, occupied with prayers and fasts, offering petitions to God for the public peace of the world. Then, when the heresy had calmed down a little, at the earnest request of the monks, he presided over the Medicius monastery. But when that plague broke out again, and the heresy, in the days of the impious Emperor Leo, gathered strength, he was expelled from his flock as a worshiper of the venerable icons who adhered to the precepts of the holy patriarchs; and being subjected to bitter hardships, he was shut up in a dark prison. There, as a most valiant athlete, having overthrown the soul-destroying error, he departed to Christ, whom he had longed for.
The Memory of our Holy Father Hilarius the Wonderworker.
Hilarius the Wonderworker, having become a monk in the first flower of his youth, and taking up his cross upon his shoulders, followed the Lord who was crucified for us. When he had subjected the affections of the flesh by self-control, he surpassed all the monks in every virtue. For, shutting himself up in a dark little cell, and becoming far from every tumult, he shone with an imperturbable spirit. Wherefore he was also deemed worthy of the priesthood and performed miracles. For he rebuked the animals which were harming the sprouting seeds and drove them from the field; he repressed a fountain of hail by shed prayers; he irrigated the thirsty earth with rains; he parted the currents of a river, like the prophet Elisha; he healed the withered hand of a man, and granted sight to the blind; and having performed many other miracles, he departed in peace to the Lord.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The Fifth Day.
The Contest of Saint Irene the Martyr.
Irene, the martyr of Christ, was the daughter of the petty king Licinius. Since she was beautiful, she was shut up by her father in a high tower, being six years of age, with thirteen handmaidens. There, taught by a divine angel the mysteries of God, she was not long after baptized by Timothy, a disciple of the holy Apostle Paul, who had arrived there. As for the idols which her father had given her, that she might
worship, she broke them and cast them down. Then her father, having become enraged, had her tied to a wild horse in order that she might be destroyed. But she herself suffered no harm; for her father died, the horse having bitten his hand and severed it; but she, having prayed, raised him up. Then he too believed in God, and others, about three thousand [people]. And again, the saint, having been seized by the governor Ampelianus, and after being tortured in many ways and not being persuaded to deny Christ, was perfected by the sword and buried.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The Sixth Day.
Memory of Job the Just, and conqueror of many struggles.
Blessed Job was from the region of Ausitis, which is situated on the borders of Judæa and Arabia, a son of the sons of Esau, so as to be the fifth from Abraham. Previously his name had been Jobab. He prophesied for thirty-five years, preceding the incarnation of Christ by one thousand nine hundred and twenty-five years. Being called just by the testimony of God, the devil sought to afflict him. But since God desired to render him more glorious, He handed him over to the devil: who not only stripped him of his wealth and his children, but also striking him, cast him down to the dunghill, wounded and covered in sores. But the saint, having withstood all temptations, and having given thanks to God in all things, covered the devil with utmost shame. Having later obtained on earth double the wealth, and having taken a wife and begotten children, and having exhibited himself as grateful to God according to custom, he ended his life.
And the memory of our holy Father Pachomius.
Saint Pachomius, our father, having been seized in the time of persecution, was cast into prison. But as he was not yet initiated, nor did he well know the dogma of the faith, he asked God to teach him. An angel of God therefore approaching, instructed him in all truth. When the persecution had ceased, he embraced the solitary life: and he progressed in virtue such that he was deemed worthy of the conversation of an angel, and learned from him the order and habit of monks. For from him was formed the angelic institution of the solitary life. After these things he roused many monasteries to the glory of God: and having worked miracles, and having served God in all things until old age, he migrated to Him rejoicing, having obtained an eternal kingdom in the heavens, and life everlasting and without end.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The Seventh Day.
Memory of the sign of the cross which appeared in the heaven.
In the reign of Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, and while Cyril was archbishop of Jerusalem, on the days of holy Pentecost, at the third hour of the day, there appeared the sign of the life-giving cross, fashioned from...
light in the heavens, in the sight of all the people, stretched out above the holy Golgotha, where our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified, and extending as far as the holy mount of Olives, which by the brightness of its shimmering rays obscured the rays of the sun. Wherefore Christians of every age, young and old, together with infants and nursing children, betook themselves to the holy church of God; and with immeasurable joy, they sent up glory and thanksgiving unto God with fervent contrition for the wondrous miracle. Concerning this, the holy Cyril also wrote to Constantius, confirming him in the orthodox faith.
And the contest of the holy martyr Acacius.
Acacius, the martyr of Christ, was in the time of the emperor Maximianus, from the region of Cappadocia, serving in the cohort of the *Scholae*. But being recognized as a Christian, he was seized and brought to the governor of the region, and having confessed Christ, he was severely beaten. Then, being sent on to another governor, and bound with many other prisoners, he was led to Byzantium; and having been flayed over his entire body with cruel scourges and tortures, he was cast into prison. There, divine angels stood by and restored him to health; and when all those who were in the prison saw him so suddenly restored to health, they themselves also believed in Christ, and were beheaded. Then, being brought out of the prison and sent on to another governor, and again tortured, he was beheaded; and his remains were laid to rest in a place called Staurium.
SAME MONTH.
II.
Commemoration of the holy John the Theologian on account of the holy ash.
The man-loving and all-good God of ours, not only deemed those who struggled for Him—His holy disciples and apostles, prophets and martyrs, and all those who have pleased Him—worthy of the kingdom of heaven and eternal blessings, but He also showed the places in which they walked or were buried to be full of graces, and illumined them with many miracles. For the tomb in which the great Apostle and Evangelist John was buried, just prior to his translation, by the assent of the Holy Spirit, suddenly sends forth and exudes each year, on the eighth day of the month of May, a holy ash, which the local inhabitants call "Manna." Those who approach and receive this ash use it for the deliverance from all manner of maladies, for the healing of souls, and for the soundness of bodies, glorifying God and venerating His servant, the Theologian.
And the commemoration of our holy Father Arsenius the Great.
Arsenius, our Father among the saints, was from the old
Rome, deacon of the most holy Church of God. On account of his knowledge and virtues, he was chosen by Theodosius the Great, the emperor, to instruct his children, Arcadius and Honorius, not only in letters but also in virtues. He was so honored by the emperor that he was called the Father of the emperors. But he, hating crowds and fleeing the emperor of the earth, loved the solitary life and desired the heavenly King; he asked Him to direct him in the way, that he might know how he should be saved. He heard, therefore, a voice from heaven saying to him three times: "Arsenius, flee from men, and you shall be saved." And immediately, having changed his garments and assumed the habit of a poor man, he departed into Egypt and undertook the solitary life: and after having struggled as no one else, he departed to God in deep old age.
EODEM MENSE. Die nona.
The Contest of the holy prophet Isaiah.
Isaiah, the great prophet of God, had Jerusalem as his fatherland; he was the uncle of king Manasseh, the son of Hezekiah. Because he rebuked him for his iniquities, he was sawn in two with a saw and ended his life, and was buried near the waters which king Hezekiah had diverted, covering the land on account of enemies. But God made the sign of Siloam for the sake of the prophet. For when, before he died, he was thirsty, he prayed that water might gush forth; and immediately water was sent to him from it: and on account of this it had the surname Siloe, which is interpreted as "sent." And of old, indeed, the holy relics of the prophet lay, as they say, near the waters of Siloam, and near the tomb of the kings David and Solomon. But finally, transferred to Constantinople, they were deposited near the Blachernae, in the church of the holy martyr Laurence.
And the contest of the holy martyr Christopher.
Regarding this holy man, certain wonderful and stupendous things are reported by some, namely that he first had the face of a dog and devoured men, and finally, when he had believed in Christ, he changed his form. But the matter did not happen so; but some suspected him thus because he was a pagan, and fierce, and terrible. He was, however, during the reign of Decius, and having been captured in battle by a count, since he was unable to speak Greek, he prayed to God: and an angel was sent to him, saying: "Take heart." And touching his lips, he made him speak Greek. Having therefore entered the city, he preached Christ. But the guards sent, captured him. And when his staff blossomed, they believed in Christ, and together with him were baptized at Antioch by the holy Babylas, where he was also called Christopher. Afterwards, brought to the emperor, he was first subjected to many tortures, and at last was beheaded.
And the contest of the holy martyrs Epimachus and Gordianus.
Epimachus and Gordianus were martyrs of Christ
from the great and ancient Rome. But because they confessed Christ, they were seized by the idolaters and handed over to the governor of the region, and being compelled to deny Christ and to sacrifice to the idols, and not being persuaded, they were severely beaten; and being suspended, they were torn with iron claws. Then, being taken down from the stakes, they were shut up in prison, having been granted a time of reprieve so that they might repent and live. But even while in prison, they did not cease to pray and to give thanks to God that they were counted worthy to struggle for his sake. After some days, having been brought out of prison again and subjected to many and various tortures, their holy heads were cut off with the sword.
The contest of the holy martyr Codratus, and of those in his company.
Codratus, the martyr of Christ, lived during the reigns of Decius and Valerian in the city of Nicomedia. Because of his confession of Christ, he was seized by the heathens together with his company, bound, and brought before the proconsul of the city. Being interrogated, he freely confessed Christ. He was therefore stretched out upon the ground and struck with dry ox-sinews; and having stained the ground with his blood, he was committed to prison. Then, being taken by the proconsul to Nicaea, he was tortured. And some who feared the torments and wished to sacrifice, he strengthened by reminding them of the fear of God; and the proconsul cast these into the fire and burned them. Codratus, being led from city to city and sanctifying them all with his blood, reached Hermopolis and was beheaded.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The tenth day.
The contest of the holy martyr Hesychius.
Hesychius, the martyr of Christ, lived under the emperor Maximian; he was first in the palace, and held the rank of master. While Maximian was staying at Antioch, he commanded that no Christian should serve as a soldier, but that whoever wished to confess Christ should ungird their belts and live as a private individual. And many having chosen an inglorious life rather than honor in perdition, among their number was the great Hesychius. When the emperor learned of this, he stripped him of his costly garments, and having clothed him in a hair-shirt [colobium], condemned him to live together with the women. And after some days, summoning him, he said: "Tell me, Hesychius, are you not ashamed to live in such disgrace?" But he replied: "The honor that comes from you is fleeting." Then the emperor ordered a millstone to be tied to his neck and had him cast into the Orontes river, where he received his blessed end, having attained the kingdom of heaven.
And the memorial of our holy Father Hesychius the Confessor.
He was from the region of the Armenians. Desiring...
to become a monk and to live in tranquility, he descended into the maritime regions. But as he was traveling to a high mountain, demons entered into two men, John and Hilarion, and they made it their business to meet him and to ask him where he was going. And when they learned this, they said, "The place is full of wild beasts and robbers." But he said, "I have committed deeds worthy of death, and I am going there to flee from death." And they answered, "You fear death from men, but do you not fear it from wild beasts?" Then, recognizing the ambush of the demons, he warded them off by making the sign of the cross and cast them out of those men. He himself went on to the place he had desired, built a chapel, and spent a solitary life there, pouring out constant prayers to God and becoming admirable in the exercise of virtues. And having performed many miracles, he ceased to live. His relics, however, were translated into the city of Amasea.
And the contest of the holy Apostle Simon the Zealot.
Simon, the great apostle of Christ, who is surnamed the Zealot, was in the upper room together with the holy apostles; and upon receiving the visible operation of the Spirit in the likeness of a dove and in tongues of fire, he became wholly fiery and was filled with divine zeal. He freely burned up all the error of the many gods like stubble; and he traversed almost the whole earth, illuminating and enlightening it with his words of doctrine and the light of piety. Whence he rightly and truly received the name of Zelotes, and he obtained the double crown of confession. For he traversed Mauretania, all the region of the Africans, and all Libya, and brought many of the infidels to the Lord. And finally, having journeyed into Britain, he was fastened to a cross and thus surrendered his spirit to God.
And the contest of the holy martyr Alphaeus and his company.
Alphaeus, Philadelphus, and Cyrinus, martyrs of Christ, were from the region of Italy, noble and wealthy, the sons of Vitalius, the prefect of that region. Having learned piety from a certain Christian named Onesimus, and having been baptized, they preached Christ. At that time, a prefect having been sent from the city of Rome with imperial letters into that region of Italy, to oversee the slaughter of all Christians, these men were reported to his notice and, being arrested and bound with chains, were sent to Rome together with Onesimus and Erasmus, and fourteen other men, to Licinius. By him they were delivered to the governor Diomedes and were led away to Puteoli. And Onesimus, indeed, having had a great stone placed upon his chest, gave up his spirit. But Erasmus, together with the remaining fourteen, was beheaded. And the aforementioned three were sent to Sicily and were put to death there.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE ELEVENTH.
A 93 Commemoration of the birthday of Constantinople.
When the greatest of emperors and most Christian Constantine had taken the city of Byzantium, and having built it much larger than it formerly was, and having changed its name to his own, he called it Constantinople instead of Byzantium. After he had completed the walls and the buildings within it, and the holy churches, he dedicated it to our most glorious Lady, the Theotokos and Ever-Virgin Mary, offering thanks beyond measure. Along with the most holy patriarch, and the clergy, and the people, he performed a supplication and went up to the Forum, where the citizens had erected a column of him, bearing the holy nails of Christ our God in its head; and in the lower part, at its base, it contains the twelve baskets of the remains that were left over from the five loaves. From that time, therefore, the custom has prevailed that this festival is celebrated unto the present day.
And the contest of the holy martyr Mocius.
Mocius, the holy martyr of Christ, was from the city of Byzantium, the son of Christian parents, Euphrates and Eustathia, who traced their origin from Old Rome. Being a presbyter of the Church of Christ, he exhorted all to abstain from idols, and to honor Christ, and to worship Him as God and Lord of all. One day, when a sacrifice was being performed by the governor, and the people were offering, he was moved by divine zeal, and running up, he overturned the altar and scattered the offerings. Being seized, therefore, he was punished and cast into the fire; but he was seen in the midst of the flame with three men chanting, of whom the face of one shone brighter than the sun, and he himself came out unharmed, but the flame consumed those who stood around, and the governor as well. Then he was sent to Heraclea in Thrace, where he was beheaded and buried. Afterwards, when Constantine the Great had built a temple, he brought his relics and deposited them therein.
And the contest of the holy martyr Dioscorides.
Dioscorides, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Smyrna. Being a Christian, he preached Christ openly, and taught all who came to him in His name; and he turned many of the infidels from their ancestral error which they had received from their forefathers, and baptized them. Having been seized by the idolaters, who could not bear to hear Christ being preached openly, he was scourged. Then, having been bound, he was delivered to the governor. And having been questioned by him, and having confessed himself a Christian, he was tortured and sent off to prison, where he endured severe trials for many days. Afterwards, he was taken out of the prison and was again compelled to deny Christ; and since he refused to do so, he was suspended, and being [tortured]... And persisting in his...
confession of Christ, he was put to death by the order of the governor.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The Twelfth.
Memory of our holy Father Epiphanius, Bishop of Cyprus.
Our holy Father Epiphanius was from the region of Phoenicia, born of Jewish parents. But while they persisted in the worship of the Law, he himself ran to Christ and, having been baptized, became a monk. Afterwards, he was ordained Bishop of Cyprus, and served God in such a way that he was found worthy to perform miracles. As he struggled for the orthodox faith, he endured many trials from the heterodox; and in order to strengthen the truth with his words and to drive the heretics from the Church, he traveled to Constantinople. Being compelled by Eudoxia to sign for the exile of Chrysostom, he could not be induced to do so. But when she threatened that, unless he did this, she would open the temples of the idols, he allowed himself to be persuaded and signed. When Chrysostom learned of this, he wrote to him: "Epiphanius, since you have consented to my exile, you shall not sit upon your throne." He, however, wrote back: "Athlete John, be beaten, and conquer." Eventually, sailing to Cyprus, he ended his life upon the ship.
And the memory of our holy Father Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople.
Our holy Father Germanus lived during the reign of Heraclius, the son of the Patrician Justinian, whom the son of Heraclius, out of envy, killed; and he had Germanus himself made a eunuch, and appointed him to the clergy of the Great Church. He first gave himself over to the meditation of the divine Scriptures, and to religious exercise, and devoted himself entirely to the acquisition of other virtues. Afterwards he was ordained Bishop of the church of Cyzicus. Then, being transferred from Cyzicus, he was promoted to the cathedra of Constantinople, becoming Patriarch. There he illuminated the people with his teaching, and explained the deeper mysteries of the divine Scriptures, and continued until the reign of Leo the Isaurian. When he saw him turning away from the holy images, and was able to persuade him neither by reasons nor by exhortations to desist from his heresy, he laid his omophorion—that is, his pallium—upon the holy table, and went away to his own house. There he lived a quiet life, where, offering constant prayers to God, he departed to God at the age of ninety.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The Thirteenth.
The Passion of the holy martyr Glyceria.
Glyceria was a martyr of Christ in the times of the Emperor Antoninus and the governor Sabinus, in the city of Trajanopolis in Thrace. When, one day, the governor was sacrificing to the idols, she, armed on her forehead with the venerable sign of the cross, approached him and professed herself a Christian and a servant of Christ. Then, at the urging of the governor...
that she should sacrifice, she entered the temple of the idols, and having prayed to Christ, she cast down the image of Jupiter and shattered it. For this reason, she was suspended by her hair and torn with iron claws, and cast into prison, where she was fed by an angel. Then, brought out of prison, she was thrown into a fiery furnace; but the fire being extinguished by a divine dew, she emerged unharmed. Then she was scalped, and having been locked away in prison and healed by an angel, she caused the jailer to believe in Christ; he was immediately beheaded. The holy woman, having been exposed to wild beasts, was perfected. And her relics were deposited in the city of Heraclea in Thrace.
And the contest of the holy martyr Alexander.
Alexander, the martyr of Christ, was in the time of the Emperor Maximian, serving in the army under the Count Numerian. When the count with the cohort subject to him was sacrificing to the idols, Alexander alone not only refused to sacrifice to the idols, but also called the count and those with him deluded, and worshippers of demons. Seized therefore, he was led to Maximian, and being questioned, and having confessed Christ, he was severely beaten. Then he was handed over to the governor Tiberianus, to be tortured on the journey from the city of Rome as far as Byzantium. And first indeed he was scorched with fire on his sides; then he was whipped with thorny rods, his mother following him and urging him to have a ready and cheerful spirit. When he was brought to Beroea in chains, and by his prayers brought forth water, he persuaded many of the idolaters to embrace the faith of Christ; and having arrived in the city of Drizipara in Thrace, he received death by the sword.
And the memory of the holy confessor Sergius.
Sergius, the confessor of Christ, was born in Constantinople of noble and wealthy parents. But as he venerated the divine and holy images, he was seized by the Iconoclasts. And being brought before the impious Emperor Leo, he was compelled, sometimes by blandishments, sometimes by threats, to abandon the veneration of the holy images. But not being persuaded, but rather regarding the tyrant as a loathsome thing, and counting his words and threats as nonsense, he declared with great confidence of spirit that the holy images ought to be venerated, and deservedly honored by all Christians, just as if that honor were being offered to the prototype. Then, having a rope tied around his neck, he was dragged through the market-place like a criminal. Then he was thrown into prison, and having been fined and stripped of his wealth, he was sent into exile with his wife, Irene, and his children. Where, having endured many tribulations and various hardships, he migrated to the Lord.
And the memory of our holy Father Pausicacus.
Our holy Father Pausicacus was from the city of Apamea, born of pious parents. Since he was a physician by profession, he traveled through cities and regions, healing...
all the sick without charge. Then, hating the world and loving Christ, he withdrew into a monastery and became a monk; and he progressed so much in virtue—fasting, keeping vigil, and occupying himself with constant prayers—that he was deemed worthy of great gifts. His food was only modest bread, and water likewise. Because of his virtue, he was appointed Bishop of Synada by Cyriacus, Patriarch of Constantinople, although he was unwilling, during the reign of Maurice, whom he had also healed of a most grave disease. Afterwards, guiding correctly the flock entrusted to him, he lived until the reign of the impious Leo the Iconoclast; and in extreme old age he departed to the Lord.
OF THE SAME MONTH.
The fourteenth day.
Contest of the holy martyr Isidore.
Isidore, the martyr of Christ, lived during the reign of Decius, and was from the city of Alexandria. While he was fulfilling the duty of an *optio* in the military, he set out for the island of Chios with a fleet of ships, which Numerius commanded; and he was denounced by Julius the centurion to this same Numerius as being a Christian. Therefore, having been seized and brought before him, and being asked whether he confessed Christ, he said: "I confess Christ, as the maker of heaven, earth, and sea, and I believe in Him as truly God and the Son of God, born for the salvation of men from the holy Virgin Mary, and become man without seed and without corruption." By these teachings and words, he astonished him, and was first tortured with various torments. But since he bore an immutable spirit toward Christ, and endured the punishments nobly, he was finally beheaded with a sword and received the crown of martyrdom.
And the contest of the holy martyr Maximus.
Maximus, the martyr of Christ, burning with divine zeal, when he saw idolaters not only dedicating themselves to idols, but also tricking others into error and compelling them to worship them and hold them as gods, groaned and was saddened, and prayed to God that He might compose the persecution; and at the same time, preaching Christ now secretly, now openly and freely, he was converting many of those who came to him to the Lord, and baptizing them. On one day, however, when victims were being sacrificed, and all the Greeks were eagerly running to the abominable sacrifices, and were sacrificing not only animals but even humans, he, unable to bear the wickedness, stood in their midst, openly rebuked them, calling the idols soulless stones and wood, which could not even help themselves. Then, being seized by the unbelievers, and first tortured with various torments, he was finally stoned. And thus he departed to the Lord. D
ON THE FIFTEENTH DAY OF THE SAME MONTH.
Memory of our holy Father Theodore the Sanctified.
Our holy Father Theodore, who on account of his holiness and purity earned the title of "the Sanctified," loved God from infancy. Anticipating religious exercise, he meditated diligently upon the law of God. Thus he became wholly pure, a vessel chosen and useful for the performance of the commandments, and a temple and holy dwelling-place of God. Having surpassed all visible, corruptible things that fall under the eyes, and having lifted his mind to the intelligible things—those which can neither be seen nor corrupted—he became a companion-in-dwellings and like-minded with the holy Pachomius, appearing as a peer to the saints of his circle. Whence, having appeared worthy of the great title of being called "the Sanctified," he abounded in the power of many miracles. And for this reason, having become wondrous and famous to all, and having profited many not only by his speech but also by the conduct of his life, he departed to God in deep old age.
Memory of the holy Achillius, Bishop of Larissa.
Achillius the Wonderworker flourished during the reign of Constantine the Great. Being the son of Christian parents, he was taught piety by them, and was instructed in the teachings of external sages. Then, having also diligently studied the divine Scripture, and having disciplined himself in word and virtue, he was ordained high priest of Larissa. And having demonstrated many achievements and miracles, he was also present at the council in Nicaea together with the divine Fathers, against the heretic Arius; and, having contended well for the dogmas of Orthodoxy, and having put the heretics to shame, he was admired by all. After returning from Nicaea to his own throne, and having worked many miracles, and having erected various great temples to the glory of God and His saints, he departed to Him rejoicing.
Struggle of the holy martyr Heraclius and those with him.
The martyrs of Christ, Heraclius, Paulinus, and Benedimus, being from the city of Athens and being Christians, preached the name of Christ with boldness, exhorting all idolaters to turn away from vain idols and to be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. On this account, having been seized by the idolaters, they were delivered to the governor of Athens. And when they were questioned according to custom, they confessed Christ, teaching that He is the true God and Creator of creation; but that the idols are false figments, manufactured from stones and wood and the works of art. Therefore, having angered the governor by speaking the truth, they were beaten severely; and having first passed through every other torment, they were later cast into a great furnace of fire together with their disciples, and were perfected.
The contest of the holy martyr Peter and those with him.
Peter, a martyr of Christ, was from the city of Lampsacus. Being seized by the idolaters, he was handed over to the governor of Abydos. When he was told to sacrifice to the idols and refused, his body was broken with wooden rods and he yielded up his spirit. A Paul and Andrew, however, who were serving under the same governor of Abydos, went with him to Athens. When they were seized, along with Dionysius and Christina, they were ordered to be kept in prison. But instructed by the holy Christina, they abandoned the ancestral error of the idols and came to Christ. Since they were known to be Christians, they were first subjected to many torments because they would not sacrifice to the unclean demons, and were later stoned to death. The holy Christina threw herself upon them and, having wept, gave her sacred head to be cut off.
The contest of the holy martyrs Simeon, Isaacius, and Bachthisoes.
Simeon, Isaacius, and Bachthisoes, martyrs of Christ, were from the region of Persia in the time of the impious Sapor. Being Christians, they were seized by the fire-worshippers and handed over to Sapor; they were forced to deny Christ and to sacrifice to the sun and fire. They answered, saying: "We do not deny Christ, since He is the true God and Creator of all creatures; but we turn away from the sun and the fire, as they are His creatures." By this they stirred the tyrant to anger. For this reason, they were bound by their hands and feet to four posts and were cruelly beaten. Afterward, they were thrown into prison and consumed no food for seven days. Brought out from the prison after this, and having endured various torments, they finally and willingly offered their precious and sacred heads to be cut off, and were thus perfected.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The sixteenth day.
The contest of the holy martyrs Abdas and Abdiesus, bishops, and those with them.
The holy Abdiesus, who was a bishop in Persia, having been denounced to the king of the Persians by his own nephew, who was a deacon, was seized together with thirty-nine other Christians and brought before him. When interrogated, he confessed Christ. He was then sent to the brother of the king, so that he might be punished by him. But he confuted and astonished even him with his divinely-wise words. For this reason, he was bound with cords and squeezed between pieces of wood, and his bones were broken. Then he was thrown into prison as one dead, tasting no food for many days. After this, Abdas the bishop was also seized, with twenty-eight men—presbyters, and deacons, and holy virgins, and women—and they were shut up in the prison, where they were instructed by the bishop
Finally, after a few days, they were taken out of the prison and all were beheaded.
The memory of our holy Father George, bishop of Mitylene.
Our holy Father George, having loved God from his childhood and hated the world, retreated into a certain monastery to become a monk, and by the loftiness of his humble spirit he cast down the pride of the demons. Since he was merciful beyond measure, he generously gave his own bread to the poor daily. When his virtue became widely known, he was ordained bishop of Mitylene through the earnest prayers of the people. Having taken charge of the church, he governed it well; being an opponent of every heresy and a champion of orthodoxy, he freed it from errors by refuting the mistakes of the heterodox and defending orthodox doctrine. Foreknowing his own passing, he died and was buried, having ensured that his own tomb would spring forth with healings and emit the graces of all kinds of miracles, by which all the ailments of those who approach him with faith are healed.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The seventeenth day. The memory of the holy apostle Andronicus, one of the Seventy, and Junia.
Andronicus, the apostle of Christ, having traveled over the whole world as if he had wings by which he was carried, and preaching Christ, uprooted every error from its foundations; he planted all piety and knowledge of God, having with him as a partner and assistant in the divine preaching the admirable Junia, who was dead to the world and the flesh, and who lived and served Christ alone. Wherefore, drawing many of the unbelievers to the knowledge of God and bringing them to Christ, and making them sons of light and day through divine baptism, they destroyed the shrines of idols and built churches for Christ everywhere. Of these saints the great apostle Paul, the luminary of the world, makes mention in his Epistles, saying, "Salute Andronicus and Junia." When, therefore, they had cast out unclean spirits from men and healed incurable diseases, they migrated to the Lord.
And the martyrdom of the holy martyr Solochon and those with him.
The martyr of Christ, Solochon, lived during the reign of Maximian; he was an Egyptian by birth, a soldier by profession, enlisted in the order commanded by the tribune of the region, along with three thousand other soldiers. When, because of a certain matter, he had come to Chalcedon with the tribune by the emperor's command, the same emperor commanded the commanders that they, and each with their own soldiers, should sacrifice to the idols, and that each with their own ranks should offer victims according to custom; and similarly the tribune and those who were with him. But while everyone was offering sacrifices, three only resisted the will of the emperor, professing themselves to be Christians: Solochon and two other
soldiers. And they were beaten to such an extent that their loins swelled and their heads became unnaturally enlarged. 104 Now the two of them died while being scourged; but Solochon lived for a little while longer. Then the tribune, made excessively angry, took a sharpened reed and drove it into his ear, and by this means killed him.
And the memory of Stephen, patriarch of Constantinople.
This man was the son of the illustrious Basil, emperor of the Romans; but because of his high-minded character, his religious prudence, and his moderation of spirit, along with the loftiness of his virtue, while he was still a youth, by the vote of the emperor, the holy synod, and the entire clergy and people—and what is more important to say, by the good pleasure and judgment of God—he was ordained patriarch of Constantinople. Being installed upon the great and holy throne, and having undertaken the care of the great flock, he applied his soul to the governance of the Churches of God. In this office he proved to be a most vigilant guardian and a true shepherd, leading his sheep to the pastures of the orthodox faith, showing mercy to the poor, defending widows and orphans, and rescuing others who were oppressed by injuries from the hands of the unjust. Since he conducted himself in this way, and macerated his flesh with temperance, he departed to Christ in the very flower of his age.
OF THE SAME MONTH.
The eighteenth day.
The contest of the holy martyr Theodotus and his companions.
Theodotus, martyr of Christ, with eight holy virgins—Tecusa, Alexandra, Claudia, Phaina, Euphrasia, Matrona, Julia, and Theodota—were from the city of Ancyra in Galatia. Since the governor of the city had ordered food prepared for Christians to be sprinkled with offerings to the idols so that those who ate of it might be defiled, he himself, under the guise of trade, bought wheat and made bread, which he then distributed to the needy Christians. But he also entered the prisons, confirming the faithful; among whom were the holy virgins, one of whom, named Tecusa, was his aunt. These were bound with stones 105 and drowned in a lake situated near the city. But when Theodotus had collected their remains, he buried them. Being subsequently discovered and seized, he was first subjected to torments, and finally put to death by the sword.
OF THE SAME MONTH.
The nineteenth day.
The contest of the holy hieromartyr Patricius, bishop of Prusa, and his companions.
Our holy Father Patricius was bishop of the city of Prusa. When he came to those who approached him to be taught the faith of Christ, he was seized and brought before the governor of Bithynia: at which point, upon being interrogated, he freely confessed Christ. But when the governor said that gods ought to be honored—Zeus, and Apollo, and Dionysius, and the others, who are
whose providence causes the hot waters to spring forth for the benefit of mankind—the saint answered that the hot waters spring forth by the power of Christ, and not of the idols, which are inanimate wood and senseless stones. For this reason, he was forcibly thrown into the very boiling hot waters, but came out unharmed, while all the executioners were burned to death. And after having been tortured in various ways previously, he finally received his end by the sword, together with Acacius, Menander, and Polyanus, his disciples.
And the contest of the holy martyr Colluthus.
The martyr of Christ, Colluthus, lived during the reign of Maximian, and was from a city of the Thebaid in Egypt. Because of his confession of Christ, he was seized by those who worshipped the idols and handed over to the governor of the region; and having been neither enticed by flatteries nor terrified by threats, he freely confessed Christ. For this reason, he was first suspended head-downward with a great stone tied to his neck. And while being whipped by the executioners, he said: "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us." Afterwards, being taken down from the wood upon which he had been suspended, he was compelled to go into the temple of the idols and offer sacrifice. And because he refused to do this, he received sentence to be committed to the flames; and having been thrown into a furnace that was intensely heated, he had the end of his temporal life.
And the contest of the holy martyr Philetærus and those with him.
Philetærus, the martyr of Christ, was born and bred in the city of the Nicomedians, the son of Tatianus the ex-prefect, a man of tall stature, handsome, white as snow, having the hair of his head and beard glistening like gold. Being a Christian, he was seized by the infidels and brought before the impious emperor Diocletian; and having reproved him for the evil things he was doing, and called him an enemy of Christ, he was severely beaten. And having been thrown into a furnace of fire, he came out unharmed, whereat Diocletian was amazed and released him. But after the death of Diocletian, when Maximian, his son-in-law, had taken over the empire, the saint was again seized; and having been punished in many ways, he then performed miracles and caused many to believe in Christ, and to be perfected, some by the sword and others by fire. Similarly, the martyr Cyriaca was consumed by fire, and the count who guarded them was finally beheaded together with the saint.
IN THE SAME MONTH.
The twentieth day.
The contest of the holy martyr Thalelæus and those with him.
Thalelæus, the martyr of Christ, lived in the reign of the emperor Numerian and was a physician by profession. Having been seized in the city of Anazarbus in Cilicia, he was brought to Theodore
the governor, who ordered the executioners to bore through his ankles and to hang him head downwards. And when the executioners attempted to do this, being struck with madness by divine power, they bored through and hung up a piece of the wood that lay nearby instead of the saint, and believing that they were mocking the governor, they were beaten. From these, Alexander and Asterius, having seen the miracle, believed in Christ and were beheaded. Moreover, the governor desiring with his own hands to bore through the holy ankles, was unable to rise from his throne, his backside having become stuck to the throne, and his hands having withered. Again, many believed in the Lord. Then, through the prayers of the saint, the governor was healed, and rising from the throne, he beheaded him.
And the contest of the holy martyr Ascalon.
This man was from the region of the Thebaid in Egypt; and having been seized on account of his faith in Christ, he was brought in bonds to the governor Arianus. By whom, upon being interrogated, as he freely professed Christ, he was hung upon the rack and his sides were torn with iron claws. Then, having been thrust into prison as if dead, when he saw the governor crossing the river in a boat, he prayed that he might not reach the land before he confessed in writing the divinity of Christ. Then, indeed, the governor was detained in the river and could not cross it. To whom the saint said: "It shall not be permitted to you to leave this place unless you confess in writing that Christ is God." And so, receiving the paper, the governor wrote that the God of the Christians is great, and that there is no other existing besides Him. Which being done, he immediately left, and ordered the saint to be brought before him, and to be hung, and his sides to be burned with fiery torches; finally, having been bound to a stone, he was cast into the river, where he received the end of his martyrdom.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The twenty-first day.
Memory of the most pious and great emperors Constantine and Helena.
Constantine the Great, and the first of the Christian emperors, was the son of Constantius, the Roman Caesar, and of Helena; of Constantius, I say, who was surnamed Chlorus, and who alone among the other emperors used to invoke the providence from above, and refrain from idols. Therefore, seeing the Christians subjected to torments, he felt compassion, and taught his son to implore in wars the help of the divine providence, and not that of idols. Hence, after the death of his father, while invoking the supernal providence, he saw in heaven the venerable cross, and heard a voice saying to him: "Constantine, in this conquer"; and he cast down the enemy. Thereafter, having obtained the empire, he indeed overturned idols; but he raised up churches, and founded cities; and he discovered the cross of Christ through his mother Helena. And when he had done many things rightly, he departed to the Lord.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-SECOND DAY.
Certamen of the holy martyr Basiliscus.
Basiliscus, the martyr of Christ, lived during the reign of Maximian; he was from the region of the Armenians, and was a nephew of the holy great martyr Theodore. Having previously contended alongside the holy Eutropius and Cleonicus, who were soldiers of the holy Theodore, when they were perfected for Christ’s sake, he was left behind in prison. Beseeching God that he might complete the course of his witness, he was urged by Him to join his kinsmen, as he was destined to undergo martyrdom in Comana. Having therefore taken leave of his own people, he was seized by the governor Agrippa and led as a prisoner to Comana. And working miracles along the way, he persuaded many to believe in Christ. Upon arriving at Comana, and having prayed, he brought down fire from heaven, which burned the temple of Apollo and the idol. Because of this, he was beheaded and thrown into the river. Later, his relics were recovered and deposited in Comana.
And the memory of the holy apostle Jude.
Jude, the divine apostle, after the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, having taken up a divine zeal, traveled through every city and region, preaching Christ with a loud voice and His resurrection from the dead, announcing Him to all, and demonstrating Him to be the judge of the living and the dead. He explained how, for our salvation, being the Word and Son of God the Father, He emptied Himself, came down to earth, and becoming incarnate of the Holy Spirit and the ever-virgin Mary, became man, taking on the whole of Adam except for sin. He was tempted, treated with contumely, reviled, slapped by the hand which He Himself had formed, was cast out, and finally nailed to the cross, was buried, and rose again, appeared to the apostles, ascended, and sits at the right hand of the Father in the heavens, and is coming again to judge the living and the dead. Having taught these things, and baptized many of the unbelievers, he departed in peace to the Lord.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-THIRD DAY.
Memory of our holy Father Simeon on the Wondrous Mountain.
Our holy Father Simeon was from Antioch in Syria, and he flourished in the reign of Justinian the Elder. He was conceived according to a promise, for the Forerunner and Baptist had announced this to his mother. When he was born, while he was suckling, he refused the left breast, God thus indicating that he would love the right path of the commandments. When he had grown and left the world behind, he took to the mountain; and going to a monastery where he strove beyond human endurance, he became a monk. He shone forth in virtue to such a degree that he even performed stupendous miracles. Thereafter, descending from the mountain, he ascended upon a pillar, having stood upon it
for eighteen years. And having arrived at the wondrous mountain, he ascended a rock and endured there for ten years. Then, having ascended a small pillar, he continued for forty-five years, so that the time of his life was eighty-five years; of which he spent seventy-nine in the ascetic life, and departed to God.
And the memorial of our holy father and confessor Michael, bishop of Synnada.
Our holy father and confessor of Christ, Michael, was a pious monk and one who feared God; and because of his virtuous manner of life, he was consecrated bishop of Synnada in the times of the Iconoclast emperor Leo. But because he continued struggling for the orthodox faith, teaching the Lord’s people things pertaining to salvation, and striking the heretics with his words as with arrows and driving them from his flock, he stirred the apostate emperor to anger. Being summoned, therefore, by him, he was compelled to renounce the veneration of the all-venerable icons. And when he steadfastly refused to do this, he was subjected to most harsh exiles: where, having endured very many tribulations for the sake of the truth and the upright dogmas, and having persevered immutable until the end, he received the end of this life rejoicing, adorned with a double crown, namely, that of the priesthood and of confession.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The twenty-fourth day.
The contest of the holy martyr Meletius the general and his companions, one thousand two hundred and fifty.
Meletius, the martyr of Christ, was a general in the time of the emperor Antoninus, from the region of lower Galatia. Being a Christian, he prayed that God would utterly destroy the error of the idols. But the demons, knowing their own ruin, entered into dogs and lamented their own destruction, the dogs wandering about, howling, and filling the people with terror; whom holy Meletius, together with the soldiers under him, destroyed by the sword; and furthermore, demolishing the temples of the heathens, he shattered the idols that were in them. Wherefore, having been apprehended by Maximus the governor, together with the counts who were with him, he was compelled to sacrifice to the idols. But when he would not even listen to such a thing, he and his counts were beaten with iron balls. Then the holy Meletius, having been suspended on a pine tree and fastened with nails, was brought to his end; but Stephanus and Joannes the counts were beheaded.
And the contest of the holy martyr Sarapion and his companions.
Sarapion, the martyr of Christ, was by birth an Egyptian; but at the time when the holy Meletius was undergoing his contest, having arrived from Egypt and seeing him and those with him being crowned by martyrdom, he believed in Christ. And having been apprehended shortly thereafter, he was cast into prison: where
he was ordained bishop by a divine angel, that he might baptize those who were still unilluminated, but who were to suffer martyrdom for Christ on that day. For the kinsmen of holy Meletius, and of the counts, and of the soldiers, along with the women and children, gathering together, said with a loud voice: "We too are Christians." Then, having provoked the governor to anger, the bishop Sarapion, along with Callinicus the magician who had turned to the faith, was beheaded; but Theodorus and Faustus, along with the men who had believed, were committed to the flames and met their end; and the remaining multitude, cut down by wood [clubs], perished.
OF THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-FIFTH DAY.
The Contest of the holy martyr Therapon.
We do not know whence Christ’s holy martyr Therapon originated, or of what parents he was born, or in what times he lived, as his records, it seems, have perished with the lapse of time. This alone, however, we have learned: that he became a monk and bishop of Cyprus, and that he finished the athletic contest and was brought to Christ through blood, having been fully assured of this not only from the unwritten tradition of our forefathers, but also from his icons. And this pertains to what happened earlier. Later, however, when the Saracens intended to attack Cyprus, the saint appeared to his sacristan and said to him: "Arise quickly, and taking my relics, transport them to Constantinople. For the enemies of the cross of Christ are about to land on this island and will lay these places waste." His relics were therefore transported and deposited in Constantinople, where they pour forth healings.
And the memorial of our holy Father and confessor John the Psychaitee.
John, our Father among the saints, having loved Christ from infancy and imitated the ways of Elias and John the Forerunner, abandoned the world; and going away to the laura of Psychaita, he became a monk; and he gave himself over to such austerity that he received from God the gift of driving out demons and curing diseases. But as he struggled during the time of the iconoclasts and championed the orthodox doctrines, he was reported to the one exercising tyranny, and being summoned, he was compelled to renounce [the faith] and to sign the tome of impiety. But, refusing to do this, and instead rebuking the emperor and calling him a heretic, he was exiled. There, having endured many tribulations from the lawless and unjust iconoclasts, he changed his life [for death].
And the contest of the holy holy-martyr Therapon.
Therapon, the holy martyr of Christ, being a priest—
of the holy church in Sardis, and because through his teaching he converted many of the unbelievers to our Lord Jesus Christ and baptized them, he was seized by the governor Valerian, bound, and thrown into prison. Being brought out from there, he was taken bound to Synaus, and near the river he was stretched out supine upon the pavement, fastened to four stakes, and beaten so severely that his flesh was lacerated by the rods. The earth, irrigated by his blood, produced a very large oak plant, which is seen to this day evergreen, healing every disease and every infirmity of those who approach it. After this, he was led away into the Thracesian Theme, near the river Hermus, in the bishopric of Satalos; and having been subjected to many torments and afflictions, he finally received the crown of martyrdom.
And the contest of the holy martyr Pancharius.
Pancharius, a martyr of Christ, was born and raised in ancient Rome, and had faithful parents. But when he was honored with temporal rank by the idolatrous emperors and was familiar to them, he turned aside from the straight path through the operation of the devil, denied Christ, and joined himself to the idols. Wherefore, being accepted by the idolatrous emperors, he lived his life in great honor. When his mother understood this, weeping much, she signified to him by letter that he should withdraw from the worship of idols and return to Christ, recalling to his memory the punishments, the Gehenna, and the prison prepared for those who had denied Christ. But he, having received the letters and being stung in his soul, returned to the religion: when this was known, the emperor ordered him to be beheaded.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The twenty-sixth day.
Memory of the holy apostle Carpus, one of the seventy.
He was counted among the seventy disciples and apostles by Christ Himself; and serving the great Paul in his preaching, and carrying his divine epistles to those to whom he was sending them, he brought many of the Gentiles to the faith of Christ. And having his mind illuminated by the brightness of the Paraclete, like an inaccessible star rising from the East, he illuminated the whole world with his divine teachings, performing great miracles daily and casting out most wicked spirits, and bringing cities and peoples to the faith of Christ. Consequently, he suffered many afflictions from the unbelievers. But with a manly spirit, taking up the laborious contest of martyrdom, he did not fear the angry temper of the princes. Wherefore, since he had glorified God in his members, he was gloriously glorified by Him: and departing in peace, he delivered his spirit into the hands of God.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-SEVENTH DAY.
Contest of the holy martyrs Theodora and Didymus.
St. Theodora flourished in the times of Diocletian. When, having been brought before the prefect of Alexandria, she confessed Christ, she was cast into a brothel; but having poured forth prayers to God, she preserved herself incorrupt. For a certain Christian, Didymus by name, moved by God, entered into her presence in military attire. She, however, struck with fear, fled into a corner of the house. But Didymus, bidding her to be of good courage—being assured that she would suffer nothing of what she feared—clothed her in his military garment and commanded her to go out from the house; while he himself, putting on her female garment and covering his head with a veil, remained in her place. But when a certain profligate entered, and realizing that the person in the female guise was a man, he reported the whole matter to the prefect. Wherefore, the saint was immediately apprehended and beheaded. After this, St. Theodora was also seized, and when her head had been severed by the sword, her body was cast into the fire.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-EIGHTH DAY.
Contest of the holy martyr Heliconis.
Heliconis, the martyr of Christ, lived under the emperors Gordian and Philip, hailing from the city of Thessalonica. Being apprehended and brought before the duke of Corinth, and having confessed Christ, she was first bound by her feet to an ox-yoke, and her heels were lacerated; then, being shorn of her hair, she suffered fire over her whole body. Yet, preserved unharmed, she entered the temple of the idols, and by prayer she overturned the images of the gods. After this, her breasts were cut off. And when Justin the proconsul had succeeded to the place of the duke, the holy martyr was brought to him and cast into a burning furnace. But as the flames did not touch her—but rather consumed seventy men of the soldiers—she was stretched out upon a brazen bed heated by coals beneath. But the archangels Michael and Gabriel appeared and preserved her unharmed. Then, being thrown to the wild beasts, she suffered no harm from them, but one hundred and twenty men perished by their teeth. And then, having received the sentence of death by the sword at last, she was beheaded.
Contest of the holy hieromartyr Helladius.
Helladius, the holy martyr of Christ, having purified himself from his youth, was constituted bishop by the vote of God. And having been entrusted with the care of the Church, he governed it as an excellent shepherd. But because he had brought many of the Gentiles to Christ, he was seized and shut up in prison. And when the tyrants brought him forward in bonds, then his virtue shone forth the more and illuminated the souls of the faithful more brightly. For, pressing forward bravely into the contests, and speaking with all boldness for piety, and having openly confessed Christ, he was subjected to very many tortures. And as his body was shredded severely with scourges, Christ
appeared and healed him. After this, the tyrants, filled with rage, cast the saint into the fire. Remaining unharmed therein, he drew many to the faith of Christ. Finally, being most grievously beaten, he surrendered his spirit to God, having attained the immortal kingdom.
And the passion of the holy martyrs Crescens, Paul, and Dioscorides.
The martyrs of Christ, Crescens, Paul, and Dioscorides, residing in the city of Rome, and by their teaching bringing many of the infidels to Christ and enlightening them day by day, were denounced to the prefect of the city and, by his order, were seized and thrust into prison, receiving a command to teach no one in the name of Christ. But when they did not cease to teach those who were bound with them—many of whom believed—even in the prison, they were led out of the prison and beaten cruelly, having first been compelled to deny Christ and then to enter the temple of Jupiter and sacrifice to the idols that were therein. But when they refused to do this, and instead proclaimed Christ to all with a loud voice, they were cast into a great furnace of burning fire, and there, like the three holy children of old, glorifying God, they fulfilled their martyrdom.
ON THE SAME MONTH, The twenty-ninth day. Memory of the holy Fathers who first gathered at Nicaea against Arius.
After the most holy Peter, patriarch of Alexandria, Achillas was ordained, and after him, Alexander. In his times, a certain presbyter of the Church named Arius, to whom the exposition of the divine Scriptures had been entrusted, when he saw that Alexander had been preferred to the patriarchate according to the constitution of Saint Peter, was moved by envy. C Since he could not construct calumnies against him, he armed his tongue against the orthodox faith, vomiting forth blasphemies against the Son of God, and saying that He was a creature and not consubstantial with the Father. Wherefore, being cast out from the Church and holding conventicles, he rent the Church. When Constantine the Great learned of this, having convoked the holy synod at Nicaea, he condemned Arius and relegated him into exile; but he embraced the holy bishops kindly and dismissed each to his own lands.
And the passion of the holy virgin martyr Theodosia.
Theodosia, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Tyre. When she was eighteen years old, having been denounced as a Christian and seized by the idolaters, she was led in bonds and brought before the governor Urbanus; having been interrogated by him, she professed Christ. And when she was compelled to deny Him and to sacrifice to the idols, and would not do so, she was beaten most savagely with raw thongs upon her breasts and flanks, and her bones were crushed; and she was so torn that her entrails appeared. Thus bruised by scourges, she bore her torments in silence. When
she had recovered her breath a little, she was asked by the governor whether she was willing to sacrifice to the gods. But she, opening her mouth and fixing her eyes intently upon him, answered with a smile on her face: "You are mistaken, O man; do you not know that I have been accounted worthy of the fellowship of the martyrs of Christ?" Then the governor, becoming enraged, cast her into the sea, where she received her blessed end.
And the contest of the holy martyr Olbianus, bishop of the Aneorum. Olbianus, the holy martyr of Christ, lived during the reign of Maximian, and was bishop of the Church of the Aneorum. Being seized by the governor Julius, he was delivered to prison, with the instruction received that he should not teach in the name of Christ. But he, preaching Christ all the more freely, proclaimed what concerned Him to everyone, constantly and without fear. For this reason, he was cast out of prison, stripped of his garments, and beaten severely; and with red-hot awls he was pierced in his belly, sides, and entrails, and was again cast into prison as if dead. But being cured by the appearing of Christ to him, he was brought again to the governor for a second examination. And when the governor—having changed his mind—entreated him to sacrifice to the idols, he again confessed Christ. Then, being cast into a great furnace, he was brought to perfection.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The thirtieth day.
Memory of our holy Father Isaacius, the confessor.
Our holy Father Isaacius, coming from the regions of the East, arrived in Constantinople in the reign of Valens the heretic, and there lived a tranquil life in a monastery. And when the same emperor was moving his entire army against the Goths, Isaacius met him and said: "O Emperor, open the churches to the orthodox if you wish to return alive from the war." But the emperor, becoming enraged, ordered the holy man to be beaten and shut up in prison until he should return. Then the holy man said: "If you do return, then God has not spoken by me; but you shall flee from the face of your enemies, and by fire you shall have the end of your life." And this came to pass. For having turned to flight and hidden himself in a straw storehouse, he was burned within it, the Goths casting fire upon it. With this prophecy, therefore, and many other glorious deeds, the saint was made illustrious and fell asleep in peace.
And the contest of the holy martyrs Eusebius, Romanus, Mentius, Charalampus, and Christina, and of the multitude of the holy ones who suffered martyrdom in Nicomedia.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The thirty-first day.
Contest of the holy martyr Hermias.
Hermias, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Comana, serving as a soldier in the reign of Antoninus, being already advanced in age and having gray hair.
But having been seized for his confession of Christ, he is brought before Sebastian the Duke, and is compelled by him to sacrifice to the idols. But when he refused to do so, he is beaten upon his cheeks with stones; then his facial skin is flayed, and his teeth are pulled out. Soon, thrown into a burning furnace and having emerged from it without any harm, he is ordered to eat poisoned food. But having consumed this also without any damage, he caused the man who had prepared it to believe in Christ, and to be beheaded for His sake. Then all the nerves of his body are stretched, and having been thrown into a boiling cauldron, he emerged unharmed. Then, having had his eyes gouged out and having been hung upside down, he was finally beheaded.
MONTH OF JUNE
The first day
Contest of the holy martyr Justin the philosopher.
Justin, the most wise martyr of Christ, was from Neapolis in Syria, a man who was a philosopher and possessed of great clarity of mind. Loving Christ, and turning away from those who hated Him, he was inflamed with divine zeal every day. For this reason, having gone to Rome during the reign of Antoninus, when he had written a book against the error of the idols and in favor of the faith of the Christians, he presented it to the emperor. The emperor, having admired his wisdom and knowledge, not only did not kill him, but rather commended him. But because in his dissertations to the idolaters he showed the worship of idols to be deceptive, and confirmed the religion of the Christians with written arguments, he incurred the envy of the philosopher Crescens, and, being hated by him, was sought out by treachery until he was destroyed by him.
Contest of the holy martyr Justin and his companions.
These saints also were staying in Rome, teaching in the name of Christ. Having been seized by the prefect of the city, they were cast into prison, and after several days, having been led out from there, they were brought before him. The prefect, after many and various interrogations, asked Justin thus: "Tell me, Justin," he said, "if you are beaten with lashes and decapitated, are you completely certain that you are going to ascend to heaven?" Justin said: "I hope to inherit the kingdom of heaven, if I willingly endure these torments." To this the prefect: "Do you therefore think that you are to ascend to heaven, and there receive a retribution of certain good things?" Justin said: "I do not merely think so, but I hold it with the most certain persuasion." Then, by order of the prefect, along with his holy companions, he was beheaded.
THE SAME MONTH
The second day
Memory of our holy Father and confessor Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople.
The divine pontiff Nicephorus was from Constantinople
born and bred in the time of the impious Constantine, and had for parents Theodorus and Eudocia. Since Theodorus was a scribe of imperial mandates, he was accused of being a worshipper of divine images, was beaten, and was soon deported into exile to Mylasa, where he died. His son, Nicephorus, being also a scribe, having renounced his dignity, wealth, and glory, made for the city on the Propontis; where, devoting himself to God and to his own soul, he attained great virtue. After the death of the most blessed patriarch Tarasius, he was appointed patriarch of Constantinople by the emperor Nicephorus, father of Stauracius. And he lasted until the reign of Leo the Iconoclast, by whom he was also exiled and cast into prison, departing to the Lord at the age of seventy; of which years he spent nine in the high priesthood, and thirteen in exile.
THE SAME MONTH. The third day.
The contest of the holy martyr Lucillianus and his companions.
Lucillianus, the martyr of Christ, lived during the reign of Aurelian; he had formerly been a priest of the idols in the city of Nicomedia, now advanced in age. Having been converted to the faith in Christ, he was seized and handed over to the count Silvanus; and, not being persuaded to deny Christ, his face was crushed with stones, and after being beaten with rods, he was hung up by his head on a beam. Then, being cast into prison, he found there four children detained for the sake of the faith in Christ—Claudius, Hypatius, Paul, and Dionysius—and, filled with joy, he confirmed them in the faith. And together with them he was brought again before the count, and not being persuaded to deny Christ, he was thrown into a furnace of fire. And having emerged unharmed, he was led bound with the children to Byzantium. The children were beheaded; but he himself was fixed to a cross and finished his life.
And the contest of the holy martyr Paula the virgin.
The martyr of Christ, Paula, being present at the contest and struggles of the holy Lucillianus and the children, both in the prison and along the way, wiped away their blood and the sores of their wounds with a sponge, healing the bodies of the saints to the best of her ability; for she was born of Christian and faithful parents. And this was her work: to visit those in prisons and to heal and nourish those who were suffering martyrdom for Christ. On account of this, therefore, she was seized and brought before the count Silvanus. And not being persuaded to sacrifice to idols, she was beaten severely and, her body torn to pieces by the blows of rods, she recovered her health through the assistance of an angel. And having been brought again before the count, she was cast into a furnace of fire. And having emerged unharmed, she too was sent to Byzantium, and was beheaded in the same place where also the holy Lucillianus was.
OF THE SAME MONTH. Fourth Day. Memorial of our holy Father Metrophanes, Patriarch of Constantinople.
Our holy Father Metrophanes lived in the time of the great Constantine, and was bishop of Byzantium, a kinsman of the Emperor Probus. When the Great Constantine had enlarged the buildings of Byzantium and, having changed its name, had called it Constantinople, he was promoted to the patriarchal dignity, holding the place second to that of Rome. When the first synod was gathered at Nicaea, the patriarch, because of his old age and illness, being deficient in strength, designated the first presbyter, Alexander—whom he had also named his successor—to act in his stead in the conduct of the council. After the Emperor and the holy synod had returned, when he had designated by vote Alexander as the first and Paul the confessor as the second successor to himself, and had prayed for good things for the Emperor and the synod, he rested; his relics were deposited in his own church.
OF THE SAME MONTH. Fifth Day. Struggle of the holy martyrs Marcian, Nicander, and their companions.
Marcian and Nicander, martyrs of Christ, together with their companions, were born in Egypt. Having been seized by the prefect on account of their confession of Christ, and being compelled by force to deny Christ and to worship idols, and refusing to do so, they were first received with cruel lashes: presently their sides were scorched with lamps; then they were suspended and lacerated with iron hooks until their flesh fell to the ground. Afterward, half-dead, they were thrust into prison. An angel of God appearing to them, they were healed; and so, after many days, they came out of prison whole and unharmed. But having been led to the tribunal of the prefect, because they had converted many of the unbelievers to the Lord on account of this miracle, they were again cast into prison, where they surrendered their souls to God.
OF THE SAME MONTH. Sixth Day. Struggle of the holy martyr women Cyria, Valeria, and Marcia.
Cyria, a martyr of Christ, and Valeria, and Marcia, hailing from the city of Caesarea in Palestine, having been taught by a certain Christian, renounced idols and impure sacrifices, approached Christ, and were baptized. Then indeed they lived a quiet life at home, persevering in much piety, in virtue, in fasting, in prayer, and in vigil. And they implored God that the imposture of idols being utterly extirpated, the Christian faith might shine throughout the whole world, and the persecution against the saints might cease. While they were doing these things, they were denounced by the idolaters to the prefect of the region and were compelled by him to deny Christ and to worship idols:
and not consenting to do these things, they were tortured, and being scourged, they were brought to their end in these very punishments.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE SEVENTH DAY.
The contest and translation of the relics of the holy martyr Theodotus.
Theodotus, the martyr of Christ, was from the region of Galatia, from the village of Malos. While he was burying the relics of the holy martyrs, he was denounced to the prefect of Ancyra, and having been seized, he was imprisoned. Then, being brought to interrogation, he strongly opposed the prefect, and mocked the gods of the Greeks, and called those who worshipped them foolish and wretched.
