Then, being severely beaten, he was hung upon a tree, and his sides were scorched with torches, and his flesh was torn. And after this, having received the sentence to be beheaded by the sword, he prayed, and thus his head was cut off. A certain presbyter, Phronto by name, seeing his relics being guarded by soldiers, went to them and treated them with wine, and when they had fallen asleep, he took the relics, and having placed them upon his mule, he carried them away and buried them in his own village, where they pour forth healings to this day.
And the contest of the holy martyrs Nicander and Marcian.
Nicander and Marcian, the martyrs of Christ, were soldiers by rank, but pious Christians who feared God. While serving under the prefect Maximus, since they were sent by him, together with the soldiers under them, to capture Christians and lead them to him, they would urge some to flee; others they would indeed capture, but, sparing them, they took care of their needs in every way. When the prefect learned this from the idolaters, he was grieved; and having called them to himself, he inquired whether what he had heard about them was true. They, not knowing how to lie, not only affirmed that what they were asked about was true, but also confessed with boldness that they were Christians. Wherefore, having first been subjected to many tortures, they were afterwards beheaded of their precious and sacred heads.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE EIGHTH DAY.
The translation of the relics of the holy martyr Theodore the Stratelates.
Theodore, the martyr of Christ, lived during the reign of Licinius. Born of noble parents in the city of Euchaita, he was educated by them in the faith, and having grown up to be a brave man, he followed a military life and was soon appointed general (stratelates) of Pontic Heraclea. He was also very fair of face and wise in knowledge. When Licinius learned this and desired to see him, he summoned him to come to him, in order to sacrifice with him to the gods. But he sent a message back to him: "It is rather for you, Emperor, to come here, so that the..."
your command. Persuaded by these words, the emperor departed quickly. But the martyr, meeting him as befitted the emperor, followed him with honor. But then Licinius said, "Come, Theodore, let us sacrifice to the gods." He replied, "Order them to be first delivered to me, that I may take them home and worship them there, and then at last I will sacrifice to them." Having received the silver-wrought images of the gods, he smashed them, and gave them to the poor; and upon this being known, he was punished, and thereafter beheaded. His relics were translated from there and deposited in Euchaia, near Euchaita.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The ninth day.
The Contest of the Holy Martyr Pelagia of Antioch
She, having been accused before the prefect and fearing for her virginity, prayed to God; and having modestly covered herself, she climbed to the top of the house where she was being detained by the order of the prefect, and casting herself from it, she rendered her soul to God. The venerable John Chrysostom honored her with encomia, both for her undefiled chastity and for the excellence of her exercises in virtue.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The tenth day.
The Contest of the Holy Martyrs Alexander and Antonina
These were from the village of Cardamus. The holy Antonina was leading a respectful and holy life, when she was arrested by Festus; and not wishing to deny Christ or worship demons, she was condemned to a brothel. But when she had remained fasting for three days, a light shone in the night, and there was thunder, by which the doors of the prison were shattered, and a voice came from heaven to her, saying, "Arise, and take food." When therefore she had prayed and eaten, she was again brought before the prefect, by whose order, because she could not be induced to sacrifice to idols, she was trampled underfoot and beaten with palm rods; and she was cast again into the brothel. Alexander, revealed by an angel, entered (for it was thought he did this to satisfy his lust, as he was a youth of about twenty-eight years of age), and having wrapped the head of the holy woman in his cloak, he led her out of the brothel; and he himself remained in her place. A little later, when soldiers had approached to shame the holy woman, the matter was revealed. Alexander was therefore led before the prefect, and he was first beaten with palm rods; afterwards, when he and the holy woman had been seized, both had the extremities of their feet and hands cut off. Finally, they were cast into a pit of fire, having had their whole bodies smeared with melted pitch; and thus they received a blessed end. Their festival is celebrated in the monastery of Maximinus, situated in Constantinople, where their relics were deposited, from which the healings of many diseases flow forth.
And the contest of the holy martyr Timothy, bishop of Prusa. He lived under Julian the Apostate, guiding the church allotted to him well, and feeding the people within it with spiritual nourishment. Excelling in various miracles, by the application of the veil which covered the consecrated loaves, he burst asunder and killed the great dragon which, through the malice of the man-slaying, ancient dragon who dwelt in that place, was killing passersby, and even destroying beasts just with its breath, and which had rendered the road between the city of Prusa and the Hot Springs impassable and unreachable. He was beheaded by the order of Julian the Apostate, who, having heard of the wonders he performed, sent men to kill him. His service is celebrated in his most holy martyrdom, which is inside the pious hospital in the Deutero.
And the memory of our holy Father Canis. He flourished under the reign of Theodosius the Great, born of Theodotus, his father, and Theophane, his mother, who were pious and God-loving people dwelling in the region of the Cappadocians. It is said of his mother that she abstained from all rich food while she carried him in her womb, and that, when born, the infant would always abstain from the left breast. If the mother ever ate more delicate food, he would not touch even the right breast. So, having been baptized and weaned, and passed the first stage of childhood, he bade farewell to all and took to the mountain. Having entered a small cave, he shut himself therein, dedicating himself to prayer and fasting, and once a week he tasted a very small amount of raw vegetables without salt, and he continued thus for seventy-three years. Because the place was very prone to flooding, and the cave was besieged by much moisture, the hair of his head and his beard fell out. Having lived thus for very many years, the blessed man departed to the Lord.
IN THE SAME MONTH, THE FOURTEENTH.
The contest of the holy apostles Bartholomew and Barnabas.
Of these, the holy Bartholomew was one of the twelve disciples; having preached the Gospel to the Indians called the Happy, and having delivered to them the Gospel according to Matthew, he was crucified and finished his life gloriously in Abarnopolis. His body, placed in a leaden coffin, was cast into the sea; but by divine providence, it was carried as far as Sicily to the island of Lipari and, having appeared there, it was buried. From his holy and precious coffin, sources of many miracles gush forth, and to all who faithfully pray to him, he gives speedy healing, and they return home with joy and gladness.
Barnabas, also called Joseph in the Acts of the Apostles, was one of the Seventy and was appointed a companion of Paul in his travels. His name
is interpreted "Son of consolation." He was of the tribe of Levi, and was born and educated on the island of Cyprus. He was the first to preach the Gospel of Christ in Jerusalem, Rome, and Alexandria. Having set out for Cyprus, he was stoned by the Jews and Greeks and delivered to the fire. His body was taken up by the Apostle and Evangelist Mark and deposited in a certain cave. Then, when he had sailed to Ephesus and come to Paul, he informed him of the death of Barnabas. Mark mourned for Barnabas for a very long time. It is said that he was buried together with the Gospel of Matthew which had been written by his own hand, which was found later along with the apostolic body; whence the faithful received the privilege that this island of theirs should be subjected to no other bishop, but should be ordained by its own bishop.
EODEM MENSE. Die duodecima.
Memoria sancti Patris nostri Onuphrii.
Our holy Father Onuphrius indeed drew his origin from the region of Egypt; but he spent his time in a coenobium located near Thermopolis in Thebes. But when he heard of the life of the prophets Elijah and John the Forerunner, he imitated them, left the coenobium, sought the desert, and lived there for sixty years, during which time he saw no human being at all; until a certain monk named Paphnutius, having progressed into the interior desert to seek a blessing from holy men, found him. And when they had sat down together, as Paphnutius wished to know what had occurred during that long interval, Onuphrius replied: "All of us who inhabit the desert feed on herbs, but we receive the holy Communion from an angel." And as Paphnutius was already contemplating his departure, Onuphrius added: "Stay, my son, yet today, since the end of my life is at hand, and commit me to the grave." And having said these things, he suddenly expired, and was buried in the rock, covered by half of the cloak of the same Paphnutius; for he was naked.
Et certamen sanctæ Antoninæ martyris.
The martyr of Christ, Antonina, became renowned in Nicæa under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. Being a Christian, she was seized by the governor, beaten with scourges, and cast into prison; afterwards, she was led out of prison, seized upon the rack, and her sides were torn. Soon she was placed upon burning coals; then her hands were pierced with glowing awls, from which she emitted a most sweet odor; finally, with her ankles pierced, she was again shut up in prison: where, cured by the visitation of Christ, she persevered in custody for two years, troubled by hunger, thirst, and other hardships. After this, extracted from custody and compelled to deny Christ, since she would by no means consent, she was thrown into a lake, where she joyfully received a blessed end.
EODEM MENSE. Die decima tertia.
Certamen sanctæ martyris Aquilinæ.
The martyr of Christ, Aquilina, was [martyred] in the reign of Trajan...
born in the city of Byblos in Phoenicia, the daughter of a certain Eutolmius, an illustrious man. At five years of age, she received baptism from Eutalius the bishop; and becoming ten years old, she taught her young companions to abstain from the worship of idols and led them by the hand to the faith in Christ. For this reason, having been denounced to the provincial governor by a certain idolater named Nicander, she was seized. And having been brought for questioning, she confessed the name of Christ before all, and was cruelly beaten; and her ears were so scorched with red-hot iron awls that blood flowed from her nostrils and smoke issued from her head. Then, having received the sentence of beheading by the sword, she departed to the Lord, whom she had longed for.
EODEM MENSE. Die decima quarta.
Commemoratio sancti prophetæ Elisæi.
The great and glorious prophet of God, Elisha, was from Judea, from the land of Reboim, born of his father Josaphat. Now, at the time of his birth, a great sign occurred. For the golden heifer set up in Silom lowed with such a loud voice that it was heard in Jerusalem, so that even the priest, moved by this monstrosity, said: "A great prophet is born today in Jerusalem, who shall destroy the graven images, and break in pieces the molten images, and will work great wonders." And this indeed came to pass; for he healed the sterile waters of Jericho by casting salt into them, and he raised the dead, and cleansed Naaman the Syrian, who was a leper, and struck with leprosy his own servant Giezi, who was greedy for money and disobedient; and having prophesied much concerning the coming of Christ, he died and was buried in Samaria, in the city of Sebaste.
And the commemoration of the holy hieromartyr Cyril, bishop of Crete.
The divine hieromartyr Cyril flourished in the reign of the emperor Maximian, adorned with every virtue, being the bishop of the holy church in Crete. Being ninety-five years of age, and having two servants, Theophanes and Theocharistus, he was going with them to one of the monasteries. And seeing on the way some idolaters sacrificing to idols, he groaned. And having been recognized as a Christian, he was seized by them and shut up in prison; and praying therein, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him: "Cyril, I have need of thy work in Rome." And the doors being opened, he went also to Rome. And having strengthened the brethren, he returned again to Crete. And having been seized by the ruler, he received the sentence of beheading by the sword. And having been placed upon a wagon, because he could not walk on account of his old age, and having been brought to the place of execution, he was beheaded.
And the commemoration of our holy Father Methodius, patriarch of Constantinople.
Our holy Father Methodius was from...
Sicily; having become a monk, and having attained every virtue through various exercises, he finally reached Constantinople. And because the persecution of the iconoclasts was growing, he settled there in a monastery constructed in a certain location of the mountain of the diocese of Chios. And because he undertook to overthrow the heresy of the iconoclasts with learned arguments and Scriptural passages, and to set forth the orthodox faith to the most holy churches of God, he endured many temptations and various afflictions. But when Theophilus the emperor departed this life, and the orthodox faith shone forth, he was summoned by Theodora the empress and her son Michael, according to the prediction of the holy Joannicius, and was ordained patriarch of Constantinople. And having held the episcopate for four years and three months, he passed away.
SAME MONTH.
Day the fifteenth.
The struggle of the holy martyr Dulas.
The martyr of Christ, Dulas, was a prefect of the region of Cilicia; but because he worshipped Christ, he was cast down from his rank and brought in bonds to the governor Maximus. And first indeed he is beaten with rods; next, because he mocked the idols, he is cast onto burning coals; afterward, his head having been anointed with oil, he was compelled to place it upon burning charcoals. Then his loins were cut with swords and lacerated with sharp potsherds. After this, being asked by the prefect how he could think that Christ, who was made of flesh, is God, he set forth all His economy in a brief account. Then, truly, having been suspended, he was flayed for so long until all his bones were laid bare and his entrails poured out. And thus he was compelled to run twenty miles as he was dragged along, and at the same time being most cruelly beaten by the lictors with rods, he delivered his spirit to God.
SAME MONTH.
Day the sixteenth.
Commemoration of our holy Father Tychon the wonderworker.
Tychon the wonderworker, the offspring of pious parents, was consecrated to God by them. Afterward, having been taught the sacred letters, he was ordained a deacon by the bishop of Trimethus. Upon his death, he himself was raised to the episcopal throne by the great Epiphanius. And having turned not a few from error to the Lord, and having performed many miracles, he migrated to the Lord, of which I shall relate only two. Once his father had handed over loaves to the boy to sell—for he was a baker—but the boy distributed the price to the needy. And when his father discovered the matter, he was moved against him; but the boy, going to his storehouse, showed it to his father filled with wheat: wherefore both glorified God. One day, finding a shoot of a vine, he made it take root in the ground; which even to this day brings forth early grapes, which they harvest mature at the time of his commemoration.
And the commemoration of the holy prophet Amos.
Amos, the glorious and great prophet, was born in the country of Zabulon, in the land of the river Jordan. He was the father of Isaiah the great prophet. He prophesied for fifty years, guiding the transgressing people and rebuking the king of the Jews for his lawless deeds and injustices, by which he provoked God to anger. He predicted much concerning the coming of Christ, the destruction of the Jews, the overthrow of idols, and the captivity of the people. For this reason, he stirred up against himself Amaziah, the priest of the idol of Bethel, by whom he was attacked with false accusations because he had rebuked him for the error of the golden calves. And for this, having been struck on the temple with a staff by his son, while he was still breathing, he returned to his own land. And after two days, having surrendered his soul to God, he was buried with his fathers.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE SEVENTEENTH DAY.
The contest of the holy martyrs Manuel, Sabel, and Ismael.
Manuel, Sabel, and Ismael, the martyrs of Christ, were from the country of Persia, sons of a father who was an archmage and a mother who was a Christian. Having been taught the sacred scriptures and piety by a certain Christian named Eunicus, they believed in and worshipped Christ. During the reign of Julian the Apostate, they were sent by the King of Persia as envoys to Constantinople for the sake of peace. And seeing the apostate on the other side at Chalcedon sacrificing to idols, they were grieved. And being recognized, they were denounced to the apostate. And being brought before him, they rebuked him. Whereupon, having been beaten severely and having their ankles pierced, and having been hung up, their armpits were burned with torches of fire. Afterwards, the holy Manuel was nailed to a piece of wood by his head and his loins, and pierced with arrows; finally, he was led away with his brothers to the place of the condemned, and they were all beheaded together.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE EIGHTEENTH DAY.
The contest of the holy martyrs Leontius, Hypatius, and Theodulus.
Leontius, the martyr of Christ, originated from the country of Hellas. Because of his valor, he became a commander and resided in Tripoli of Phoenicia, openly worshipping Christ and providing for the poor. Having learned of this, Hadrian, the governor of Phoenicia, who had recently been appointed by Vespasian, Caesar of the Romans, sent to him Hypatius the tribune with two soldiers, one of whom was called Theodulus, to summon him. The tribune, however, suffering from a dangerous fever, heard a voice saying to him, "If you wish to live, invoke the God of Leontius three times." And having done this, he recovered. And when Theodulus heard this voice, he believed, and both were baptized. When the governor learned of this, he seized both and beheaded
them. And he ordered the holy Leontius to be beaten in prison, and the Lord received him after he was beaten.
EODEM MENSE.
Die decima nona.
Certamen sancti martyris Zosimi.
Zosimus, the martyr of Christ, originated from Apollonias in the region of Sozopolis during the reign of Trajan. While he was serving as a soldier under Domitian, the governor of Pisidian Antioch, he cast aside his weapons and, fleeing to the Church of God, was deemed worthy of baptism in Christ. Having been seized, he was led in chains to the governor and, upon being questioned, confessed himself to be a Christian. Stretched out by his four limbs, he was beaten most severely; shortly after, he was suspended on the rack and tormented, and was placed upon a red-hot bronze bed. As the fire turned into dew, many of the unbelievers were struck by this miracle and believed in Christ. After this, his feet were pierced with nails, and being bound to untamed horses, he was forced to run alongside the governor as he traveled to the city of the Caneotae, having remained fasting for three days. Finally, being called again for examination, as he freely confessed Christ, he was beheaded.
Et certamen sancti Judæ apostoli.
Judas, the apostle of Christ, whom the holy apostle and Evangelist Luke in the Acts calls by this name (but by the remaining apostles and evangelists Matthew and Mark is called Thaddaeus), was a brother according to the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, inasmuch as he was the son of Joseph the Betrothed and brother of James the Brother-of-God; he who wrote an Epistle for all, full of light and rich in the doctrines of the Holy Spirit. Strengthened by Christ himself and filled with the Holy Spirit, he dispelled all error and illuminated all the faithful. Having gone into Mesopotamia and proclaiming the Gospel, he converted many of the unbelievers to the Lord, and proceeding to the city of Edessa, he relieved Abgar the Toparch of his disease. Finally, he sought the city of Arat; and there, having been nailed to a cross and pierced with arrows, he reached the end of his life.
EODEM MENSE.
Die vicesima.
Certamen sacrosancti martyris Methodii episcopi Patarorum.
Methodius, the holy martyr of Christ, consecrated himself from infancy as an honorable vessel to God, becoming a receptacle of the divine Spirit. Wherefore, he was deemed worthy of the pontificate by the vote of God, and having been created bishop of the church of Patara, he ruled his flock in excellent fashion. Perceiving, however, the spreading heresy of Origen, as an excellent pastor, he burned it with the divine fire of his own words. But since the hostile devil could not endure his boldness and steadfastness, [he armed his] ministers for his destruction. And he, even before...
his martyrdom was accomplished, having put on a life-giving mortification and reckoning himself dead every day, according to the divine apostle Paul, offered his holy and blessed head to be cut off by the sword, and departed to the Lord, rejoicing and exulting.
ON THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-FIRST DAY.
The contest of the holy martyr Julian in Egypt.
Julian, the martyr of Christ, was in Egypt during the reign of Diocletian. Worshipping Christ, he built a very large monastery in which he glorified God. Upon learning this, the governor sent soldiers and seized him, while he burnt the monastery, cremating all the bishops, priests, and monks he found therein. Then, after scourging the saint, he threw him into prison. Bringing him out again, he led him in bonds before him; and Celtius, the son of the governor, seeing angels standing by the saint, believed in Christ, along with many others. A dead man, being carried upon a bier, suddenly arose and cried out, "I have been brought back to life because Julian prayed!" And again many believed in Christ. Therefore, the governor, in his anger, had the skin of the head of Julian, as well as that of Celtius, flayed. The governor's wife, seeing this, believed, and together with her son and the others, she was beheaded alongside the holy Julian.
ON THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-SECOND DAY.
The contest of our holy Father Eusebius, Bishop of Samosata.
Eusebius, the hieromartyr of Christ, was Bishop of Samosata under the Emperor Constantius, and was a burning zealot of the orthodox faith. But because the emperor held the views of Arius, and once threatened to cut off his hand if he did not produce and hand over the decree written by the great Meletius, it is said that he stretched out both his hands and said that he would rather have both his hands cut off than betray the decree. After the deaths of Constantius and Julian, he was driven from his own see by Valens, who was also an Arian, and was exiled to the river Ister. And after the death of Valens, returning to his own church, he attained the end of a martyr. For an Arian woman threw a roof tile from a rooftop upon his head as he was passing by, and it struck him. Surviving for a little while, he charged those with him to inflict no punishment upon the woman; and thus he reached his end.
ON THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-THIRD DAY.
The contest of the holy martyrs Zeno and Zenas.
Zeno and Zenas, the martyrs of Christ, were from the city of Philadelphia in Arabia. Zeno, indeed, was of the military order
he prayed to God continually. He would dismiss those who came for the sake of profit, after confirming them and teaching them what pertains to salvation. And thus he passed his days, enduring the hardships of cold and heat; and when he had been enriched with the power of miracles and had served God in all things, he migrated to Him.
And the commemoration of our holy Father Sampson the Xenodochos.
Our holy Father Sampson was from old Rome, a kinsman of the great Constantine. Having distributed all his patrimony among the needy, he became indigent for Christ's sake, came to Constantinople, and lived intent upon prayer in the temples of the holy prophets. Having secured leisure, he meditated upon the divinely inspired Scriptures. Because of such virtues, when he became known to the Patriarch Menas, he was ordained a presbyter of the Great Church; and he subsequently became a saving harbor for those laboring and for the sick. For, being learned in the art of medicine, he even healed the Emperor Justinian of an incurable malady, by whom he was held in the highest regard and love. He therefore founded a Xenodochion for the relief of the poor and the infirm; and having performed many notable works and miracles, he fell asleep in peace. His relics were deposited in the temple of the holy martyr Mocius.
IN THE SAME MONTH. The twenty-eighth day. The finding of the relics of the holy martyrs Cyrus and John.
Cyrus and John, the martyrs of Christ, flourished under the Emperor Diocletian. Cyrus was from the city of Alexandria, and John was from the city of Edessa, both physicians by profession. Having recognized each other due to their common calling, they traveled through every island and territory, healing not only bodies but also souls. And since they made many Christians more eager and ready to undergo martyrdom, they were denounced to the prefect of that place. And having first been subjected to tortures by him, they were finally beheaded. And although their precious relics were at one time concealed, they were later revealed in Alexandria under the Emperor Arcadius and Theophilus, Patriarch of Alexandria; they continue to the present day to perform innumerable miracles to the glory of Christ and our God, for whom they suffered, whose anniversary we, all the faithful, celebrate annually.
IN THE SAME MONTH. The twenty-ninth day.
The Contest of the holy great apostles Peter and Paul.
Peter, the great apostle of Christ, was from the city of Bethsaida, the son of Jonah, the true brother of Andrew the First-called. Being a fisherman and poor, he took the daughter of Aristobulus, brother of the apostle Barnabas, from whom he also had children. At the time when the Forerunner was cast into prison, he himself, in the lake of Gennesaret...
was fishing, and having been called by Christ as He passed by the lake, he followed Him with his brother, and became His disciple. Paul, however, being a Hebrew and himself from the city of Tarsus, after the assumption of the Lord Jesus, persecuted His Church. But being called, he too became His disciple; and having traversed with Peter almost the whole world, he preached Christ. And finally, both having departed to Rome, they suffered for Christ under Nero: Peter, indeed, being crucified head downwards, and Paul being beheaded.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The Thirtieth Day. The Synaxis of the Twelve Holy Apostles.
Although each of the holy apostles suffered martyrdom at a different time, the Church of God, because of their surpassing honor, celebrates this synaxis immediately after the memorial of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and praises them all together, as those who illuminated the world. First, therefore, worthy of praises is Peter, the fervent disciple, who under Nero was crucified head downwards. Second is Paul, the vessel of election, who was beheaded under the same. Third is Andrew, the first-called, who was fastened to a tree by Aegeas. Fourth is James of Zebedee, who was slain by the sword by Herod. Fifth is his brother John, who was buried alive and then translated. Sixth is Philip, suspended from a wall by the Greeks. Seventh is Thomas the Didymus, pierced by lances by the Indians. Eighth is Bartholomew, who was crucified. Ninth is Matthew, overwhelmed by stones. Tenth is James of Alphaeus. Eleventh is Simon the Zealot. Twelfth is Judas of James, suspended and transfixed with arrows.
MONTH OF JULY. The First Day. The Contest of the Holy Unmercenaries Cosmas and Damian, who were renowned at Rome.
Cosmas and Damian, martyrs of Christ, were renowned during the reign of Carinus. Since they were physicians by profession, they wandered over every place, healing all the infirm, and demanding no other reward from those whom they cured than that they should embrace the faith of Christ. But those who were seduced by idolatry, thinking that they performed their cures by magic arts, reported them to the emperor, wherefore being seized, they were compelled to deny Christ: which, when they refused to do, they prepared themselves for tortures. But by the power of Christ they recalled the emperor Carinus from his error; they cured him, for he was suffering from a luxation of the neck, and they caused not only him to believe in Christ, but also all his household. Hence, being held in honor, they suffered the envy of their master. Therefore, having been led by him to the mountain to gather herbs, they were stoned.
And the commemoration of our holy Father Peter.
Our holy Father Peter was born in Constantinople during the reign of the most pious Empress Irene, the son of Constantine the patrician, from whom he was taught all Greek and Christian literature. Then, having taken a wife, he became a patrician, and because of his singular virtue, he was appointed by the Emperor Nicephorus, father of Stauracius, as Domestic of the Schools, and he campaigned with the emperor against the Bulgarians. But when, after the slaughter of the emperor and the flight of his son Stauracius, he was captured along with fifty others, through his poured-out prayers—the holy John the Theologian appearing to him—he was freed from his bonds. Renouncing the world, he became a monk and practiced asceticism on Mount Olympus with the holy Joannicius. After the latter had passed away, he departed for the royal city, and settled in the house which he himself had built in the place called Evander’s, and having made manifest all virtues, and performed many miracles, he ended his life.
ON THE SAME DAY.
The Deposition of the precious robe of the most holy Theotokos.
During the reign of Leo the Great, two brothers of patrician rank, Galbius and Candidus, were seized with a desire to go and venerate the holy places in Jerusalem. Having fulfilled their longing, they went to Palestine, and having lodged in the house of an old Hebrew woman, they saw there a multitude of the sick lying about. Having inquired, they learned that the precious robe of the Theotokos was kept in that place. They asked, therefore, that they might be allowed to venerate it, and they were admitted. Then, having secretly taken the measurements of the chest by night, they went off to Jerusalem and prepared a similar chest; returning to the same house, they placed the chest which they had brought in place of the original, which they took away, and carried it to Constantinople, depositing it in their own suburb, called Blachernae, glorifying God along with the emperor and the people for such a treasure acquired.
And the contest of the holy martyr Hyacinth.
The martyr of Christ, Hyacinth, was born in the region of Phrygia, where he was also trained in piety. Having gone to the city of Cyme, he healed those who were sick in the name of Christ. Having been recognized by the idolaters, he was seized and surrendered to the governor of the region. Being compelled to sacrifice to the idols, and not being persuaded, he was tortured; and having prayed to God, he delivered the governor over to an unclean spirit; and having worked a miracle, he healed him, and he believed in Christ, and he was released. Then, having been seized by the inhabitants of Cyme, he was punished. And again, having prayed, and shaken the city, and crushed the idols, he persuaded many to believe in Christ. And after these things, having been seized by Clearchus the
governor, and his legs broken, he was cast into prison. And having been released from prison, and wandering through every land, and healing those who were sick, he himself, having fallen ill, departed to the Lord.
And commemoration of our holy Father Juvenalis.
Our holy Father Juvenalis was in the days of Theodosius the Younger. He became the successor of the most holy Cyril as third Patriarch of Jerusalem. He was present at the Ephesian Synod of the two hundred holy Fathers, and shone with words and dogmas along with the ever-memorable Cyril, Patriarch of Alexandria. He also reached the fourth Synod of Chalcedon, in the days of the Emperor Marcian, the founder of the temple of the Blachernae; to whom, when he asked where the immaculate body of the Mother of God had been deposited, so that he might take care to transfer it, he replied that he knew nothing of it from Scripture; but that he had been taught by ancient tradition that it had been taken up, with only the burial clothes left in the sepulcher. The emperor then, having had these transferred, deposited them in the Blachernae. The holy Juvenalis, having returned to his own church, fell asleep in peace.
OF THE SAME MONTH.
The third day.
The contest of the holy martyrs Marcus and Mocianus.
Marcus and Mocianus, martyrs of Christ, because they confessed Christ, were apprehended by the prefect Maximus, who attempted to compel them to deny the Christian religion and submit themselves to the superstition of idols. But while they were being tortured, a certain little boy who was standing by the altar of the sacrifices reproved the prefect, saying that he was acting unjustly. Wherefore, having been bound and beaten with scourges, together with a certain Christian named Paul who was present and was encouraging the holy men, he was cast into prison. Then, sentence of death was passed upon the holy men, and while they were in chains they were being led to death, they were praying to God and giving thanks to Him that they had been judged worthy to suffer martyrdom for his sake. Their wives, however, with their children, followed them weeping as far as the place of execution: where, having arrived, they were beheaded, their wives receiving their venerable heads.
And commemoration of our holy Father Anatolius, Patriarch of Constantinople.
Our holy Father Anatolius was born in the city of Alexandria, and was a presbyter of the most holy Church of God in the time of Theodosius the Younger. On account of his virtue and wisdom, he was sent as apocrisiarius to Constantinople by Dioscorus, the heretical patriarch of Alexandria, who was led by the hope that he would share his own perverted dogma and support it. But he participated in the fourth Synod of Chalcedon, and together with the six hundred and thirty holy Fathers, he struck Dioscorus with an anathema; for he had been deposed by Dioscorus in the Ephesian brigand synod, and had endured injustice from the heretics, and the name of the holy Flavian
he restored to the diptychs; and he struck all the heretics with the sentence of excommunication. Finally, having been chosen patriarch of Constantinople, and having rightly governed his flock, he departed to God.
The contest of the holy martyr Hyacinth.
Hyacinth, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Caesarea in Cappadocia; and being a chamberlain, and serving at the table of the lawless emperor Trajan in Rome, he worshipped Christ. Being therefore denounced by the idolaters, and arrested, he was forced to sacrifice to the idols and to eat of unclean foods. But since he refused to be persuaded to do this, and confessed Christ even more clearly, saying that He alone is God and Lord of all, he was on that account beaten severely and cast into prison. And the emperor having commanded the jailer not to bring him clean bread, but to set before him only foods sacrificed to idols, since he stayed for many days without tasting them, but remained fasting, he surrendered his spirit to God.
The contest of the holy martyrs Theodotus and Theodota.
These holy martyrs also, having been seized for their confession of Christ by the impious Trajan, and compelled to deny the truth and to sacrifice to idols, and being unable to be brought to this, were tormented in various ways and cast into the same prison in which the holy martyr Hyacinth had been shut up; and having been instructed by him, and more fully confirmed in the faith of Christ, they were reported to the emperor Trajan by the guards who were idolaters. And after the death of the holy Hyacinth, they were brought out of prison and stood before him. Again being forced to eat the polluted foods, they rebuked him and execrated the error of the idols. Then, suspended from wooden beams and lacerated, they were burned with torches. Finally, being taken down from the beams, they met the end of life by the sword, surrendering their souls to God.
ON THE SAME MONTH. Fourth day.
The contest of the holy hieromartyr Theodore, bishop of Cyrene.
Theodore the hieromartyr was in Cyrene during the reign of Diocletian; and having well learned the art of calligraphy, and preparing many books, he provided them to the Christians for the praising of God. Being therefore denounced by his own son to the prefect of the city, he was arrested along with many other Christians, with whom was the holy Lucia. And being asked for the books which he had written, and not producing them, he was beaten severely. And being forced to approach the altar and to burn incense, he ran forward and kicked it, overturning it. Then, suspended from a beam and fastened with nails, and his tongue having been cut out, he...
suspended on the wood, was nailed, and his tongue was cut out; and having been taken down from the wood, he was locked in prison. And seeing him healed, many men and women believed in the Lord, who also were beheaded along with him.
And the commemoration of our holy Father Andrew, Archbishop of Crete, the Hierosolymite, and of holy Lampadus, who was in Irenopolis.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The fifth day.
153 Commemoration of holy Martha, mother of holy Simeon on the Wonderful Mountain.
Holy Martha, mother of our holy Father Simeon the Stylite, attained every virtue through the highest exercise. Having, moreover, great confidence in the Virgin Theotokos, she was perpetually sitting in her temple, praying to her for the salvation of the whole world. Wherefore, before her departure from the body, having been divinely taught, she secretly understood the eternal goods laid up for her. And then, indeed, she departed with good hope; but afterward, appearing to those running to her holy relics and telling of those goods, which the eye of the body did not see, which God prepared for those who love Him, she brought incredible joy. Thus the Lord glorifies those who glorify Him, together with our Lady the Theotokos, who gave birth to Him without seed and without corruption.
And the contest of holy Agnes the martyr.
Martyr of Christ, Agnes, adorned with morals corresponding to her name, having called many unchaste women away from their shameful deeds by her admonitions and exhortations, brought them to the faith of Christ. Therefore, having been seized by the prefect of that place, she was tormented; and since she refused to sacrifice to idols, she was ordered to be led to a brothel, so that she might be defiled by the incontinent. But she, trusting in Christ, to whom she kept her faith and chastity, was preserved unstained and pure, being protected by a divine angel, who did not permit anyone to approach her; of whom one, having dared to approach, suddenly fell down dead. The prefect, hearing this, summoned her and prayed that she might raise the dead man. And so, the saint praying, the deceased immediately revived. But the prefect, thinking that she had accomplished this by magical art, handed her over to be burned by flames. D
154 And the contest of holy martyr Cyprilla.
Cyprilla, martyr of Christ, born in Cyrene during the reign of the emperor Diocletian, of Christian parents, remained in widowhood for twenty-eight years after her husband died two years after their marriage. But when Theodore, the most holy bishop of Cyrene, was captured and thrust into prison, it happened that, being afflicted with a headache, she came to him for the sake of a cure; and having been cured by him, she began to minister to him with Lucia and Aroa, pious women. But after the passing of holy Theodore, having been brought to the governor, and having professed Christ, she was first beaten: then, receiving hot coals, by the lictors of his
hands she was compelled to offer incense to the gods. But she cried out: "This is not," she said, "a voluntary offering: for I sacrifice to my Christ." Having spoken these words, she was hoisted upon a rack and, being torn, she yielded up her spirit.
And the commemoration of the holy Hilarion of the monastery of the Dalmatians.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The Sixth Day.
The commemoration of our holy Father Sisoes the Great.
Blessed Sisoes, having loved God from infancy, and having taken up his cross upon his shoulders, followed him; and having overcome the conflict of invisible enemies, he joyfully withdrew to the laborious struggles of monastic discipline. Having attained the peak of humility, he received the grace of miracles. For he both raised the dead, and drove demons from men, and healed the sick, and performed many other miracles. He was also, in familiar gatherings, clear-minded, and moderate in spirit, and pleasant in his replies, from which many things have been written down for the benefit of others. Moreover, he corrected not a few of the fallen brothers, by fitting examples turning them toward repentance. He also had this characteristic, that he never condemned any man. Having lived in this manner an angelic life, he departed to God, whom he desired, receiving the eternal kingdom prepared for him.
And the struggle of the holy martyr Lucia, and those with her.
Christ’s martyr, the virgin Lucia, was another from the Lucia who was a virgin of Sicily; she was from the region of Campania. Having been seized by the governor of that region, she was punished. But having performed miracles, she persuaded him to believe in Christ; and not only was she released by him, but she also received a house and maidservants and lived in quiet, praying to God for him. After the passage of twenty years, both desiring to undergo martyrdom for Christ, they abandoned everything, and taking their own servants, they approached the governor of the region, delivering themselves up voluntarily. And having been questioned and having confessed Christ, they were tormented in various ways. But as they remained for a long time in the faith of Christ, they received the sentence of beheading. And so, being beheaded together with the rest of their companions, they finished their life in this manner, having obtained their crown in Christ.
And the struggle of the holy hieromartyr Astius, bishop of Dyrrachium.
Astius the hieromartyr was during the reign of Trajan; and having been seized by the idolaters, he was handed over to the governor Agricolaus, and upon being exhorted to deny Christ and to sacrifice to the idols, and not being persuaded, he was consigned to prison. But before he was seized, of this sort
he beheld a dream: he saw himself standing upon a rock smeared with pitch and oil. Having woken up, he said to his clergy: "Brothers, it behooves me to suffer for Christ; as for the rest, let each of you go where he may be able to save himself." Having said this, he was seized, as has been narrated, and brought before Agricolaus; and when he had confessed Christ, he was cast into prison. Being led out from prison, he was beaten with leaden whips. Soon he was smeared with honey and hung upon a wooden beam in the heat of the day, so that, being consumed by the bites of wasps and flies, he might perish. And as that happened, bearing the torture with thanksgiving, he surrendered his soul.
And the commemoration of the holy martyr Phocas, and of the miracle that occurred. Leo, surnamed Pontianus, recounted that that Sisinnios, who is called Stibarus, while sailing in the royal fleet, was captured by the Saracens; and, being bound with a double chain, he was thrown into prison. Constrained by such necessity, he fled to God and His holy martyr Phocas. "Holy martyr Phocas," he would say, "have mercy on me, and deliver me from the distress of my bonds that holds me." Then, having fallen asleep, he saw the saint appearing to him in the garb of a priest, and saying to him: "Arise, and depart." Having woken up, he found the chains shattered, himself loosed, and the prison opened. Wherefore, taking to flight, he arrived home; and, mindful of the benefit received, he continued to celebrate the memory of the saint with much thanksgiving, and to glorify God, who bestows such graces upon His saints.
And the contest of the holy martyr Isaurus and his companions. Isaurus, a deacon of the mysteries of Christ, and his companions, were by birth Athenians; and in the reign of Numerian, having departed from their own fatherland, they went away to the city of Apolloniades. There, being warned by an angel of God, they entered a cave where Felix, Peregrinus, and Hermias—who were themselves also Christians—dwelt. Upon seeing the holy Isaurus, they were affected with such great joy that, having distributed their property to the poor, they resolved to follow him and live under his discipline. Their kinsmen, having discovered this, tried in vain to turn them from their purpose and call them back to their own homes, and so they accused them before the governor; who, having arrested them, ordered them to be beheaded. But Isaurus, the deacon of Christ, and his companions, were bound in chains and sent to the son of the governor for interrogation, by whom they were cast into the flames; yet when they emerged from them unharmed, they led many to the faith of Christ. Moved by this, the governor ordered them to be put to death by the sword.
OF THE SAME MONTH.
The seventh day.
And the contest of the holy martyr Peregrinus and his companions.
The martyrs of Christ, Peregrinus, Lucianus, Pom-
peius, Hesychius, Papias, Saturnilus, and Germanus were from the land of Italy. In the reign of Trajan, when a persecution against the Christians had been stirred up, they boarded a ship and arrived at Dyrrachium. Having seen the holy hieromartyr Astius smeared with honey for his confession of Christ and suspended on a wooden frame, being stung by wasps and flies, they called him blessed. Because of this they were recognized and seized by the officers. When they were interrogated and confessed Christ, they were delivered to the governor Agricola; by his order they were bound, cast into a ship, and thrown into the Adriatic Sea, where they received their blessed end. The sea cast up their relics, which were buried in the sand, and later, having been revealed to the Archbishop of Alexandria, they were honorably interred.
And the memory of Saint Thomas on Mount Maleo.
Our holy Father Thomas, while he was in the world, was illustrious and conspicuous for his wealth and power; indeed, he also won many trophies against the Barbarians. But when, for the love of Christ, he renounced the world and the most troublesome agitation of secular life, he became a monk and grew so much more illustrious that, like a pillar of fire amidst the darkness of the night, he seemed to shine by the visitation of the great prophet Elijah, whose manner of life he also emulated. He cultivated perpetual silence and prayer to God on the mountain which they call Maleo. Wherefore, having received the gift of healings, he cast out demons and, by his prayers to God, caused a spring of water to gush forth. He restored sight to the blind and agility to the lame. And having performed many other miracles in the name of Christ, having become wonder to all men, and having served God as much as is possible for a man, he departed to Him with joy and rejoicing.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The eighth day.
The Contest of the Holy Great Martyr Procopius.
The great martyr Procopius was born in the city of Aelia to a Christian father and a pagan mother during the reign of Diocletian. After the death of his father, he was raised by his mother and presented to Diocletian himself, so that he might be promoted to honors. Therefore, having been created Duke of Alexandria, he was sent there to wage war—not only against enemies, but also against Christians. As he was proceeding toward his home, a voice falling from heaven reached him, saying: "Young man, cease fighting against my servants, lest you die." Moreover, the figure of the cross was shown to him. Wherefore, having gone to Scythopolis, he ordered a goldsmith to come to him and commanded him to fashion a cross according to the figure that had been shown to him, which he then wore. But when he had brought back trophies from the Saracens and had returned home, he was denounced by his mother to the emperor for being a Christian. Therefore, having been subjected to various tortures and having performed miracles himself, he not only convinced many others to believe in Christ, but also his own
mother, and some women, with whom he was beheaded and departed to God.
OF THE SAME MONTH.
The ninth day.
The contest of the holy martyr Cyril.
The holy martyr Cyril, having been increased by the Christian faith and divine virtues, was appointed bishop of the Church in Crete. And having well governed the flock and increased the Lord’s people through teaching and exhortation, when a persecution was stirred up, he was seized by the idolaters and, having been bound, was delivered to the governor. And having been cast into the fire, and having come out of it unhurt, the bonds with which he was bound having been burned, and the wood by which the flame was fed having been reduced to ashes, he was set free by the governor, who wondered at the event and condemned the emperor's edicts as unjust. And at that time, the matter happened thus. But afterward, the governor, seeing many embracing the faith in Christ and fearing the anger of the emperor, seized the saint and, even against his will, condemned him to be beheaded; and in this way, he procured for him an immortal life and the everlasting blessedness of the kingdom of heaven.
And the contest of the holy martyr Patermuthius and his companions.
Patermuthius and his companions, while Julian the Apostate was exercising his tyranny, had sought seclusion and a quiet life in the Egyptian desert. But when the same Apostate was preparing an expedition against the Persians, they were denounced by the idolaters and, being seized, were presented before him. Now, Patermuthius was seventy-five years of age, and Copres was forty-five. And so, being separated from one another, they were compelled to deny Christ. But Copres, taken by the enticements of the Apostate, fell from the faith. When Patermuthius learned of this, he wept and prayed to God for him. Shortly after, he himself was brought in, and seeing Copres clothed in splendid garments, he wept. But Copres, recognizing that the cause of his tears was his own fall, began to cry out with a loud voice: "I am no longer a Julianite, but a servant of Christ." On account of this, his tongue was cut out, and he was cast into the fire together with Patermuthius; and when a certain Alexander saw them completely unharmed by the fire, he embraced the faith in Christ and, rejoicing together with them, was beheaded by the sword.
And the contest of the holy martyrs Bianor and Silvanus.
Bianor, the martyr of Christ, was born in the region of Pisidia. On account of his confession of Christ, he was seized by Severianus, the prefect of Isauria, and after being tempted in vain to abjure Christ, he was placed upon the rack and most cruelly lacerated with iron claws. Soon, his armpits were burned with glowing iron balls, his teeth were pulled out, and his ears were cut off. When a certain soldier named Silvanus saw that he was bravely enduring these things, he believed in Christ; and immediately his own tongue was cut out, and he was also beheaded. Bianor, however, the victor of many contests, having had his ankles pierced, and his...
right eye gouged out, and the skin of his head flayed off, was cast into prison. And on the following day, while he was still breathing a little, he was brought out of the prison and, carried by the executioners, he was beheaded.
The Contest of the Holy Martyr Apollonius
The martyr of Christ, Apollonius, was from the land of Lydia, from the city of Sardis, but he went about all the cities and the region, teaching the word of the truth and turning many of the infidels to the Lord. Being accused, therefore, by the idolaters to the governor of the city of Iconium, he was seized and, brought in chains, he was presented before him. And when asked, he confessed himself a servant of Christ. And being compelled to swear by the fortune of the emperor, he said, "It is not lawful to swear by a mortal emperor, and especially one who does not acknowledge God, the Creator of the world." Having said these things, by order of the governor, he was beaten very severely; and soon being placed on the rack and fastened with iron nails, he gave up his spirit to God. And thus, having finished the course of his martyrdom, he obtained the kingdom of the heavens.
And a commemoration of the myriad holy Fathers who were burned and suffocated in the caves by Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, because of Isidore the presbyter.
ON THE SAME MONTH
The 15th
The Contest of the holy forty-five martyrs who suffered martyrdom in Nicopolis
The forty-five martyrs of Christ flourished during the reign of Licinius and the administration of Lysias; they were led by Leontius, Maurice, Daniel, and Antony. Having been seized, therefore, they were presented to the Duke Lysias in Nicopolis of Armenia. And when they confessed Christ but spat upon the idols, they were beaten and their mouths and faces were crushed with stones, and they were cast into prison, remaining without food for many days. And seeing their constancy, the soldiers who were guarding them believed in Christ. Then, being brought out of the prison, and having their legs cut off with axes, some while already dead, and others while still breathing, they were cast into a furnace of fire and were perfected, having received the immortal kingdom prepared for them by Christ from the foundation of the world.
ON THE SAME MONTH
The 16th
The Contest of the holy martyr Marcianus
Marcianus, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Iconium. Being young, he was taught the faith in Christ. And having been baptized, he preached the truth, and rebuked the deception and weakness of the idols, and silenced the idolaters. Being seized, therefore, by them, he was handed over to the governor. And, being brought to trial, he was compelled, now by promises of corruptible and temporary honor, now by threats, to deny Christ and—
to sacrifice to the idols. Not being persuaded by the governor’s words, but rather confessing Christ before the people, he was beaten and shut up in prison. After this, having emerged from imprisonment in bonds, and standing before the governor, and persisting in the same confession, his face was flayed with iron, his sinews were severed, and his tongue was cut out with a sword and placed upon burning coals. Finally, being beheaded, he completed his course of martyrdom.
*And a remembrance of the miracle of the all-praised martyr Euphemia.*
In the reign of Theodosius the Younger, a certain Eutyches, a monk and presbyter, became the author of the heresy, teaching that there is one nature in Christ our Lord. Having been deposed for this reason by Flavian, the patriarch of Constantinople, he did not, however, cease to disturb the Church. But the holy Marcian, having obtained the empire, called a council of six hundred and thirty Fathers. And a discussion having arisen with the heretics, it pleased all that two tomes should be set forth, one of the orthodox, and one of the heretics, and that the chest of the martyr should be opened, and the tomes placed upon her breast, and that they should be held by her. And when this was done, after many days they opened the chest, and found the tome of the heretics lying under her feet, and the one of the orthodox held in her hand. And thus the heretics were confused, but the orthodox rejoiced.
*And the struggle of the holy martyr Cindaeus.*
Christ’s martyr Cindaeus was a presbyter of the church in the city of Side; in the reign of Diocletian, having been denounced to the prefect Stratonicus because he worshipped Christ, he was seized and, having iron shoes with sharp nails fastened to his feet, he was compelled to run along the road that leads to what is called the Sacred Gate, being beaten by the executioners. Since the executioners had orders to burn him, they met a certain poor man carrying a load of wood, intending to sell it, and they wanted to snatch it for free and burn the saint with it. But he, having produced the price, gave it to the poor man, and placing the wood upon his own shoulders, he reached the place of execution. And having kindled the furnace, he entered into it; and at that time, having come out unharmed, he persuaded the priest of the idols, together with his wife, to believe in Christ. Later, having prayed, he surrendered his spirit. His remains were buried honorably.
*On the same day. 12th.*
*The struggle of the holy martyrs Proclus and Hilarius.*
Proclus and Hilarius, martyrs of Christ, were from the city of Ancyra, in the reign of Trajan, being Christians, and preaching Christ, many of the unbelievers they turned to the --
Lord. Proclus, being the first to be seized by the idolaters, was brought before the governor. When examined, and confessing Christ all the more, he was handed over to the magistrate Maximinus; by whom he was suspended, and his flesh torn with iron claws, and his stomach and sides burned with flaming torches. After this, a sentence being passed that he should be shot with arrows, he was led naked to the place of execution. But as he greeted his nephew Hilarius, who met him on the way, his doing so was the cause of him also being seized. And he, having been bound to a stake and pierced by arrows, yielded up his spirit. But Hilarius, having been beaten and his flesh torn, and having been dragged naked for several miles, was finally beheaded with a sword.
And the contest of the holy martyr Golinduch.
The martyr of Christ, Golinduch, lived in Persia in the reign of Maurice; and having been given in marriage to a certain chief of the Magi, an angel of God appeared to her at one time in her sleep, and showed her a splendid place, where the righteous were dancing, and another, dark, in which idolaters were being tormented. And as she attempted to enter the bright place, she was prohibited, the angel saying, "Unless you become a Christian, you shall by no means enter here." Awakening, she immediately received baptism. And this having been discovered by her husband and the king, she was shut up in the prison of Lethe, and then into a pit where there was a dragon; and after many years, having been brought out, she was tormented in various ways. Finally, wearing a seal of wax upon her neck, she was led to execution. But the angel took the seal safe and sound and handed it to the executioner; and he, seeing the saint grieving because she was not suffering for Christ, struck her on the neck with a sword, and though he caused blood to flow, he did not behead her. Having lived after these things and benefited many, she migrated to the Lord.
ON THE SAME MONTH. THE THIRTEENTH DAY.
The contest of the holy martyr Serapion.
Serapion, the martyr of Christ, lived in the time of the emperor Severus, a man pious and noble in his manner of life. Being seized by the idolaters because of his confession of Christ, he was delivered to Aquila, the governor of that region. And having stood before him, and being asked what religion he belonged to, he confessed Christ with boldness. Being therefore severely beaten for Christ, and his whole body torn with sharp iron hooks, he was sent back to prison, to be consumed by hunger and thirst. After many days had passed, he was brought out of custody and stood bound before the governor. And since he bore no mark of a wound or scar on his whole body, because he had been immediately healed by Christ, he brought amazement to all, and persuaded many to believe in Christ. Whereupon the governor, fearing lest he should bring even more to Christ, delivered him to be burned with flames; and in this way, having finished the contest of immortality, he was perfected.
And the Contest of the Holy Martyr Myrope
The martyr of Christ, Myrope, lived during the reign of Decius; she was born on the island of Chios, and traveled to the city of the Ephesians. There, she collected the myrrh flowing from the relics of the holy martyrs and apostles, and healed the sick; hence she received the name Myrope [Myrrh-bearer]. Upon returning to the island of Chios, and finding that Saint Isidore had been martyred and perfected for Christ, she took up his relics and hid them away with her. When many were seized and tortured on account of the removal of the relics, she revealed herself, confessing that she had taken and hidden the body. Therefore, she was seized by the governor Numerianus—the same who had tortured Saint Isidore—and was cruelly beaten and cast into prison. There, having received the promise of the good things reserved for her through an apparition of Saint Isidore, she surrendered her spirit to God.
ON THE SAME MONTH. THE FOURTEENTH DAY.
The Contest of the Holy Martyr Justus
Justus, a martyr of Christ, was from the city of Rome and served in the rank of the Numeri. Once, while returning from battle, he saw a crystal cross, and from the cross he heard a voice speaking and commanding him to abandon idols and believe in Christ. He returned at once to Rome, where he distributed his patrimony to the poor, and, happy and content in the faith of Christ, he resolved to live thereafter in private seclusion. When the tribune learned of this, he ordered that Justus be seized; and, having made an attempt in vain to make him deny Christ, he had him bound in chains and sent to the governor Magnentius. Because he persisted the more firmly in the faith of Christ, he was lashed with raw leather strips; then a red-hot iron helmet was placed upon his head; soon after, he was laid naked upon burning coals; and finally, being cast into a great furnace of fire, he surrendered his spirit to God.
And the Commemoration of our Holy Father Onesimus the Thaumaturge
Saint Onesimus was born in the city of Caesarea in Palestine during the reign of Diocletian, the son of pious parents who, as report has it, had been baptized by a divine angel, and had been informed by the same angel of the conception and name of their son. Having been born and raised in the discipline and admonition of the Lord, he set out for one of the monasteries situated near Ephesus in which eight hundred ascetics dwelt, and became a monk, thereafter striving beyond the strength of human nature. Meanwhile, his parents, saddened by his bereavement, had become blind. When a persecution against the Christians arose, and all the ascetics had fled, he himself went to his father’s house as a stranger. And he did indeed restore his parents’ sight through prayer, yet he did not at all reveal himself to them; rather, he left a written account of the course of his life on a parchment, placing it in one of the house’s windows, and departed for Magnesia…
where having performed many miracles, he migrated to God.
And the commemoration of our holy Father Joseph, the confessor.
Our holy Father Joseph flourished during the reign of Theophilus the Iconoclast; he was the son of Photinus and Theoctiste, and brother to Theodore, the superior of the Studite monastery, who, because of his signal probity of character, was by common suffrage created bishop of Thessalonica. After a few years had passed, since he had taught the orthodox faith, he returned to the royal city by the emperor’s command. He and his brother were brought before the iconoclast emperor and were compelled in vain to renounce the adoration of the venerable icons. Theodore, indeed, was ordered to be sent into exile at the lake of Apollonias. As for Joseph, after being led through various prisons and having endured the rest of his tribulations and hardships with fortitude, he was sent back again by a certain impious man to the emperor; having been tempted in vain to subscribe to the tome of the heresy, he was thrust into a most abysmal dungeon and ended his life.
OF THE SAME MONTH. THE FIFTEENTH DAY.
The contest of the holy martyrs Cyricus and Julitta.
Julitta, the martyr of Christ, flourished under the emperor Diocletian, from the city of Iconium. When the persecution prevailed at Iconium, taking her son Cyricus, who was three years old, she withdrew to Seleucia; encountering the same persecution there, she set out for Tarsus. There, Alexander the governor, a cruel and savage man, was harassing the saints. Having been seized and separated from her child, she was subjected to tortures. The governor, placing the child upon his knees, meanwhile attempted to lure him with blandishments. But the child, turning his face away from him and fixing his gaze upon his mother, called upon the name of Christ with a stammering voice and strove to go to his mother. Wherefore, he was kicked by the cruel beast and thrown down the steps; having struck his head against a stone and crushed it, he gave up his spirit. But his mother, glorifying God after many tortures, was herself beheaded.
And the contest of the holy martyr Abudimus.
The martyr of Christ, Abudimus, flourished under the emperor Diocletian, from the island of Tenedos. Having been seized and strongly urged to renounce Christ, he was not persuaded; but rather, he confessed His divinity with boldness. Wherefore, he was later stretched out for scourging and was struck by nine soldiers. And when the impious executioners forced him to taste of meat offered to idols, he resisted. Wherefore, he was lacerated by them with iron claws; and having been tempted in vain with many other tortures, he was finally beheaded. And behold, at mid-day, the martyr appeared to Diocletian with angels holding swords, and with heavenly terror
he struck him, and says: "Behold, the man of the true God whom you think to be dead; but God, by His own assistance, shows him to you, as he is stronger than the fellow-workers of the demons." The lawless one, who ought to have been converted by the patience of God and to have believed in Christ, became rather more enraged and delivered the body of the martyr to the flames.
The struggle of the holy martyrs Antiochus and Cyriacus.
Antiochus, a martyr of Christ, was from Sebaste, by profession a physician, going about all the cities and healing those who were in sickness. But having been seized by the governor Adrian, he was first afflicted with many tortures; afterwards, being cast into a cauldron and not burned, he is led to be exposed to wild beasts, to which the beasts, rejoicing and moving about at his feet, were fawning upon him. But one leopard, with a human voice, reproached the governor. Meanwhile, the holy man was praying, and by his prayers he dissolved all the idols into dust. Finally, he was beheaded, and milk flowed from his neck along with the blood. Cyriacus, the executioner who had decapitated the saint, having seen the miracle and having gained confidence, confessed himself a Christian and, pronouncing an anathema upon the idols of Adrian, he himself was also beheaded and added to the holy Antiochus. And thus, having been perfected, they received from the heavenly and great King the kingdom of heaven.
The struggle of the holy martyr Paul and his company.
These were Egyptians by race; having been captured and led to the city of Diocesarea, they were presented to the governor; and having been tested, they confessed our true God. Their left feet were burned, and their right eyes were gouged out; and they were perfected by sword and fire. And many other men and women were with them who had confessed the name of Christ. And the holy Thea, having been stretched upon a rack, was flayed; and her sister Valentina, attacking the judge, overturned the altar with her foot; wherefore she too was flayed most cruelly. But Paul, the holy martyr, after receiving the death sentence by the sword, and standing, prayed for Christians, for Jews, for Samaritans, for Greeks, and for other nations, that they might come to the knowledge of God, and that the persecution against the Christians might cease. By doing this he moved everyone to pity and tears, and after this was beheaded.
IN THE SAME MONTH.
The sixteenth day.
Commemoration of the holy Council of Chalcedon of six hundred and thirty Fathers.
After the condemnation of the impious Arius, which took place by the three hundred holy Fathers in Nicaea, Eutyches the heretic, inspired by the devil, wished to renew his heresy, saying that there is one nature in Christ after the union. But after the death of Theodosius the son of Arcadius, the holy Marcian, having gained the empire, convened...
in Chalcedon a holy synod of six hundred and thirty God-bearing Fathers; and he overthrew not only the unhappy and miserable Eutyches and his accomplices, but also utterly destroyed Arianism, confirming and establishing the holy symbol of the holy Fathers, and anathematizing all heretics. In this task, the holy great martyr Euphemia co-operated, and, as if living, she provided the definition of the orthodox faith to the orthodox.
The contest of the holy martyrs Onesiphorus and Porphyrius.
The martyr of Christ, Onesiphorus, was by origin from the city of Iconium, and was a kinsman of the empress Tryphaena; he dwelt in the city of Iconium.
Where
, having received the great apostle Paul, he was taught by him the word of truth, and having been baptized along with his whole house, he preached Christ. For this reason, being persecuted, he departed from Iconium and dwelt in Parium. Being wealthy, he took great care of the poor. Also, when Paul was departing for Jerusalem, he gave much money for the ministry of the brethren, and he followed him as he was being sent in chains to Rome, and at his exhortation returned again to Parium. Having been seized by the governor together with his servant Porphyrius, he was tortured: then, being bound to wild horses and dragged for fourteen miles, he gave up his spirit. And Porphyrius also, having suffered torments along with him in all the struggles which he endured for God, ended his life.
The contest of the holy martyr Athenogenes.
Athenogenes, the hieromartyr of Christ, was by origin from Sebaste during the reign of Diocletian. Having been seized by the governor together with his ten disciples, and having endured many tortures with them for the love of Christ, he finally received his end by the sword. It is told concerning him, that before he was seized, having departed to the monastery, he did not find his disciples; for they had been previously seized. But he blessed a doe that ran to meet him, which he had reared in the monastery, and prayed that it might not be captured by hunters, nor its offspring; but that it should, at each recurring year, keep his memory, and also that which was to be born of it. And so it happened. For it is seen that after the reading of the holy Gospels, the doe enters the church, and having offered her fawn to the saint, she goes out again. And those who are gathered in the church, sacrificing it, celebrate the glory and honor of the hieromartyr.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
THE SEVENTEENTH.
The contest of the holy martyr Marina.
Marina, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Antioch in Pisidia
daughter of Edesimus, a priest of idols. Being a Christian, she was seized and brought before the governor Olymbrius; and although she was subjected to many tortures, she in no way denied Christ, mocking the weakness and vanity of the idols. She was therefore cast into prison, where a great dragon appeared to her, having serpents around its neck, which, hissing around the saint, threatened to devour her. But she, signing herself and forming the sign of the cross, killed it. Then she was thrown into a lake of water; and a dove appearing, blessed the water and baptized her. Having gone forth from the lake and being brought again before the governor, and having freely confessed Christ, she received the sentence of death. And when she had reached the place of execution and had prayed for a long time, she was beheaded.
ON THE SAME MONTH. THE EIGHTEENTH.
The contest of the holy martyr Emilianus.
Emilianus, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Dorostolum in Lower Moesia, in the times of Julian the Apostate. Although he was a slave to a certain Greek, he was by profession a Christian. Having found an opportunity, he took a hammer and entered the temple of the idols, and smashed all of the statues, and scattered the sacrifices. The idolaters, not knowing who had done this, seized a certain farmer and began to beat him, and dragged him before the governor. Then the saint, seeing this, surrendered himself, saying, "I am the one who did this." When he was brought before the governor, he rebuked his folly, as one who put his faith in vain idols. Wherefore he provoked him to anger; and though he was beaten most severely with rods, and remained steadfast in his confession of Christ, he was delivered to the fire. And in the midst of it, blessing and praising God, he gave up his holy soul.
And the contest of the holy martyr Hyacinth, in the city of Amastris.
Hyacinth, the martyr of Christ, was born of pious parents, having for his father Theoclitus and for his mother Neonilla, under Heraclius, bishop of Amastris. This name was imposed upon him by an angel. And when he had reached the age of three, by the invocation of Christ he raised a dead child to life. As he grew in age and virtue, anticipating the wisdom of old age, he performed many miracles in the meantime. Seeing the idolaters superstitiously worshipping trees—specifically a tall and cultivated elm—he cut it down. Having been seized, therefore, he was brought before the ruler and the leading men of the city of Amastris. And having been severely beaten, and his teeth plucked out by the roots, he was bound with ropes and dragged outside the city, and pierced with sharp reeds. Then, having been cast into prison, he surrendered his spirit to God. His relics, however, were deposited in that same city, perpetually pouring forth healings.
And the contest of the holy martyr Theodosia.
Theodosia, the martyr of Christ, lived during the reign of Constan-
stantine Caballinus, from the city of Constantinople, a daughter of pious parents. After her father and mother had passed away, having given all the property that had been left to her to the poor, she entered a monastery and became a nun. When Leo the Iconoclast had seized imperial power, and had cast the most holy patriarch Germanus from his throne, and was rejecting the holy images, wishing also to destroy the bronze image of our Savior in the Chalke, the holy Theodosia, having learned of this, together with other women, and having been inflamed with divine zeal, cast down and crushed the spatharios who was ascending the ladder to destroy the holy image; then, entering the patriarchy, she rebuked the heretic Anastasius. For this reason, some of the women were beheaded, but the holy Theodosia, pulled by ropes, was put to death by the horn of a rushing ox in the ox-market.
OF THE SAME MONTH. THE NINETEENTH DAY.
Commemoration of our holy Father Dius.
Our holy Father Dius was laboring during the reign of Theodosius the Great, in Antioch of Syria. Having reached the highest summit of the ascetical life, and having received a revelation from God, he set out for Constantinople and came to the place where his monastery is now founded; and since it was then a dwelling-place of demons, having driven out the evil spirits, he consecrated it to God. Having become known to the emperor for his virtue, he rescued many from temptations and brought them to God, and he built a very large temple, and performed many miracles. For having stuck his staff into the earth, it being dry, he caused it to sprout, which is seen to this day; and he caused water to gush forth, and raised a dead man. When he had fallen into sickness, and, being given up, was lying as if dead, and the patriarchs Atticus of Constantinople and Alexander of Antioch, who had come to visit him, had arrived, he suddenly regained consciousness and said, "God has granted me fifteen years." Rising, therefore, and having completed that number of years, he departed to the Lord.
And the commemoration of the holy Macrina, sister of Basil the Great.
The holy Macrina, adorned in bodily beauty and with gentle manners, was indeed joined in marriage to a man; but the union having not yet been consummated, after he had consented to this, she lived in journeyings, occupying herself with the divine Scriptures, and nurturing her own brothers as a second mother; for when all the ten children were young, she was the eldest of all. Since she passed her life in holiness and religious exercise, she was a help to many. For she was a teacher, not only of words, but also of deeds. "For whoever shall do and teach," the holy Gospel says, "he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." And when the hour of death was at hand, she philosophized together with her brother, Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, who had come to visit her
And therefore he was killed by them for this reason. For they contradicted him all the days; and the prefect of the people killed him because he was rebuked by him. He was buried honorably by his relatives in that region, when he had flown off to God, for whom he had endured many tribulations from the impious, about to receive good things, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love Him.
ON THE SAME MONTH, THE TWENTY-SECOND DAY
Commemoration of the Holy Mary Magdalene.
Mary Magdalene was from Magdala in the mountains of Syria. When she was vexed by seven demons, she was healed by Christ. Because of this benefit, she followed him and became his disciple, and was ministering to him until his passion. And when she brought ointment together with the other Mary, she was the first to see the resurrection; when at the evening of the Sabbath she saw an angel, and in the morning two angels sitting in white vestments; and again she saw the Lord Himself, whom she supposed to be the gardener, and heard him saying to her: "Touch me not."
