After the divine ascension of Christ, therefore, she went to Ephesus to the divine John, the apostle and evangelist, and there she fell asleep in holiness. And she was placed at the entrance of the cave in which the holy and blessed seven youths sleep. But later, under the Emperor Leo the Wise, her holy relics were brought, and were deposited in the monastery of Saint Lazarus which he had built.
ON THE SAME MONTH, THE TWENTY-THIRD DAY
Contest of the Holy Hieromartyr Phocas.
Phocas the hieromartyr was during the reign of Trajan, shining with blameless conduct and every kind of virtue. Having been seized, therefore, he was brought to the prefect Africanus. And when questioned, he confessed Christ. But the prefect contending with him in words, and attempting to make him blaspheme Christ, and to subject him to torments, an earthquake occurring, he suddenly fell down together with the soldiers under him, and lay as one dead. But the saint having prayed, recalled him and the soldiers to life. And having been seized again, he was sent in chains to Trajan. And in his presence, when he had preached Christ and had discoursed about His whole dispensation, he was suspended and flayed. And when he remained the more in his confession of Christ, he was cast into a burning furnace; and emerging from it unharmed, he was cast into a bath that was heated greatly and inflamed beyond measure; and there, praising God—just as the three holy youths in the furnace sprinkled with dew—he delivered up his spirit.
And the contest of the holy martyr Trophimus and his company.
Trophimus and Theophilus, martyrs of Christ, with
their holy companions, by the permission of A God, during the reign of the most impious and tyrannical Diocletian. Confessing Christ, and teaching and baptizing those who approached them in His name, they were recognized and seized, and brought before him in bonds. When they were compelled to deny Christ and to sacrifice to idols, and would not be persuaded, they were severely beaten. Being suspended on a beam, they were flayed. Then they were stoned. And after this, having been taken down from the beam, they were thrown into a great furnace. But, delivered by the grace of God from the furnace and coming out unharmed, so that not even their hair was touched by the fire, they astonished the tyrant. And finally, having bowed their necks, their holy heads were cut off.
And the commemoration of the brethren slaughtered in Bulgaria.
During the reign of Nicephorus, the father of Stauracius, it happened that a war took place between the Romans and the Bulgarians. And when the emperor had won a victory against the enemy, the people were elated and indulged in food and drink. But the remaining Bulgarians, incited by the devil, attacked the Roman army by night, and captured and killed the emperor himself; and those under his command, some they slew and some they took captive. Hence, those who did not find time to escape perished immediately; but those who were able to flee to the nearby mountains escaped unharmed. Those, however, who came into the power of the enemy were urged to deny Christ (for the Bulgarians did not yet know Him), and since they would not do so, they were subjected to various and harsh kinds of death: some were beheaded with the sword, others were suspended and suffocated, others were pierced through with missiles and thus finished their course. And others, condemned to imprisonment and famine, completed the course of martyrdom.
And the contest of the holy hieromartyrs Apollinaris and Vitalius, bishop of Ravenna, and Apollonius, and the martyr Eugenius, and Susanna in Leucate.
IN THE SAME MONTH.
The twenty-fourth day.
The contest of the holy martyr Christina.
Christina, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Tyre. Having a father who was a commander, she was taken by him to a high tower so that she might not be seen by anyone, he having taken his own gods up to the tower and commanded her to sacrifice to them and worship them. But she, understanding their weakness, paid no heed to them at all; but looking out of the window at the beauty of the sky, and discerning the Creator from His works, she shattered the idols and cast them down. Being therefore discovered and brought down from the tower, she was subjected to every torture by her own father. Then, thrust into custody, she received food from an angel; and having been thrown into the sea, she had the water as a baptism. Afterward, she came out of the sea, and was again cast into prison.
having received the water for baptism, and having gone out of the sea, they were shut up again in prison. After the death of her father, having been brought for examination to the governor Diones, she was beaten severely. And having performed miracles, she caused many to believe in Christ. And having had her breasts cut off, and having been pierced through the heart with spears, she was perfected.
IN THE SAME MONTH, THE TWENTY-FIFTH.
Commemoration of Saint Anna, the mother of the Theotokos.
Anna, the venerable mother of our glorious Lady the Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary, was of the tribe of Levi, from Bethlehem of Judea, the daughter of Matthan the priest. This Matthan was serving in the priesthood during the reign of Cleopatra, before the reign of Herod the son of Antipater. He had three daughters: Maria, Soben, and Anna. The first daughter was married in Bethlehem and gave birth to Salome, who is also called Maria. The second also married in Bethlehem and gave birth to Elisabeth, the mother of the Forerunner. Anna married in the land of Galilee and gave birth to Mary the Theotokos; so that Salome, Elisabeth, and the Theotokos were the daughters of three sisters. Anna, as we have said, having brought forth the great benefit, the salvation of the world, the immaculate and faultless Theotokos, and having reared her and brought her into the temple of the Lord, and having dedicated her to God, departed with joy to Him.
And the commemoration of Saint Eupraxia.
Saint Eupraxia flourished during the reign of Theodosius, to whom she was related; she was the daughter of Antigonus the senator. Upon his death, she was brought by her mother, Eupraxia, to the emperor as their kinsman and guardian, and she lived under his protection. Having been betrothed to a certain senator, since he died before the marriage could be consummated, she distributed her wealth to the poor and, together with her mother, withdrew to the city of Thebes in Egypt. Having entered the monastery where one hundred nuns resided, she took the habit. She remained in the monastery, living a life equal to the angels. Her mother went around her estates in the East, sold them, gave a portion to the poor, and donated a portion to the churches, then returned to the monastery and, after living a short time longer, fell asleep. After this, Eupraxia arrived at the summit of virtue and, having performed miracles, rested in the Lord.
And the commemoration of Saint Olympias.
Saint Olympias lived during the reign of Arcadius and Honorius, the sons of Theodosius the Great. She was the daughter of Acundus the comes, and the granddaughter of Ablabius the prefect; she was called a bride but was the wife of no man. For he who had taken her as his wife having departed to the Lord, she remained both virgin and widow. She spent all the days of her life in fastings, in prayers, and in the greatest liberality toward the poor. And the property that she possessed...
distributing all she had to the needy, and emptying all her wealth for the care of the priests of Christ, she especially honored the blessed John Chrysostom, serving him in his infirmities. But after he had suffered unjust exile by the empress Eudoxia, she herself was finally adorned with the crown of confession. For she was banished for the sake of the truth and endured many tribulations. But until the end, giving thanks to God, she gave up her spirit.
*And the commemoration of our holy Fathers, who were gathered in the fifth synod.*
In the seventh year of the emperor Justinian, Anthimus the heretic became Patriarch of Constantinople, who had formerly been Bishop of Trebizond, but being transferred from there, he ascended the great throne of the imperial city. But being a heretic, he was cast out by the orthodox, and in his place, Menas, the most holy presbyter of the Church of Constantinople and administrator of the Xenodochium of Sampson, was ordained by Agapetus, Pope of great Rome. In his time there appeared Severus and Peter, men carrying every heresy within themselves, who disturbed the Church of Christ, vexing the orthodox. Wherefore the emperor Justinian convened a synod of one hundred and sixty-five holy Fathers in Constantinople, and he anathematized them and their followers, as well as every heresy. Since then, the Church of God, observing such a commemoration, glorifies God.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The twenty-sixth day.
*The Contest of the holy hieromartyr Hermolaus and his companions.*
Hermolaus the hieromartyr, and his companions Hermippus and Hermocrates, were presbyters from the clergy of the Church of Nicomedia, survivors of the twenty thousand holy ones whom the impious Maximian burned in the church. They were hidden in a certain small house. But after Saint Panteleemon was seized and brought for questioning before the impious Maximian, he was compelled to indicate where Hermolaus was hiding; and since he did not know how to lie, he confessed the location. Therefore Hermolaus, Hermippus, and Hermocrates were captured, bound, and brought to the tyrant; they freely confessed Christ, and they mocked the idols and reviled them, and they called those who believed in them miserable. Wherefore, having been tortured with various torments, they were beheaded: and thus having been perfected, they received an indissoluble kingdom and eternal life.
*And the contest of the holy martyr Sanctus and his companions.*
These men lived under the emperor Marcus Antoninus, and were from the city of Ravenna in the province of Italy. Because they confessed Christ, they were seized by the governor of the province, and were first afflicted with the harshest punishments,
being forced to deny Christ. And since they would not do this, they were delivered into prison. Afterwards, being brought out of prison, they were tortured again. For one had heated bronze plates applied to his sides; another was delivered to beasts; another was seated upon a red-hot iron throne. And a certain woman, having been scourged from morning until evening, and hung upon a piece of wood, and thrown to the beasts, and tied to horses and dragged for a long time, gave up her spirit. The rest, having been cast into prison, were strangled with ropes and thrown to the dogs to be devoured; and their remains, having remained untouched, were thrown into the river Rhone.
And the commemoration of the venerable John of the Palaeolaura, and of the holy Maurice.
OF THE SAME MONTH. 27th Day. Contest of the holy great martyr Panteleemon.
Panteleemon, the greatest martyr of Christ, was from the city of Nicomedia, the son of Eustorgius, a pagan, and Eubula, a Christian, and a physician by profession. He learned this art from Euphrosynus, who enjoyed the greatest reputation among physicians; but he received the faith of Christ from the priest Hermolaus, by whom he was also baptized. Because of this, he also restored to life a child who had been struck by a viper and died, and he made a blind man see; and he performed many other miracles. Having been denounced to the Emperor Maximian, and arrested, and having confessed Christ, he was tortured in various ways. And finally, having received the sentence of the sword, having been bound in chains, and having reached the place of his perfection, he was tied to an olive tree. And having had his head cut off, he shed blood and milk; which is seen even to this day, and provides healings to all the faithful who approach.
And the commemoration of the holy Anthusa.
The venerable Anthusa flourished during the reign of Constantine Caballinus. Having renounced the world and having desired Christ, she lived in mountains and caves. And having found a certain holy monk and priest sitting in the districts of Mantineum, she took him as one to be imitated in asceticism. And she advanced so much in virtue that she even entered a furnace that was burning fiercely without being burned. But after the death of Sisinnios, the most holy priest, having been denounced by Caballinus for honoring and worshipping the holy icons, she was forced by those who were sent to her to deny their veneration. And because she did not consent, she was beaten severely. But when she revealed to the Emperor’s wife, who was unable to give birth, that she would bear two children, a male and a female; when this happened, she was released from the torture. And thus she caused the Empress to be so disposed toward her that she was held by her in place of a mother. And in this manner she fell asleep.
OF THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-EIGHTH DAY.
The contest of the holy martyr Eustathius of Ancyra.
Eustathius, a martyr of Christ, was a soldier by profession and a Christian by religion. Brought before Cornelius, the governor of Ancyra, and questioned, he confessed Christ with boldness. Wherefore he was severely beaten, his vertebrae were pierced, and being bound with ropes, he was dragged from the city of Ancyra as far as the river Sangarius, while the governor followed and watched. There, being locked in a casket, he was cast into the river. But by the will of God, a divine angel arrived, brought the casket to the land, and the saint was found within it unharmed, chanting: "He that dwelleth in the aid of the Most High," and the rest. When the governor learned this, he was filled with shame, and drawing his sword, he killed himself. The holy martyr, praying and having become a partaker of the divine gift through a dove sent to him from heaven, surrendered his spirit into the hands of the appearing angel; and his relics were deposited in the same city of Ancyra.
And the contest of the holy martyr Acacius.
Acacius, a martyr of Christ, was illustrious in the reign of Licinius. Brought before him, and having confessed Christ, he was hung up and his flesh torn. Then he was handed over to the prefect Terentius, by whose command he was thrown into a red-hot pot filled with pitch, oil, and fat. Having suffered no harm, he was forced to follow the prefect as he departed for Apamea and Apolloniada, and having been brought there into the temple of idols, by pouring out prayers he shattered all the statues. After this, he was handed over to a tribune, and having been severely beaten, he fought with wild beasts. Soon after, he was cast into a furnace and remained unharmed. But the tribune, thinking the furnace had cooled, approached to look, and was himself consumed by the flame and reduced to dust. But Acacius was handed over to the governor Possidonius, and wearing heavy iron chains, was led to Miletus; and having there again shattered the idols, he was beheaded, and blood and milk poured from the wound.
And the contest of the holy apostles Prochorus, Nicanor, and those with them.
OF THE SAME MONTH. THE TWENTY-NINTH DAY.
The contest of the holy martyr Callinicus.
Callinicus, a martyr of Christ, was from the region of Cilicia, and being a Christian and teaching the word of Christ, he exhorted men to abstain from vain things and to acknowledge Christ as the maker of all things. Wherefore he was seized and brought before the governor, and was subjected by him to every kind of torture; soon, having been fitted with iron shoes spiked with sharp nails, he was forced to run before the horses as far as the city of Gangra, which is sixty stades away. And having covered the sixty stades on foot, and seeing the soldiers who were leading him away faint from thirst, he poured out prayers
and brought forth water from the earth and gave them to drink. But when he arrived at the city of Gangra, he was cast into prison. And after a few days, having been brought out of prison and compelled to deny Christ, and refusing to be persuaded, he finished his life in the fire. And his venerable relic was laid by the hands of Christians in the very place of his completion.
And the commemoration of our holy Father and confessor John, metropolitan of Chalcedon.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The thirtieth day.
Commemoration of the blessed John the soldier. B 
He served in the army under Julian the Apostate. Having therefore been sent with other soldiers for the persecution against the Christians, he seemed to those who saw him to be a persecutor, but secretly he championed the Christians; to some, before they were captured, he signaled that they should flee, and for others, after they had been seized, he devised a secret escape. And he showed sympathy not only to these, but he also supplied the necessities to the needy. And he adorned his life with prayers and fastings, and visitations of the sick, and consolations of the afflicted, and ordered it according to the rule of honesty. Having lived in this manner, he rested in the Lord; and he was laid in the place where foreigners were also buried. But later, he made himself known to a certain woman through a vision: for appearing to her, he revealed his deeds in life and the name by which he was called. Performing also many other miracles, he also checks the flight of slaves.
And the commemoration of the holy apostles Silas, Silvanus, Crescens, Epaenetus, and Andronicus.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The thirty-first day.
The Contest of the holy martyr Julitta
C 
Julitta, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Having a lawsuit against a certain greedy and violent man, who, intending to claim for himself the abundance of this land, had transferred to himself fields, and animals, and villages, and servants, and all the equipment of life, making light of justice and God, and relying on slanderers, false witnesses, and bribes offered to the judges: when she stood before the judge and began to expose the man's tyrannical usurpation, she was accused by him of being a Christian. And paying no regard to any of the present things, but despising them all, she said: "Let life and its glory depart. For I will not deny the creator and maker of all things." Therefore, the unjust judge immediately delivered her to the flames. The furnace, having embraced the body of the holy woman like a splendid bridal chamber, sent her soul to the heavenly realm, but it preserved her venerable body whole and incorrupt for her relatives and for all the faithful.
And the commemoration of our holy Father Eudocimus the Younger.
This blessed man lived during the reign of Theophilus, the enemy of Christ,
whose parents were of Cappadocian lineage; they had combined the splendor of the age (for they were patricians) with the orthodox religion. Wherefore Eudocimus, being excellently reared by them in virtue, was promoted by Theophilus to the rank of Candidatus and was also appointed to a military command, first in the province of Cappadocia, and then in the district of Charsianum. He was everywhere a just balance and a rule, observing all equality, bestowing most abundant alms daily, adorning the churches, defending widows and orphans, and, in short, mirroring every form of virtue. Having lived in this manner according to God, he was eventually seized by a bodily illness and rendered his spirit unto God. His relatives, fulfilling his mandate, buried him with his garments and shoes, and God glorified him with many miracles.
IN THE MONTH OF AUGUST
The first day.
The struggle of the holy Maccabees.
Eleazar, that most illustrious man who dwelt in Jerusalem, was the teacher of the seven sons of the holy Solomonis. But when Jerusalem had been depopulated by King Seleucus, and the people of the Hebrews led into captivity, these also were detained and were compelled to taste of the sacrifices of the Gentiles and to eat polluted foods. But they were never persuaded; rather, struggling for the laws of their fathers, they were subjected to diverse tortures. First, indeed, Eleazar was harshly beaten and cast into the fire, and praying, he delivered his spirit to God. Then the boys, in the order in which they were born, being brought one after another, and exposed to torments, racks, wheels, and fire, were fulfilled for the sake of piety, truly showing a mind that possessed sovereign authority over the passions. And thirdly, their mother Solomonis voluntarily entering the furnace, died upon her own sons.
And the struggle of the holy martyr Leontius and his companions.
The martyrs of Christ, Leontius and Alexander, together with their holy companions, lived during the reign of the emperor Diocletian and were from the region of Pamphylia. Being from diverse places, yet having one purpose towards our Lord Jesus Christ, inasmuch as they were born of Christian parents, having therefore taken counsel together and holding all the affairs of this world as nothing, they reached the temple of Diana. And being there, they overturned all the idols. Being discovered, therefore, and seized, they were beaten severely, and were torn with iron claws, and their eyes were pierced with awls; and being delivered to prison, they remained for many days without food. Afterwards, brought forth from the prison, they were exposed to wild beasts. But the beasts did not touch them. Finally, having received the sentence by the sword, they were beheaded.
B']
The Contest of the Holy Hieromartyr Stephen and His Companions
Stephen the hieromartyr was during the reign of Valerian, a native of ancient Rome. While he was hiding because of the persecution in a small dwelling, he used to baptize the Gentiles who came to him and would ordain deacons and presbyters, and he prayed to God for the salvation of the world. Having also healed the daughter of Emesius the tribune of the plebs, he persuaded him to be baptized; and not only him, but also a multitude of men and women, who were perfected through various tortures. Gathering their relics, the high priest Stephen buried them honorably. Afterward, being compelled to enter the temple of Mars and to worship, he entered, and having prayed, he threw down the idol. After this, while he was performing the sacred rites, he was beheaded; and he was laid to rest in that very chair, together with his disciple, who held in his hand the holy symbol of the faith.
And the Finding of the Relics of the Holy Martyr Dadas and His Companions
These holy martyrs were during the reign of the emperor Maximian in the city of Dorostolon in the region of Thrace. Having been seized and brought before the governor, they were compelled to sacrifice to the idols. And as they did not obey, they were cast into prison. While the holy Maximus was reading the divine Scriptures to his fellow martyrs, they fell asleep and saw the devil holding weapons of war and fighting against them. And having been awakened, they saw an angel of God giving them courage. Afterward, they were cruelly beaten, and having received the sentence [to be executed] by the sword, they were led to the place of the condemned, and there their heads were cut off on the twenty-eighth day of April. Their precious relics were found through an angel on the second day of August; these now lie in the church of the holy Theotokos located in the district of Vigilantia, performing many healings for those who come to them.
And the Translation of the Relics of the Holy Protomartyr Stephen
During the reign of Constantine the Great, the relic of the holy Protomartyr Stephen was revealed. For a certain man, a presbyter named Lucian, who lived in the village where it lay hidden under the earth, found it through a divine vision. For the first champion appeared to him three times and made himself known. And when John the archbishop learned of this, he was filled with joy and traveled to the place with the clergy. And having dug, he found the casket. Suddenly there was a great earthquake, and a most sweet fragrance.
IN THE SAME MONTH. The Third Day. Memory of the Holy Dalmatus, Faustus, and Isaacius
The blessed Isaacius was previously practicing virtue in the desert
and having subdued the affections of the body and conquered the demons, afterwards by divine providence came to Constantinople, and dwelling in one of the city's monasteries, which is now called the Dalmatos [Monastery], through his virtue and teaching he persuaded many to forsake the world and become monks and be saved. Among whom were Dalmatus and his son Faustus. For the latter, being a soldier in the times of the Emperor Theodosius, having one day encountered the saint by chance, and having tasted of his conversation, he deserted both his wife and children, and taking with him only his son Faustus, came to him and became a monk, tonsuring his son as well. And thus they labored, so as to become renowned before the emperor and senate, and performed many wonders for the glory of God; and thus after the death of Isaacius they finished their lives.
IN THE SAME MONTH.
The Fourth Day.
The Contest of the Holy Martyr Ia and those with her.
This woman flourished in the time of Sapor, King of the Persians, being of very advanced age. She was seized, along with nine thousand Christian captives who were taken away and given over to the chief magi to be tormented with various kinds of torture; and along with them, this blessed woman bore these tortures with a constant mind: and after she had been vexed with many punishments, she was beheaded.
The contest of the holy martyr Eleutherius the cubicularius.
Eleutherius, the martyr of Christ, was a native of the city of Byzantium in the time of the Emperor Maximian, one of the senators, and also numbered among the emperor's intimate eunuchs. Since he had pleased God through instruction in His commandments, yet had not been perfected by the divine baptism, and wishing to be baptized, he asked the emperor to allow him to go to his own suburban estate. Having obtained the favor, he went to the river Sangarius, and having built a subterranean church there, and having brought a presbyter, he was baptized there. But wishing to flee the emperor, he feigned illness. When Maximian learned of this, he came to the place, and having seen with his own eyes the temple and the arrangement of the altar, he burned with anger; and having seized Eleutherius, he first subjected him to dire tortures: shortly thereafter he cut off his head. D
IN THE SAME MONTH.
The Fifth Day.
The Contest of the Holy Martyr Eusignius.
Eusignius, the martyr of Christ, was from the great city of Antioch, and served as a military commander in the times of Constantius, father of the great Constantine; and he lived until the times of Julian the Apostate. Being apprehended for the sake of the Christian faith, he was subjected to questioning. And when he rebuked the apostate for having forsaken the true God and approached vain idols as if they were gods, he was beaten with cudgels and tormented with harsh tortures. After he had been punished severely
for he was one hundred and ten years old), he was thrown into prison. And having been brought out of prison after some days, and having stood again before the apostate, he was compelled to deny Christ and sacrifice to the idols. And as he would not be persuaded, but rather rebuked the tyrant again, his head was cut off with a sword; and thus he was perfected, having received an unfading crown and eternal life.
ON THE SAME MONTH, THE SIXTH DAY
A 194 The Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ.
After Christ had spoken much to His disciples about dangers and certain sorrowful things, and had affirmed that these things belonged to the present life, but that good things are in hope, wishing to show them what that glory is with which He is to come, He took them up to a high mountain apart, and was transfigured before them; and His face shone as the sun, and His garments became as brilliant as the light. And Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with Him. He took only three of the others as being the most excellent; but He brought Moses and Elijah into their midst, correcting the incorrect opinions concerning Him held by many. For since some said He was Elijah, and others Jeremiah, for this reason He presented these men, so that He might show the disciples the distinction between the servants and the Lord, and might persuade them that He has power over both death and life.
ON THE SAME MONTH, THE SEVENTH DAY
The Contest of The Holy Martyr Dometius.
Dometius, the martyr of Christ, was from the region of Phrygia during the tyranny of Julian the Apostate. Seeing that many were yielding to the tyrant, and that the number of those who were denying Christ and worshipping idols was increasing daily, he was distressed and indignant, and was seized with great sorrow. One day, therefore, when the chariot races were being held, and a sacrifice was being offered to the unclean demons, he could not endure it; but, inflamed by divine zeal, he stood in the middle of the theater, and with a loud voice anathematized the apostate Julian, spit upon the idolaters, and mocked the falsely named gods. Having therefore been seized and bound securely, he was delivered to the governor; and after having endured many tortures, he was shut up in prison. And after a few days, having been brought out of prison and forced to deny Christ, and not being persuaded, his sacred head was cut off by the sword.
And the commemoration of the slaughter of the Persians and of the Avars.
During the reign of Heraclius, Chosroes, the king of the Persians, sent a general with a force of many men. And he devastated the entire Roman state. This same general came even to Chalcedon, desiring to take also
the city of Constantinople. Heraclius, however, wishing to create a diversion against the Persians, and being short of troops, left the city to his son Constantine and departed secretly. Having boarded a ship and navigated the straits, he eluded the Persians, and having gathered an army and marched into Persia, he laid the region waste. The leader of the Avars, becoming aware that Heraclius was in Persia, broke the peace treaty, came as far as the Golden Gate, and waged war. The city was thus besieged by both land and sea. But the people of God, along with the patriarch, having instituted public prayers and carrying the icon of the most holy Mother of God, drove away the enemies. Since that time, the city has celebrated such a procession in thanksgiving.
And the commemoration of the pious empresses Pulcheria and Irene.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The eighth day.
The Contest of the Holy Martyr Marinus
Christ’s martyr Marinus lived during the reign of Diocletian and was from the city of Anazarbus. Being a Christian and leading many of the unbelievers to Christ and baptizing them, he was denounced to the prefect Lysias. Being seized and standing before him, he confessed Christ, was beaten severely, and, having heavy irons placed upon him, was cast into prison. The next day, he was led to the interrogation, and because he was compelled to deny Christ and sacrifice to idols, and did not consent to do so, he was suspended by his feet from a rack and beaten with whips. Then he was burned with torches; and having remained in his confession of Christ until his last breath, he received the sentence of death by the sword. Being dragged outside the city, his holy head was cut off. His body, thrown to the dogs to be eaten, was committed to burial by a certain pious man named Xanthius.
And the contest of our holy Father Emilianus, Bishop of Cyzicus
Our holy Father and great priest-martyr and confessor Emilianus lived during the times of those emperors who were hostile to icons, and was bishop of the city of Cyzicus. He shone forth not only in piety and knowledge and the other qualities worthy of true bishops, but also in mercy toward the poor, compassion, long-suffering, and kindness. He possessed a divine zeal for the orthodox faith; and he rebuked with boldness those who did not show adoration and honor to the sacred icons, calling them heretics and enemies of Christ. Having been denounced to the Christ-hating emperor Leo by the enemies of the truth, he was seized and brought to him in chains. Having been subjected first to countless afflictions and later banished from his fatherland, he endured many trials in exile and was brought to his end.
And the memory of our holy Father Theodosius.
Our holy Father Theodosius from his tender
obedience to the commandment of Christ, which says: "Whoever does not leave father and mother, and brothers and sisters, and fields, and house, and does not take up his cross and follow after me, cannot be my disciple"; he left everything, and taking up his cross upon his shoulders, followed Him eagerly. And having become a monk, he lived a solitary life, fleeing into the desert. Sometimes he would spend his time in the mountains, sometimes he would dwell in caves, nourishing himself on the fruits of trees and the herbs growing among the rocks; by night and by day beseeching God for his own salvation and that of the world. Leading his life in this manner, he received also the gift of miracles, and having restored health to many infirm people, he departed joyfully to God.
And the memory of our holy Father and wonderworker Myron.
Myron, the holy and great hierarch, was from the island of Crete, during the reign of Decius, and was the son of noble parents. Being joined by them in marriage to a woman, he conducted his life according to the rule of piety; and cultivating the land with all care, he fed the poor with its fruits. Having once a garden of chickpeas, he found some people in it stealing chickpeas. They, while they thought they were gathering chickpeas, were picking thorns. But he, having given them chickpeas, sent them away. Having found others also in the threshing floor who had filled their sacks with grain, and were not able to lift them, he himself placed the sacks upon their shoulders, and sent them away, warning them to depart and to steal no more. Afterwards, having been ordained presbyter, and then bishop, and never casting from his mind the mercy towards the poor, he fell asleep in peace.
And the struggle of the holy martyr Antoninus.
Antoninus, the martyr of Christ, was from the city of Alexandria, a Christian, pious, and fearing God. For this reason, having been seized by the idolaters, he was brought to the prefect; and being questioned, he confessed Christ. Having been suspended, therefore, upon a wooden frame, he was fiercely torn. And being compelled by the executioners and the soldiers standing by the prefect to deny Christ and be released from the torture, he himself, in a loud voice, proclaimed Christ to be the true God all the more; and he mocked and ridiculed the idols and those who worshipped them. Having persisted for a long time in the torments, he received the sentence of fire. And thus, having prayed and exhorted those who were present to acknowledge only Christ as God, he was cast into the furnace, and delivered his blessed soul to God.
And the struggle of the holy martyrs Eleutherius, Leonidas, and the children.
IN THE SAME MONTH. The ninth day.
The struggle of the holy apostle Matthias.
Matthias, the apostle of Christ, was first one of the seventy apostles, excelling in every virtue among
all men. But after Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve disciples, betrayed our Lord Jesus Christ out of avarice to the Jews, who were filled with envy, and after he saw that He had been scourged unto death, he went away and hanged himself, the number of the twelve was diminished. Then Peter, together with the ten disciples who were with him, persisting in prayer, cast lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles in the place of Judas Iscariot. And after this, having preached the Gospel in the outer Ethiopia and enlightened many, he was seized by the unbelievers, and after being beaten most severely, he committed his spirit to God.
The struggle of the holy martyr Julian and his companions.
These flourished in the reign of Emperor Leo the Iconoclast. Being of orthodox faith, and fearing God, and honoring the venerable images, they suffered martyrdom. For seeing him averse to the adoration of the holy images, and burning them with fire, they became jealous and grieved. And when they also saw the venerable image of Christ, which stood at the Bronze Gate, being broken down, they brought their sorrow into the open. And seizing the guardsman who had climbed the ladder to destroy the image, they threw him down with the ladder and killed him; and having moved the tyrant to anger, some were immediately put to death by the sword, being many in number, among whom were not a few women, and Maria the patrician. Others were handed over to custody, and had their faces burned, and having suffered many cruelties, were beheaded.
And the commemoration of the holy Constantine, archbishop of the imperial city.
IN THE SAME MONTH. The tenth day. The struggle of the holy martyrs Lawrence, Xystus, and Hippolytus.
These lived in the time of Emperor Decius. Xystus was born in Athens, where he also applied himself to the study of philosophy. Having come to Rome, he was ordained bishop after the death of the holy martyr Stephen. And having distributed through the hands of the deacon Lawrence the ecclesiastical funds he possessed to the poor, he said to him: "Lawrence, tomorrow we shall be handed over to Decius for examination." And according to his prediction, having been seized, and not persuaded to sacrifice to the idols, he was beheaded. Lawrence was also brought in, and when they demanded the sacred treasure from him, he placed the lame and the maimed, upon whom he had bestowed the money, onto wagons, and brought them before the emperor, saying: "These are those who guard the treasure." Then, being stretched over a grate of glowing coals, he delivered up his spirit. But the holy Hippolytus, taking their relics and burying them, was seized; and having been bound to wild horses, he was dragged to his end.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE ELEVENTH.
Contest of the holy hieromartyr Euplus.
Euplus, the martyr of Christ, flourished in the reign of Diocletian from the city of Catana on the island of Sicily. Being a deacon in the church of that same place, he instructed the people in the faith of Christ, reading aloud the Holy Scriptures. Whereupon, being denounced and seized by the governor, and urged to deny Christ, and not being persuaded, he was bound hand and foot. And being suspended on a wooden frame, he was torn with iron claws and nails, and his bones were crushed with heavy mallets. Then, being taken down from the frame, he was cast into prison, where, being thirsty and having no water to drink, he prayed and brought forth a fountain of water from the earth, and by drinking he gave thanks to God. After this, being cast out of the prison and having his ears bored through with awls, finally he was beheaded by the sword.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE TWELFTH.
Contest of the holy martyrs Photius and Anicetus.
Photius and Anicetus, the martyrs of Christ, flourished in the reign of Diocletian. Now Photius was the nephew of Anicetus. When Diocletian was haranguing the people at Nicomedia and had brought all the instruments of torture into the midst, and threatened that whoever confessed himself a Christian would be subject to death, Anicetus, who was present, declared with a loud voice that he was a Christian. And being seized, he was beaten severely, and he proved the wild beasts turned loose upon him to be gentler than sheep. Then, praying, he crushed the idol of Hercules. Having received the sentence of death by the sword and being about to be beheaded, through prayer he withered the executioner's hand. Then Photius, running up, embraced him; and being seized, he was bound with him; and both, having been tortured in various ways, were finally brought to perfection by fire.
IN THE SAME MONTH. THE THIRTEENTH.
The translation of the relics of our holy Father Maximus the Confessor.
This man lived during the times of Constantine who was called Pogonatus, who was a descendant of Heraclius. Therefore, having been welcomed with the greatest honors by the emperors who preceded him, and being capable of instructing in matters to be done in political administration by means of discussions and methods, and being taught by long experience of affairs, he was promoted to the dignity of the protosyngellos, and became an advisor to the emperors. But when the wicked and degenerate opinion of those who foolishly and impiously asserted one will concerning the economy of Christ in the flesh, removing from the midst one of the two natures, prevailed; and when certain edicts affirming this false doctrine were paraded through the marketplace and displayed upon the great church, he, not enduring to share in the impiety by communing with the ungodly, leaving behind the common
pursuits, chose rather to be an outcast in the house of God than to dwell in the tabernacles of sinners. Having therefore arrived at the monastery in Chrysopolis, he laid aside his hair, where he later became a leader. Then, inflamed by divine zeal as if by fire, he reached the elder Rome and persuaded the most blessed Pope Martin to assemble a local synod and to smite with anathema the leaders of that impious dogma who dreamed of one will in Christ. But he also composed sermons to refute those who thought this way, and writing letters with demonstrations drawn from reason and Scripture that confirm the accuracy of our faith, he disseminated them to all parts of the world. Departing from Rome along with his two disciples named Anastasius, he was arraigned before the senate, which consented to the emperor’s heresy, on the charge that, while all yielded to the emperor, he alone resisted him and stirred others to defection, inducing them through his letters to think the opposite. For this reason, he was sent into custody near Thrace; and persisting in the orthodox faith, he had his right hand and tongue amputated, and was from there banished to the region of Lazica. There, after spending three years and ministering to the needs of his own body himself, he reached the fullness of days and, after a brief illness, rested in the Lord. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Arsenius in that same land of the Lazi, where he works many miracles daily. It is said, however, that after the amputation, his tongue was miraculously restored by God, and that he spoke clearly as long as he lived. Of his two disciples, the elder Anastasius, having had his tongue and right hand cut off just like his master, was cast into distant exile; while the younger was sent to a certain fortress in Thrace, where he ended his life.
ON THE SAME MONTH. The fourteenth day.
Memorial of the holy hieromartyr Marcellus, bishop of Apamea.
This man lived under the Emperor Theodosius and hailed from the island of Cyprus, where, having been entrusted with the civil administration and governance of the province, he astonished everyone by the piety and precision he applied to official matters. Having then crossed over to the priestly order and been appointed bishop of Apamea in Syria, he performed his duties in all other respects justly and holily. He was also a fervent zealot of the faith in Christ, building churches to the glory of God and destroying temples of idols. When he could not succeed in burning one of these, which was called the temple of Zeus, because the demon inhabiting it would not permit it to be consumed or razed to the ground by any engines, the saint took water, blessed it, and sprinkled it upon a stack of wood, causing a fire to ignite and the temple to be consumed by the flames. Having been seized for this by the idolaters and cast into the fire, he received the crown.
ON THE SAME MONTH, THE FIFTEENTH DAY.
The Dormition of our most glorious Lady, the Theotokos.
When it pleased our Lord and God to take up His Mother to Himself, He announced her translation to her through an angel. Upon hearing this, she rejoiced; and ascending the Mount of Olives, having prayed, she returned to her house. And having prepared all things necessary for the burial, she awaited her Son. And when a great thunder occurred, all the apostles arrived from the ends of the earth by clouds in order to tend to her immaculate body. And having arranged herself upon the bed, she committed her holy soul into the hands of her Son and God. Her most immaculate body, having been buried by the holy apostles, was not found after the third day. For Thomas, having opened the tomb to venerate the remains (for he had arrived late), did not find it; for God had translated it to a place which He Himself knows; only the linen cloths were found.
And the contest of the holy martyr Ursicius.
The martyr of Christ, Ursicius, lived during the reign of Maximian, from the region of Illyricum, holding the rank of soldier and the dignity of tribune. Being a Christian, he was denounced to the governor by one of the soldiers under him. And having been seized, he was forced to sacrifice to the idols. Not having been persuaded, he was beaten severely. And having been bound hand and foot with thick ropes smeared with oil, tallow, resin, and pitch, and set on fire, he was burned mercilessly. And as his hands and feet were burning, he cried out and said: "Rightly and justly do I suffer. For these hands are worthy of burning, because they saved the tyrant while he was perishing in the most terrible peril of war—which I wish they had never done!" Upon hearing this, the tyrant, being overcome with shame, having immersed his hands in water and extinguished the burning, released him. But later, having been seized again, the saint was beheaded.
And the commemoration of the destruction of the Hagarenes, which took place by the mercy of God.
During the reign of Leo the Isaurian, a great multitude of Saracens came and surrounded Constantinople by land and by sea, and desired to besiege it. Seeing the necessity of the emperor, as he wished to grant them terms, they even said that guards should be stationed in the city. But the Lord, who opposes the proud, rendered their counsel void. And their leader, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing, asked that he might at least be allowed to enter through the gate of the Bosporus on horseback. And while others were entering without harm, his horse alone, rearing up, would not enter. And looking up and seeing the image of the Theotokos above the gate, he understood that this had happened to him because of his having blasphemed against her. Consequently, therefore, they returned empty-handed; and along the Aegean Sea
perished. Having reached the ships, they were struck by burning hail and perished.
IN THE SAME MONTH.
THE SIXTEENTH DAY.
The contest of the holy martyr Diomedes.
Diomedes, the martyr of Christ, had the city of Tarsus in Cilicia as his fatherland. He had learned the medical art. Yet, in the times of the Emperor Diocletian, he departed from Tarsus and traveled to Nicaea; where, through piety toward God and skill in the medical art, he earned the good favor of those who came to him. From this he was denounced to the emperor. But when those who had come to apprehend him discovered that he had already departed to the Lord, they cut off his head and brought it to the emperor; seeing which, the emperor ordered it to be brought back and joined to the corpse. Upon this being done, it is said that the soldiers who had brought it immediately recovered the use of their own eyes, which they had lost when they had cut off the head of the holy man. And his precious remains were handed over for burial by faithful and pious men.
And the contest of the holy hieromartyr Myron.
This man existed during the time of Emperor Decius, and of Antipater, governor of Achaea, as a presbyter of the Church. On the holy day of Christ’s Nativity, therefore, when Antipater had gone into the church to seize the Christians, this man, being filled with zeal, assailed him with rather harsh words. For this reason, he was suspended and mangled; subsequently, he was cast into a furnace. But the furnace preserved the holy man unharmed, while it burned up one hundred and fifty of the men who were standing around it. And the saint, being forced again to sacrifice to idols, and not being persuaded, was flayed from his shoulders to his feet. From which, taking a thong, he lashed it into the face of the proconsul. Afterwards, with his flesh torn open, he was dismembered: and Antipater, looking upon him and being filled with shame, laid hands upon him himself. He, however, having been taken thence to Cyzicus, and having received the sentence of the sword from that proconsul, was beheaded.
IN THE SAME MONTH.
THE SEVENTEENTH DAY.
The contest of the holy martyr Paul, and Juliana and their companions.
These were during the time of Emperor Aurelian, born in the city of Ptolemais, siblings in the flesh. But Paul, having meditated upon the divinely-inspired Scriptures, was obstructing the mouths of both Jews and Greeks. While, however, the emperor was spending time in the city, he was denounced, and was brought before him; and having confessed Christ, he was suspended and scraped. His sister, seeing this and crying out against the tyrant, was herself also apprehended. And having been suspended, she was scraped, and both were cast into a boiling cauldron of pitch; but having received no harm from this, they were stretched upon an iron bed that had been set on fire, and were beaten upon their loins. Afterwards, they were thrust into prison, and having received angelic food—
they were strengthened; then, having been cast out, they were beaten. Stratonicus, Codratus, and Acacius, the executioners, because they spared the saints, were beheaded along with them.
The Contest of the Holy Martyrs Strato, Philip, and Eutychian
These men, while staying in the city of Nicomedia, used to go to the theater by agreement, so as to instruct the crowd gathered there, to turn them away from the worship of idols, and to bring them to the faith of Christ. One day, therefore, the governor, seeing the theater empty of people and having learned the cause—that the crowds, being taught by the holy martyrs, had abandoned the pleasures of the spectacles and were pursuing a certain new life, having despised the ancestral gods—ordered the saints to be brought before him immediately. And when they stood before him, they confessed that they themselves held to the faith in Christ and that they taught others; being led into the theater, they were exposed to beasts. But being preserved unharmed by them, and having been tested by various modes of torture, they were finally cast into the fire, fought the contest for Christ, and having won the victory, and having received the crown of victory, they obtained the kingdom of heaven.
ON THE SAME MONTH
The Eighteenth Day
The Contest of the Holy Martyrs Florus and Laurus
These were twin brothers, stone-masons by trade. After the martyrdom for Christ of their teachers, they left their occupations in Byzantium and arrived in Illyricum. There, working at their own trade while exploring certain mines under the governor, they were later sent by him to Licinius. From him they received money to build a temple for the idols. But they gave the money to the poor, yet they built the temple; and when it was completed, they broke the idols in pieces and dedicated it to the glory of Christ. Upon learning this, Licinius cast them into a deep pit, where they committed their souls to God. In the time of Constantine the Great, their precious relics were revealed and were brought to Constantinople, and were established in the place where they now lie.
The Contest of the Holy Martyrs Hermas, Serapion, and Polyaenus
These men, having been accused by the infidels because they worshiped Christ and loathed the idols, were arrested and stood before the prefect of Rome. Having confessed with boldness their faith in Christ, they were first shut up in a most dark and foul-smelling prison. Then, being cast out of prison, and not consenting to sacrifice to the idols, they were dragged through narrow and difficult places, bound with ropes; and as they were being dragged, and being dashed against the stones, they committed their sacred souls to God. But their precious and most holy relics, some of the pious Christians, by night, going secretly and taking them up, with psalms and hymns...
have committed them to a tomb, for the glory of our true God Christ, for whom they willingly met their end.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The nineteenth.
The contest of the holy great martyr Andrew and those with him.
This man lived during the reign of Maximian, a commander of soldiers in the East under Antiochus, who held the command of the entire army. Having been sent by him, together with other commanders, against the Persians, and having called upon Christ, he routed the Persians. And at the unhoped-for victory, he drew those who were with him to the faith in Christ. Being slandered to Antiochus, they were brought before him as convicts. And to some, a bed of iron heated by fire was spread out. Others with him were nailed by their hands to square pieces of wood. Then, by the order of Antiochus, they were cast out from the borders of the province by a thousand other soldiers. But the saint, having exhorted them, brought them to the faith in Christ. When Antiochus came to know of this, he pursued them with his men and put them all to the sword. And last of all, the most glorious martyr of Christ, Andrew, the most famous among the champions.
And the contest of the holy martyr Timothy and those with him.
The glorious martyr of Christ, Timothy, was born in Palestine, in the city of Gaza, being perfected in doctrine and all manner of life. Having been detained, he stood before the prefect of Gaza; and being interrogated, and confessing himself a Christian, and explaining the economy of Christ, and His sojourn for our sake, and His incarnation in theological terms, he was beaten cruelly. And being vexed with all kinds of tortures, and yielding in no way, he was delivered to the fire and met his end. On the same day, and in the same city, Agapius and Thecla, who were detained in prison because they taught in the name of Christ and recalled many of the infidels from error to the Lord, and baptized them, standing before the prefect, were brought in, yet would not sacrifice to the idols; but, preserving the love of God undefiled, they were thrown to wild beasts and received the crown of martyrdom.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The twentieth.
Memory of the holy prophet Samuel.
Samuel the glorious and great prophet of God was born in Judea, from Mount Ephraim, of the tribe of Levi, the son of Elcana and Anna. Now Elcana had two wives, of whom one was called Anna, and the second Phænanna. And Phænanna indeed had a child; but Anna had no child. Now Elcana would go up with Anna to Silom to worship God; but the Lord had closed her womb; and
she was grieved because she was reproached by Phænanna as being barren. She prayed therefore to God, and conceived Samuel, and dedicated him to God. He was raised in the temple of the Lord. And when he reached maturity, he served before the Lord, and judged the people of Israel. He also anointed Saul as king, and afterwards David; and having reached a profound old age, he departed to God, one thousand and thirty-five years before the incarnation of Christ.
And the martyrdom of the thirty-seven holy martyrs.
certain Christian, named Severus, born in Side of Pamphylia, went about every city and region, teaching the word of Christ. And when he had come to Philippopolis, a city of Thrace, he found Apellianus the governor [who was] punishing thirty-six holy martyrs. And having openly confessed his piety, he was seized and beaten severely; and thus he was beheaded. But Memnon the centurion, having been bound to two pillars and stretched, was flayed with three thongs from head to foot: all the rest, having had their hands and feet amputated, were cast into an underground furnace, and were perfected by martyrdom.
And the commemoration of St. Theoclitus the wonderworker.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
THE TWENTY-FIRST.
The martyrdom of St. Bassa and her children.
Christ’s martyr Bassa existed in the times of the Emperor Maximian, and was a Christian from her ancestors. Having lived with Valerius, a priest of idols, she bore three sons, Theognes, Agapius, and Pistus, whom she raised in piety. But as she preached Christ, and taught those who approached her the faith in him, she was denounced to the governor of the region by her own husband. And being seized with her children, she stood before him. And first Theognes, having confessed Christ, was suspended and lacerated, while his mother stood by, encouraging him to the struggle; secondly, Agapius was beaten, and the skin of his head was torn off as far as the chest; thirdly, Pistus was subjected to various tortures. And finally, the three, having persevered in their confession of Christ until death, were beheaded together with their mother.
And the martyrdom of the holy martyr Lucius.
Lucius, the martyr of Christ, came from the city of Cyrene in Libya, he being a chief of the same city and an assessor to the governor, excelling those of his station in the magnitude of his body and the power of his wealth. And being a worshipper of idols, he fervently defended the religion of the Greeks, strongly adhering to their error. But after he saw the great holy martyr Theodore, the bishop of the same city, for Christ's
sake struggling and receiving the crown of victory, he was moved by the grace of Christ and received divine baptism. Having also persuaded the prefect to be baptized, he took him with him and sailed to Cyprus. And finding there that Christians were detained and being slaughtered for the sake of Christ, he joined himself with the martyrs, secretly giving himself up to the torturers without the prefect's knowledge. And being forced to sacrifice to idols, he could not be induced to do so in any way; nor was that all, he even kicked the altar and overturned it. Thus, the prefect having been driven to anger, his head was cut off.
EODEM MENSE. B 
Die vicesima secunda
The contest of the holy martyr Agathonicus and his companions.
Eutolmius the count, having been sent by the emperor Maximian from Nicomedia into the Pontic region to destroy the Christians, arrived at the emporium called Carpe. There, finding the holy Zoticus with his disciples confessing Christ, he slew them. Having returned from there to Nicomedia and having been informed that Princippus, by means of a certain Agathonicus, was turning the Greeks away from the worship of idols, he sent and seized both of them together with many other Christians; and he dragged them with him to the emperor who was staying in Thrace. But when he had arrived at a certain fortress called Potamus, he killed Zeno, Theoprepius, and Acindynus, as they were unable to continue the journey; and at Chalcedon he slew holy Severianus. As for Agathonicus, along with the rest of the fellow captives and Princippus, after they were cruelly beaten at Byzantium, he led them as far as Selymbria, where Maximian was staying; and there he cut off his head and those of his companions.
And the memory of Saint Anthusa, and the contest of Bishop Athanasius and his companions.
Christ the martyr Anthusa lived in the times of the emperor Valerian. She was born at Seleucia to wealthy parents, who were, however, worshippers of idols. She, however, inflamed with the desire for Christ, left her parents and her home; and taking with her Charisimus and Neophytus, her servants, pretending to depart for her nurse, she journeyed toward the city of Tarsus so that she might receive baptism. But the angel of the Lord, catching up the bishop of Tarsus, Athanasius, brought him to meet her on the way; and when there was no abundance of water there, the bishop prayed and drew water from the earth, and he baptized her and her servants. Returning to her mother afterward, and not being received, she embraced the monastic life: and having properly finished her struggle, she rested. The bishop Athanasius, however, being detained by Valerian together with Charisimus and Neophytus, and having been tortured severely beforehand, was then beheaded: and thus, having finished their martyrdom, they received the kingdom of heaven.
ON THE SAME DAY, THE TWENTY-THIRD OF THE MONTH OF AUGUST.
The contest of the holy martyrs, the priests Or and Orepse-
os. The blessed Irenaeus was a minister of Christ, together with the holy Or and the holy Orepseos, who while preaching Christ were seized by the idolaters. And standing before the governor, they were tortured in various ways; then they were cast into a fire. And suddenly, as rain poured down from above and the fire was extinguished, they emerged unharmed. After this, they were delivered to wild beasts to be devoured, but by the providence of God they were rescued even from them. Being suspended on a wooden frame, they were savagely torn; yet again, by the nod of Christ, they remained unharmed. Then the idol-worshippers, perceiving the unwavering resolve of their minds, and being driven all the more into a fury, rushed upon them with a single accord: one smote them with clubs, another crushed their teeth with stones, another pulled out their hair, while another pushed and trampled them with his heels. And at last, binding them with ropes and dragging them outside the city, they cut off their holy heads with a sword.
The contest of the holy martyr Silvanus and his companions.
B 
The holy martyrs of Christ, Silvanus, Sabinus, and Pantherius, were from the region of Thrace, in the time of the reign of Diocletian. Being Christians, they taught in the name of Christ. Wherefore, having been seized by the idolaters, they were delivered to the governor of the province. And being interrogated and having confessed Christ, they were first beaten severely. Thereafter, having been delivered into prison, they were afflicted there by hunger and thirst, pressing upon them. And after many days, being brought out of the prison, they were again compelled to deny Christ and to sacrifice to the idols; but not being persuaded, they were suspended and torn so much that their entrails were laid bare. And after that excruciating torture, receiving the sentence of the sword, they were led away bound to the slaughter: and when they arrived at the place of martyrdom, praying, they were beheaded. And having arrived [at the place of execution], they were led away as prisoners to be slain.
Memory of our holy Father Eustathius, Bishop of Antioch.
D 
Eustathius was a high priest of Christ during the reign of Constantine the Great, being Archbishop of Antioch. He was also present at the first Nicene Synod of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, being an advocate of the truth and an opponent of falsehood. Because he spoke the truth boldly, he became an enemy to the Arians. After the death of Constantine the Great, when his son Constantius, who adhered to the Arians, held the empire, Eusebius of Nicomedia, seeking the opportunity to depart and visit the temple that existed in Jerusalem, attained his wish; and having set out, he gathered together the Arian bishops. And bringing forward a woman carrying a child, [he arranged for her] to accuse him and to say that the infant was born to Eustathius,
when in fact it was not of Eustathius, but of some coppersmith.
And the memory of our holy Father Meletius, Archbishop of Antioch.
Meletius, that orthodox pastor of the Church of Christ, flourished in the times of the emperor Constantius. This Constantius, being an Arian, when he had respite from war, gathered a synod at Antioch to reject the Homousion and to substitute and proclaim the Heterousion. But since the Church of Antioch was widowed of a pastor, it was resolved first to appoint a bishop of Antioch, and then to discuss the faith. Now Meletius was at that time bishop of Sebaste, a learned man, but one who, because of the insubordination of his subjects, had abdicated his see and was living a quiet life. The heretics, therefore, thinking that he held the same views as they did, requested the emperor to appoint him as bishop of Antioch. But after he had been elected, and was asked to proclaim the truth, standing in their midst, he confirmed the Homousion and put the heretics to shame. He, in the reign of the great Theodosius, having traveled to Constantinople and installed Gregory the Theologian upon the throne, ended his life there.
And the memory of our holy Father Callinicus, Archbishop of Constantinople.
Our holy Father Callinicus was a presbyter of the Great Church. Because of his virtue, he was appointed patriarch of Constantinople by Justinian, the grandson of Heraclius, who, devising many tribulations for himself, once ordered the patriarch to offer up prayers for the destruction of the temple of the most blessed Mother of God. But he gave this answer, that there were no prayers for destroying, but only for building. Being compelled, however, by those who had been sent, to fulfill the emperor’s command, he only said: "Glory to Christ God, who endures such things." When the emperor, therefore, by reason of his perversity, was stripped of his empire, had his nose and tongue cut off, and was exiled to Cherson, and again by God’s permission had gathered strength from Bulgaria and regained the empire; the patriarch was seized by the soldiers and exiled to Rome. And having been shut up in a chamber walled in from the outside, he was brought to his end.
And the contest of the holy Hieromartyr Irenaeus, Bishop of Sirmium.
The holy martyr of Christ, Irenaeus, lived during the reign of Diocletian. Instructing those who came to him and training them in the truth of Christ, and preaching Christ openly, he was denounced by the idolaters to the prefect Probus; and having been arrested and bound in chains, he stood before him. And when he was questioned regarding his name, his station, his religion, his fatherland,
His manner of life being such, he left all things behind and confessed himself to be a servant of Jesus Christ. Having been severely beaten, he was delivered to prison, where he suffered greatly, for the prison guards had received orders not only to keep him secure, but not even to allow anyone to enter to attend to him or to bring him any necessary food. After many days, therefore, he was brought out of prison and again compelled to deny Christ and sacrifice to the idols, and as he was not persuaded, he was severely tortured; and after this, having received sentence by the sword, he was beheaded.
And the contest of the holy Hieromartyr Irenaeus.
This man lived during the reign of Marcus and Antoninus, an ancient man, who had been a successor of the holy apostles, and served as bishop in the city of Lugdunum, in the region of Gaul. And having written many books confirming the orthodox faith, he left them to the churches. From these, later generations, taking the occasions for the interpretation of the divine Scriptures, spread them throughout the whole world. Having thus become great in virtue and knowledge, after the contest for Christ and the end of the bishop Pothinus, he was appointed bishop of the aforementioned city. And having drawn many of the faithless by his words and teachings, and brought them to Christ as martyrs, at last he himself was also seized by the persecutors and, perfected by the sword, he departed to God, receiving the kingdom that was prepared for him.
OF THE SAME MONTH. The twenty-fourth day.
The contest of the holy martyr Tatianus.
Tatian, the martyr of Christ, was from the region of Gratia, and dwelling near Mantineum and teaching the faith in Christ to those among the faithless who came to him. Having been detected, he was seized by the Greeks, and bound in chains, and led to Claudiopolis, and delivered to the governor. And preaching the true faith, he was severely beaten and delivered to prison. After he had been sufficiently afflicted, he was brought out again and forced to deny Christ. And not being persuaded, he was beaten with great rods, and burned with heated irons. Then, tied with ropes, he was dragged through the middle of the city, being beaten and trampled underfoot. And when he reached the city gate, he signed himself with the sign of the precious cross, and hearing a voice from above announcing the good things prepared for him, he committed his spirit to God, and his precious relic was buried in that same city.
And the contest of the holy martyr Eutychius, disciple of the holy John the Theologian.
Eutychius, the martyr of Christ, was from Sebastopolis; but for the sake of his longing for Christ, he left behind both his country and his parents, and went to the holy John the Theologian, and became his disciple. And having imitated him in virtue, he was filled with the grace of God; and with divine zeal
of money, and not waging war on nations, but on Christians. Having been cajoled by the tyrant, therefore, and pressed by persuasive words to deny Christ, he did not yield, but was openly attacked, and beheaded, and thus reached his end. His relics were translated and deposited in the same place where those of the holy Hadrian and the other saints, and of the apostle Stachys, lie.
ON THE SAME MONTH.
The twenty-seventh day.
Memory of our holy Father Liberius.
Blessed Liberius, champion of the truth, was bishop of Rome under the emperor Constantius. Burning with zeal for the orthodox faith, he received the great Athanasius, who had been harassed by the heretics and expelled from the throne of Alexandria because he openly defended the truth. For as long as Constantine and Constans, the elder sons of the great Constantine, were alive, the orthodox faith was preserved; but when they died, and Constantius, the youngest son, who was an Arian, was left as master of affairs, the heretics prevailed. Therefore, Liberius, having greatly refuted and rebuked the impiety of the heretics, was exiled to Beroea in Thrace. But since the Romans were bound to him by faith and love, they approached the emperor and requested him; and for this reason he was sent back to Rome, and after he had rightly shepherded his flock, he passed away.
And memory of our holy Father Pœmen the anchorite.
Our holy Father Pœmen was from the region of Egypt: having abandoned the world, he withdrew with his own brothers to a monastery, and became a monk. Many years later, when their mother set out to visit them, she could not succeed: for they had closed the door against her. But while she persisted in groaning, Pœmen said to her, not looking at her: "What do you desire, O mother?" She replied: "I wish to see you." To whom Pœmen said: "In the other world we shall see one another." Hearing this, she departed. But he did not only do this thing worthy of remembrance, but also many other things. For the prefect of the region, having arrested the son of his sister on account of a crime committed, had decided to punish him with death: and having learned that he was the nephew of the holy man, he notified him, saying: "If you think it just, I will release him." To whom Pœmen replied thus: "Inquire diligently into his case: and if he is guilty of death, let him die; but if not, do as you wish." The prefect, admiring his mind, which was in no way subject to the passions, released him. The saint performed many other miracles, and rested in peace.
And memory of our holy Father Hosius, bishop of Corduba.
Hosius, bishop of Corduba, having renounced the world and embraced the monastic life, first excelled in the ascetic life: soon shining forth to all
in virtues and miracles, he was consecrated bishop of the city of Corduba by the archbishop of Rome. Having zeal for the orthodox faith, he was present at the great synod, refuting the madness of Arius and rejecting the heresy harmful to souls. But he himself even took care of convening the Council of Sardica, and held the first throne among the bishops who had gathered. Afterward, he was sent into exile by the Emperor Constantius, who was an Arian, along with many other bishops who clung tenaciously to the orthodox faith, and having suffered many dire things in that exile and endured many temptations, he departed rejoicing to God, for whom he had contended.
ON THE SAME MONTH
THE TWENTY-EIGHTH DAY [KH']
Memory of our holy Father Moses the Ethiopian.
This blessed man was an Ethiopian by birth, by color extremely black, a slave of a certain citizen, who had expelled him because of his perversity of character and habit of thievery. This man once bore a grudge against a certain shepherd who had been an obstacle to him in committing a crime, and he conceived in his mind to do away with him. But having been informed that he was beyond the Nile, which was overflowing with water, he gripped his sword in his mouth and, having placed his cloak over his head, he swam across. But the shepherd, having sensed his coming, fled and went off; he, however, slaughtered four choice rams and, binding them with a rope, he swam back across the Nile. And having eaten the meat and filled the skins with wine, he went back to his companions. I have recounted these things to show that it is possible for those who wish to be saved through repentance. But this man, finally having been pricked in the heart by a certain circumstance, gave himself up to a monastery. And he approached repentance in such a way that he also led his own accomplices to Christ. While he was sitting one time in his cell, certain robbers made an assault upon him, not knowing that it was Moses. The blessed man bound them with a rope as if they were a sack of chaff, loaded them onto his own shoulders, brought them to the church, and said to the brethren: "Since it is not permitted for me to harm anyone, and I found these men attacking me, what do you order concerning them?" They, having recognized that it was he, Moses, that famous and invincible bandit chieftain, confessed to God and they themselves renounced the world and became most excellent monks. Thus the holy elder, having lived a life pleasing to God and having overcome the demon of incontinence, died at the age of seventy-five, having also been made a presbyter and leaving seventy disciples after him.
ON THE SAME MONTH, THE 29TH DAY
The Beheading of the honorable head of the honorable, glorious prophet, Forerunner and Baptist John.
He who is testified to by Christ as being the greatest of all who are born of women, and more than the prophets...
who leaped in the womb, and proclaimed Christ to those on earth and in Hades, was the son of Zacharias the high priest and Elizabeth, born by the announcement of Gabriel. His venerable head was cut off by Herod because of the unlawful union with Herodias. He, having put on holiness from his mother's womb, having received purity, having embraced temperance, exercising himself in abstinence from food, removed from all human association, inhabited the desert as a city, living with wild beasts, clothed in camel's hair, and girded with a leather belt; and like the birds, he used food offered spontaneously by nature: he meditated assiduously upon the law of God, to whose observance and custody nothing was ever more precious to him. He transcended the very limits of nature; and he baptized the pure and immaculate Christ, who is beyond all nature.
Since therefore Herod, who was highly indulgent to lust, the tetrarch of the Judean region, had taken for himself in marriage the wife of his brother Philip, the prophet, aroused by divine zeal and armed with the weapons of truth, said to the tyrant: "It is not lawful for you to have the wife of your brother Philip." Hence came prisons and bonds for the saint, as the maddened woman drove her lover to this. Wherefore, while birthday feasts were being celebrated, and with sumptuous and voluptuous drinking bouts that devolved the host into a loss of mind, lo, a dancing-girl, the daughter of a harlot, and the reward, the slaughter of the prophet. Straightway, therefore, the head of the righteous one was brought upon a platter, and handed to the wanton and adulterous woman, still dripping blood, and uttering the same voice. These things were done in the city of Sebaste, which is at a distance of one day's journey from Jerusalem. And in the same place, where he who reigned after him, the Tetrarch, established royal houses, and where the banquet for the murder of the prophet was celebrated, there that prophetic and holy body, having been laid out by his own disciples, was hidden away. C
ON THE SAME MONTH.
Thirtieth Day.
Memory of the blessed wonderworker Fantinus.
He drew his origin from the region of the Calabrians, born to parents George and Bryena. Consecrated to God indeed from his very swaddling clothes, he is given over to a monastery; and having attained every virtue, and become a proved worker of the commandments of God, he is rendered worthy of divine revelations. And he remained fasting for twenty days. He even persevered naked for four years; struggling against innumerable calamities on account of the incursions of the Saracens. When he had continued in these things for sixty years, taking with him his disciples Vitalius and Nicephorus, he arrived at the Peloponnese: and having dwelt for a long time in Corinth, he gave many the opportunity for salvation; and seeking Athens, and having venerated the temple of the Mother of God, he repaired to Larissa; and having lingered for a long interval of time at the tomb of Saint Achillius, he set out for Thessalonica, delighted by the prodigies of the great martyr Demetrius: and for eight whole years he followed his accustomed
enjoying the wonders of the great martyr Demetrius, and for eight whole years pursuing his customary rule of temperance, he departed this life in a good old age.
ON THE SAME MONTH. THE THIRTY-FIRST DAY.
The Deposition of the Venerable Girdle of the Most Holy Theotokos.
Arcadius, son of the great Theodosius, having brought the venerable girdle of the most holy Theotokos from Jerusalem—where until that time it had been preserved together with her precious robe by a certain virgin—and having brought it to Constantinople, deposited it in an elegant reliquary, which he called the Holy Chest. Four hundred and ten years later, the Emperor Leo opened this holy chest on account of his wife Zoe, who was troubled by an impure spirit; she had been deemed worthy of a divine vision and admonished that if the venerable girdle were placed upon her, she would obtain recovery. Thus, the adorable girdle was found, looking as if it had been newly woven, shining, and marked with a golden seal, and an accompanying codicil indicating in detail the year, the indiction, and the day on which the holy girdle had been brought to Constantinople, and how it had been placed inside the reliquary by the hands of the Emperor and sealed by him. The Emperor embraced it, and by the hand of the patriarch of that time, it was spread over the Empress, delivering her from the sickness. And all, glorifying the Saviour Christ and rendering hymns of thanksgiving to His most pure Mother, deposited the holy girdle in the venerable chest in which it had been kept before.
BASILIUS JUNIOR PORPHYROGENITUS: NOVELLAE CONSTITUTIONES
